title: Guru Paramartha and His Five Disciples - Introduction
summary: In a quiet village in the fertile Tamil country, under the sprawling shade of ancient neem and tamarind trees, stood the modest ashram of Guru Paramartha. The venerable Guru was...
keywords: guru paramartha and his five disciples - introduction
full_text:
In a quiet village in the fertile Tamil country, under the sprawling shade of ancient neem and tamarind trees, stood the modest ashram of Guru Paramartha. The venerable Guru was a man of dignified demeanor, endowed with a flowing silver beard, a round and solemn belly, and an unshakeable conviction that he was the greatest philosopher, scholar, and spiritual preceptor since the dawn of creation. He spoke in slow, grand, Sanskritized phrases, frowned with immense gravity upon the simplest everyday matters, and believed that every trivial incident in life was governed by profound, occult principles of logic.

Yet nature, in her infinite sense of humor, had blessed this exalted teacher with five devoted disciples whose collective intelligence could scarcely match that of a single newborn sparrow. Their names were known far and wide throughout the district:

The first was Matti, the Blockhead, who took every metaphor, idiom, and proverb with absolute, literal seriousness. If the Guru told him to keep an eye on the door, Matti would take off his sandal, pluck out an imaginary eye, and glue his face to the wooden latch.

The second was Madayan, the Dunce, who possessed a boundless imagination and invented elaborate, scholarly explanations for things that needed no explanation at all, confusing cows with clouds and puddles with bottomless oceans.

The third was Peedan, the Clumsy Nuisance, whose fingers dropped every pot, whose feet tripped over every flat stone, and who invariably managed to douse himself with hot porridge or fall backward into mud whenever dignity was required.

The fourth was Asadan, the Ignoramus, who believed he was a master of grand debate, loudly arguing that the sun rose in the west whenever it suited his pride, and confusing his left hand with his right.

The fifth was Mudan, the Stubborn Idiot, who, once an absurd idea settled inside his skull, could not be moved by elephants, royal decrees, or the collapse of the heavens.

Surrounded by these five pillars of intellect, Guru Paramartha would sit on his woven grass mat on the ashram veranda, nodding with solemn satisfaction. 'Knowledge, my faithful children,' the Guru would proclaim in a resonant, nasal drone, 'is the supreme jewel of life. We are not like common worldly peasants who rely on base instinct; we are guided by profound philosophical logic!'

'Yes, Master!' the five disciples would chorused in unison, bowing their heads until their foreheads struck the floor with a hollow thud. 'Our Guru is the ocean of wisdom, and we are his thirsty fish!'

And thus commenced a long, celebrated cycle of misadventures, laughter, and comical disasters, wherein Guru Paramartha and his five disciples journeyed across roads, rivers, and towns, demonstrating to the laughing world that when pompous pedantry replaces practical common sense, folly reigns supreme.
moral: Pretentious pedantry without common sense turns even sacred learning into a spectacle of absurdity.

title: The Guru's Beard and Belly
summary: Guru Paramartha took extraordinary pride in two physical attributes: his magnificent, flowing silver beard, which reached down to his navel, and his round, dignified belly, whic...
full_text:
Guru Paramartha took extraordinary pride in two physical attributes: his magnificent, flowing silver beard, which reached down to his navel, and his round, dignified belly, which he regarded as the sacred storehouse of Vedic wisdom. Every morning after his prayers, the Guru sat upon a wooden stool while his five disciples performed their assigned duties of grooming.

Matti was entrusted with combing the beard with a broad sandalwood comb; Madayan stood by with a clay bowl of perfumed sesame oil; Peedan held a polished bronze mirror; Asadan fanned away flies with a palm leaf, and Mudan sat cross-legged on the floor, holding the Guru's feet to ensure he did not tip over.

One morning, while Matti was combing the silver hairs with scholarly concentration, his hand twitched and the comb caught upon a stubborn snarl. Matti tugged with earnest devotion; a single silver hair pulled loose, and the Guru let out a sharp squeal of agony: 'Ai-yo! Matti, you clumsy fool, you have uprooted a root of wisdom from my chin!'

Terrified by his master's cry, Matti fell to his knees: 'Forgive me, Master! The hair was rebellious and refused to obey the sacred comb!'

Guru Paramartha stroked his chin with immense gravity: 'A rebellious hair must be reasoned with, not yanked. But look upon my noble belly! Is it not expanding with spiritual fullness?'

Madayan leaned forward and peered at the Guru's belly with profound scientific interest: 'Revered Master, your belly is indeed expanding like the crescent moon approaching fullness. But according to my calculations, if it expands another two inches, your center of spiritual gravity will shift, and you will tilt forward and tumble onto your nose!'

Alarmed by this philosophical prognosis, the Guru questioned: 'What is the remedy, Madayan?'

'The remedy is simple, Master!' proclaimed Madayan. 'To balance the heavy belly in front, we must tie an equal counterweight of stones to your back! Thus will perfect equilibrium be restored between front and rear!'

Delighted by this scientific logic, the Guru ordered five heavy granite grinding stones fetched from the kitchen. Matti and Peedan bound the stones securely to the Guru's shoulders and back with thick coir ropes.

'Now stand up, Master, and test your divine equilibrium!' cheered Asadan.

The Guru attempted to rise. But the combined weight of his majestic belly and the heavy granite stones proved too much for his knees. He wobbled, tipped sideways, and crashed onto the floor like a felled coconut tree, knocking Peedan into the oil bowl and sending the bronze mirror flying across the room!

As the Guru groaned beneath the pile of stones and his disciples scrambled to untie him, the village washerman who had come to collect laundry peeked through the gate, shook his head, and laughed: 'A belly full of rice needs fasting, not rocks, O wise master!'

Rubbing his bruised ribs, the Guru solemnly proclaimed: 'The washerman speaks from worldly ignorance; our equilibrium was merely disturbed by an unseasonable draft!'
moral: Fussing over outer appearances and bodily dignity blinds a man to his own absurdities.

title: Counting the Disciples
summary: Having spent three days visiting a distant village fair to purchase provisions, Guru Paramartha and his five faithful disciples—Matti, Madayan, Peedan, Asadan, and Mudan—set out...
full_text:
Having spent three days visiting a distant village fair to purchase provisions, Guru Paramartha and his five faithful disciples—Matti, Madayan, Peedan, Asadan, and Mudan—set out on the dusty highway to return to their hermitage.

As they approached the outskirts of a dense, shadowy thorn forest, Matti suddenly halted and cried out in great alarm: 'Hold, brothers! We are entering a dangerous wilderness infested with brigands, ghosts, and wild boars! Before we proceed, we must count our numbers to ensure that none of us has been lost along the road!'

The Guru nodded with profound approval: 'Well spoken, Matti! Prudence is the crown of philosophy. Count our flock immediately!'

Matti stepped forward, puffed out his chest, and pointed his index finger at each companion: 'There is our revered Master, one! There is brother Madayan, two! There is brother Peedan, three! There is brother Asadan, four! And there is brother Mudan, five!'

Matti stopped, blinked his eyes, looked around, and shrieked in horror: 'Alas! We were six when we left the hermitage! Now there are only five! One of our brothers is missing! Swallowed by a demon or carried off by a tiger!'

Madayan pushed Matti aside: 'You always were a brainless blockhead, Matti! Step aside and let a scholar count!'

Madayan counted with great solemnity: 'Revered Guru, one; brother Matti, two; brother Peedan, three; brother Asadan, four; brother Mudan, five! Horror upon horror! Matti speaks the truth! There are only five of us! Our beloved brother is gone!'

Peedan counted and arrived at five; Asadan counted and arrived at five; Mudan counted and arrived at five! Finally, Guru Paramartha himself raised his ebony staff, pointed it at his disciples and counted: 'Matti, one; Madayan, two; Peedan, three; Asadan, four; Mudan, five! Merciful heavens! One of my precious disciples has vanished into thin air!'

Convinced that a tragedy had occurred, the six travelers sat down on the roadside dust, threw ashes upon their heads, beat their chests, and began to weep and wail with ear-splitting laments: 'Oh, our poor, lost brother! Which of us has perished? Who among us is dead?'

Presently, an honest village peasant passed by driving a pair of bullocks. Seeing six grown men weeping in the ditch, the peasant halted: 'What calamity has befallen you, holy men?'

The Guru sobbed: 'Good traveler, six of us set out this morning, but alas, cruel fate has stolen one away! Count us, and behold our grief—there are only five left!'

The peasant looked at the group: there stood the Guru and five disciples, six living souls in broad daylight. The peasant instantly understood that each fool had counted his companions, but had completely forgotten to count himself!

Smiling shrewdly, the peasant picked up a slender bamboo switch: 'Worry not, revered sages. I possess a magical stick of truth. Line up in a row, and as I strike each of you across your back with this wand, shout out your number loudly!'

The peasant brought the switch down across Matti's back: THWACK!
'ONE!' yelled Matti, rubbing his shoulders.
THWACK! across Madayan's back: 'TWO!' yelled Madayan.
THWACK! across Peedan: 'THREE!'
THWACK! across Asadan: 'FOUR!'
THWACK! across Mudan: 'FIVE!'
And finally, a respectful, gentle tap across the Guru's broad belly: 'SIX!' gasped the Guru.

The peasant laughed: 'Behold, holy masters! All six of you are present and accounted for!'

Overjoyed by the 'miraculous resurrection' of their missing brother, Guru Paramartha and his disciples fell at the peasant's feet, blessed his cattle, and presented him with a silver coin, marveling at the magical power of the peasant's bamboo stick!
moral: He who forgets to count himself while assessing others ends in foolish despair.

title: The Horse and the Donkey
summary: Observing that other revered spiritual masters rode upon majestic white horses with embroidered saddles when visiting wealthy patrons, Guru Paramartha decided that his own digni...
full_text:
Observing that other revered spiritual masters rode upon majestic white horses with embroidered saddles when visiting wealthy patrons, Guru Paramartha decided that his own dignity required an equine mount.

'A guru who walks on his own two feet like a common plowman,' proclaimed the Master, 'is held in light esteem. But a guru who rides a magnificent charger commands instant reverence! Go forth to the livestock fair, Matti and Madayan, and purchase for me a horse of unmatched pedigree and gentle temperament!'

The Guru handed them ten silver rupees from the ashram tin box.

Matti and Madayan hurried to the bustling town fair. Amidst the stalls of camels, goats, and cattle, they saw a cunning horse trader leading a scrawny, sway-backed, ancient gray donkey whose ears drooped like wilted plantain leaves and whose ribs looked like an upturned bamboo boat.

Matti approached the trader: 'Trader! We seek a horse for our illustrious Guru Paramartha. Does this beast belong to the noble equine race?'

The trader, recognizing the gullibility of his customers, bowed with profound reverence: 'Noble scholars! This is no common beast; this is a rare, imported Arabian steed of the royal dwarf variety! He does not grow tall because he devotes all his energy to spiritual contemplation! Notice his long, majestic ears—they are tuned to the celestial music of the spheres!'

Madayan examined the donkey's tail: 'And why does he hang his head so meekly?'

'Out of pure humility and respect for sacred philosophy!' declared the trader. 'I would not sell this celestial creature for fifty gold sovereigns, but out of devotion to your great Guru, I will surrender him for exactly ten silver rupees!'

Delighted by their extraordinary bargain, Matti and Madayan paid the ten rupees, draped a garland of marigolds around the donkey's neck, and led him triumphantly to the hermitage.

When Guru Paramartha beheld the beast, he was ecstatic: 'What a spiritual steed! Look how meekly he bows his ears! Fetch the saddle!'

The disciples threw an old wool rug across the donkey's bony back. Guru Paramartha, lifting his robes with stately grace, attempted to mount. Because of his heavy belly, it required Matti pushing from behind, Madayan pulling from the front, and Peedan lifting the Guru's left leg to hoist him into the saddle.

The instant the Guru's heavy weight settled upon the poor beast's spine, the ancient donkey groaned.

'Forward, celestial steed!' commanded the Guru, tapping the animal with his staff.

The donkey did not gallop; he did not trot. He simply lowered his head, dug his four hooves into the soft mud, and unleashed an ear-splitting, vibrating bray that rattled the tiles of the ashram roof: 'HEE-HAW! HEE-HAW! HEE-HAW!'

Startled by the demonic vibration, the Guru dropped his staff. The donkey kicked up his hind hooves with surprising vigor, pitched the Guru over his ears, and sent the great master tumbling headfirst into a large heap of cow manure beside the gate!

As the disciples rushed with buckets of water to wash their fragrant preceptor, Madayan observed philosophically: 'Revered Master, the Arabian steed was merely chanting his opening prayer of reverence! Your divine ears were unaccustomed to celestial chanting!'

Spitting straw from his mouth, the Guru nodded with immense gravity: 'You speak with wisdom, Madayan. Next time, we shall ensure our ears are plugged with cotton before we ride!'
moral: A fool who mistakes an ass for a noble steed pays the price of his own credulity.

title: The Bag of Lies
summary: One afternoon, while expounding the sacred moral treatises to his five disciples on the ashram veranda, Guru Paramartha spoke with fiery eloquence against the vice of untruthful...
full_text:
One afternoon, while expounding the sacred moral treatises to his five disciples on the ashram veranda, Guru Paramartha spoke with fiery eloquence against the vice of untruthfulness: 'Mark my words, children! A lie is not merely a spoken sound; it is a heavy, dark, tangible spiritual burden! He who tells lies accumulates a heavy sack of sins that weighs down his soul!'

Matti raised his hand, blinking with earnest literalism: 'Master, if a lie is a heavy, tangible burden, where does a liar keep his lies when he is not speaking them?'

The Guru stroked his beard, unwilling to confess that he was speaking in metaphors: 'Ahem! A confirmed liar, Matti, carries an invisible bag of lies slung across his shoulders! And when he meets honest folk, he opens his bag and scatters his deceit upon the ground!'

The five disciples gasped in awe at this revelation.

Two days later, while the Guru and his disciples were traveling through a busy market town, they passed a loud merchant who was selling brass pots, shouting: 'Come, noble patrons! These pots are forged of pure celestial gold from the Himalayas! Buy them for five coppers each!'

Hearing this blatant falsehood, Matti whispered to Madayan: 'Look! That man is scattering lies by the dozen! His invisible bag of lies must be overflowing!'

Madayan nodded with profound scientific agreement: 'We must capture his bag of lies and examine its philosophical contents!'

While the merchant was busy haggling with a customer, Matti and Madayan crept behind his stall. Seeing a large, bulging burlap sack sitting on the ground—which the merchant had filled with dried red chili peppers for his kitchen—Matti whispered: 'Here is his bag of lies! See how tightly it is tied with hemp cord!'

Snatching the heavy sack, the two disciples sprinted through the bazaar, running straight to the temple mandapam where Guru Paramartha was resting.

'Master! Master!' shouted Matti triumphantly, dropping the heavy sack at the Guru's feet. 'We have performed a magnificent philosophical service! We caught a merchant telling colossal falsehoods, and we stole his bag of lies!'

The Guru was astonished: 'You captured the bag of lies? Truly, your devotion to truth is commendable! Let us open the sack and inspect what falsehood looks like in its tangible form!'

Peedan brought an iron knife and severed the hemp cord. The Guru leaned forward with immense curiosity, sticking his face right into the mouth of the sack. Matti gave the burlap a vigorous shake to pour out the contents.

A dense, crimson cloud of fiery red chili powder billowed up directly into the Guru's eyes, nose, and open mouth!

The Guru sneezed like an erupting volcano: 'ACHOO! ACHOO! MY EYES! MY NOSE! I AM ON FIRE!'

The fiery chili powder filled the mandapam. The five disciples began coughing, sneezing, and weeping uncontrollably: 'ACHOO! ACHOO! HELP!'

Running to the temple water tank, the Guru plunged his head into the water, groaning in agony while the disciples doused themselves with cold water.

When the burning subsided, Guru Paramartha sat on the bank, his eyes red as ripe tomatoes, and proclaimed with solemn majesty: 'Behold the lesson of philosophy, my children! We have verified through practical science that lies are indeed bitter, stinging, and full of fiery torment! Never touch a liar's sack again!'

'Yes, Master!' chorused the disciples, wiping their streaming eyes in profound admiration of the Guru's wisdom.
moral: Literalism that attempts to package falsehood into a physical bundle becomes its own laughingstock.

title: Pretending to be Handicapped
summary: A severe festival season brought crowds of wealthy pilgrims to the regional temple town, and professional alms-seekers were collecting silver and gold by displaying various infi...
full_text:
A severe festival season brought crowds of wealthy pilgrims to the regional temple town, and professional alms-seekers were collecting silver and gold by displaying various infirmities: the lame were given bags of rice; the blind received copper coins, and the mute were gifted sweet rice puddings.

Observing this flourishing economy from a tea stall, Asadan whispered to Peedan: 'Look at the fortune those beggars are collecting! Our ashram treasury is empty; why should we labor in the garden when a simple display of infirmity can fill our pockets?'

Peedan hesitated: 'But brother, the revered Guru teaches that we must always be truthful!'

Asadan scoffed: 'This is not deceit; this is the philosophical enactment of suffering! I will pretend to be completely blind, and you will pretend to be deaf and mute! We will collect silver, purchase sweet jalebis, and present them to our Master!'

Peedan agreed, captivated by the thought of jalebis.

Asadan tied a dirty cloth tightly over his eyes, took a crooked stick, and began tapping the flagstones, crying in a mournful, nasal whine: 'Charity, noble pilgrims! Pity a poor, blind wanderer who has never seen the light of the sun!'

Beside him sat Peedan, rocking back and forth, pointing to his open mouth and making strange guttural noises: 'Aaah-ooh! Aaah-ooh!'

Charitable pilgrims tossed copper coins into their brass bowl. Within an hour, they had collected nearly two rupees.

Presently, a wealthy village landlord who was known for his sharp skepticism and short temper walked past. Hearing Asadan's wailing, the landlord paused, observing the two 'beggars' closely.

The landlord drew a shining silver rupee from his purse and held it out, saying softly: 'I have a whole silver rupee for the blind man, if he can tell me where my hand is!'

Asadan, eager for the silver rupee, peeked from beneath the loose edge of his blindfold, reached out his hand with perfect precision, and snatched the coin right from the landlord's palm!

'Aha!' shouted the landlord, his eyes blazing with fury. 'A blind man who spots a coin from three paces away! You are an imposter and a thief!'

The landlord raised his heavy walking staff to strike Asadan.

Seeing the stick descending, the 'deaf and mute' Peedan sprang to his feet, leaped two yards into the air, and shouted at the top of his lungs in crystal-clear speech: 'Run, Asadan, run! The landlord is going to beat your brains out!'

Hearing the deaf-mute shout with the voice of a temple bell, the gathered crowd of pilgrims gasped, then erupted in furious indignation: 'Swindlers! Rogues! They have mocked our charity!'

The angry crowd chased the two terrified disciples through the bazaar, pelting them with rotten papayas, mango skins, and old sandals. Bruised, battered, and covered in fruit pulp, Asadan and Peedan sprinted all the way back to the ashram and collapsed at Guru Paramartha's feet.

Hearing their breathless confession, the Guru stroked his beard and delivered a profound lecture: 'You failed, my children, because your philosophical enactment was incomplete! If you choose to be blind, you must blind yourself thoroughly; and if you choose to be mute, you must cut out your tongue! Half-measures in philosophy always end in rotten papayas!'

Rubbing their bruised ribs, the disciples vowed never to enter the profession of mendicancy again.
moral: Pretending infirmity to gain unearned charity brings real humiliation and pain.

title: The Sari - Krishna Gimme the Sari!
summary: During the sacred festival of Gokulashtami, the wandering drama troupe of a neighboring town enacted the famous episode of Krishna Leela upon an open-air wooden stage in the tem...
keywords: the sari - krishna gimme the sari!
full_text:
During the sacred festival of Gokulashtami, the wandering drama troupe of a neighboring town enacted the famous episode of Krishna Leela upon an open-air wooden stage in the temple square. Guru Paramartha and his five disciples sat in the front row, watching with wide, rapturous eyes.

The actors depicted the famous scene of the celestial cowherd playfully carrying away the colorful saris of the bathing maidens, climbing a kadamba tree, while the maidens pleaded from the water: 'O Krishna, give us back our saris!'

The performance moved the Guru's disciples to their very souls. As they walked back to their ashram under the starry sky, Mudan was so entranced by the drama that his mind became thoroughly unhinged.

'Did you behold the divine beauty of that scene, brothers?' sighed Mudan. 'The Lord perched upon the tree, and the colorful silk garments fluttering like rainbows! I feel the divine spirit of the cowherd stirring within my chest!'

Next morning, the local washerman had spread dozens of brightly colored, freshly washed, and ironed silk saris belonging to the village ladies upon the clean grassy bank of the river to dry in the warm sun. Crimson, emerald, saffron, and indigo silks gleamed across the meadows.

Mudan, walking down to the river to perform his ablutions, saw the sea of colored saris. The drama from the previous night ignited in his foolish brain.

'The hour of divine recreation has arrived!' shouted Mudan.

Gathering up twenty of the finest silk saris in his arms, the stubborn fool scrambled up a tall tamarind tree overlooking the river path. He draped the bright red, green, and golden saris across the boughs, sat cross-legged on a high branch, and began playing an imaginary flute on his fingers!

Presently, the village women arrived at the bank to collect their dry laundry. Finding the grass empty and looking up into the tree, they saw the Guru's disciple perched among the monkeys, draped in their silk garments!

'Hey, Mudan!' shouted the village elder's wife. 'What are you doing up there with our saris? Come down this instant and return our clothes!'

Mudan closed his eyes, swayed his head in divine ecstasy, and sang out in a high, squeaky falsetto: 'Pleaded with tears, fair maidens of Braja! Cry out: "O Krishna, give us our saris!" and perhaps the Lord will grant your prayers!'

The village women stared in disbelief, then exploded in fury. They did not recite devotional poetry; instead, they armed themselves with heavy wooden washing mallets, river stones, and wet clumps of clay!

'We will give you Krishna Leela, you impudent monkey!' shouted the women.

A barrage of stones, clay balls, and heavy mallets rained upon the tamarind tree. Mudan dodged and shrieked as a heavy mallet struck his shin and a wet clay ball hit him squarely in the ear.

Losing his balance, the 'celestial cowherd' tumbled out of the tree, falling into a dense patch of stinging nettles beneath the bank!

The angry women gave him a sound thrashing with their broom handles, retrieved their silks, and marched him in disgrace to Guru Paramartha's ashram.

The village elder's wife reprimanded the Guru: 'Control your mad disciple, O wise Master, before the village council drives you all out of the district!'

When the women departed, Guru Paramartha looked down upon the swollen, nettle-stung Mudan and delivered his judgment: 'Mudan, you were guilty of an unpardonable anachronism! The Kadamba tree of the sacred scripture was an evergreen, while you climbed a tamarind tree! The sacred Leela cannot be performed among tamarind pods!'

Applying soothing sandalwood paste to his stings, Mudan groaned in agreement, having learned that mythology and laundry banks do not mix.
moral: Religious zeal divorced from common sense and propriety leads to utter public embarrassment.

title: The Mango Tree and the Well
summary: In the back garden of the ashram grew a magnificent, ancient mango tree whose branches hung heavy with luscious, ripe, golden mangoes. The sweetest and largest fruits, however, ...
keywords: the mango tree and the well
full_text:
In the back garden of the ashram grew a magnificent, ancient mango tree whose branches hung heavy with luscious, ripe, golden mangoes. The sweetest and largest fruits, however, hung upon an overhanging bough situated directly above the gaping mouth of a deep, masonry-lined irrigation well.

Guru Paramartha, sitting on the veranda with his stomach rumbling, looked at the golden fruits and sighed: 'Ah! What heavenly ambrosia hangs from that branch! Matti, fetch me those three large mangoes over the well!'

Matti ran to the tree, but the branch was high and the well was deep. Returning to his master, Matti reported: 'Revered Master, my arms are too short, and if I shake the bough, the mangoes will fall straight down into the deep well and be lost in the water!'

Madayan stepped forward, tapping his forehead: 'Leave this engineering problem to a man of science! I have devised a flawless method: human chain logic!'

The Guru stroked his beard: 'Explain your philosophical chain, Madayan.'

'It is elementary, Master!' explained the Dunce. 'Matti will climb the tree and hold fast to the trunk. Peedan will hang from Matti's feet; Asadan will hang from Peedan's feet; Mudan will hang from Asadan's feet, and I, being the lightest and cleverest, will hang from Mudan's ankles! Thus suspended directly over the well mouth, I will pluck the three golden mangoes, pass them up the chain, and we will feast!'

The Guru nodded in profound admiration: 'A magnificent application of collective cohesion! Proceed immediately!'

The five disciples climbed the tree. Matti gripped the stout branch with all his might; Peedan grasped Matti's ankles; Asadan grabbed Peedan's feet; Mudan seized Asadan's ankles, and Madayan swung at the bottom, right above the dark, cold water of the well.

The human chain dangled in the breeze, creaking under the combined weight of five grown men.

'Can you reach the mangoes, Madayan?' called down the Guru from the garden wall.

'Just two inches more, Master!' shouted Madayan from below.

At that critical second, Matti, holding the entire chain from the top, felt an intolerable itch on the palms of his hands. The coarse bark was rough, and his fingers were slipping.

Calling down the line, Matti yelled: 'Brothers! My hands are slipping! Hold on tight to each other for one second while I let go to spit on my palms and get a better grip!'

'NO, MATTI, DON'T LET GO—' shrieked the other four disciples in chorus.

But before their warning was finished, the literal-minded Matti opened both his hands to spit on his palms!

In that single heartbeat, the entire human chain collapsed! Down tumbled Matti, Peedan, Asadan, Mudan, and Madayan, plunging headlong into the deep well with a colossal, geyser-like splash: 'KA-BLAAM!'

The icy water swallowed the five philosophers. Spluttering, choking, and thrashing, they clung to the mossy brickwork, screaming for their lives: 'HELP! MASTER! WE ARE DROWNING!'

Guru Paramartha peered over the stone rim in horror: 'Where are the mangoes?'

'Forget the mangoes, Master, throw down the rope!' wept Madayan.

It took the Guru and four neighboring farmers two hours with ropes and bullocks to haul the five dripping, shivering philosophers out of the well.

Sitting on the grass, wrapped in old blankets, Matti defended himself: 'I only wanted to secure a firmer grip, Master!'

The Guru sighed with philosophical resignation: 'Matti was merely obeying the laws of friction; it is the water that was unreasonably deep!'
moral: Do not attempt dangerous feats through inverted logic; gravity recognizes no philosophical theories.

title: The Thief and the Guru's House
summary: One moonless midnight, a professional housebreaker named Kalla entered the quiet village. Seeking easy plunder, he slipped over the garden wall of Guru Paramartha's ashram and c...
keywords: the thief and the guru's house
full_text:
One moonless midnight, a professional housebreaker named Kalla entered the quiet village. Seeking easy plunder, he slipped over the garden wall of Guru Paramartha's ashram and crept toward the open window of the central hall.

The ashram was quiet. The five disciples were snoring in a heap on the veranda, while Guru Paramartha lay awake upon his cot, suffering from a mild touch of indigestion brought on by eating unboiled lentils.

Hearing the soft scraping of the thief's iron jemmy against the wooden shutter, the Guru sat up and called out in a dignified, scholarly voice: 'Who knocks at the portal of philosophy at this unseasonable hour? Is it a seeker of divine truth, or a pilgrim with an offering of ghee?'

The thief, surprised by this gentle reception, realized he was dealing with the famous foolish Guru. Stepping boldly through the window, the thief whispered: 'I am a humble nocturnal seeker, Master! I have come to relieve you of your heavy worldly burdens!'

The Guru nodded with profound approval: 'Ah! You speak with allegorical wisdom, friend! The worldly possessions of this ashram are indeed a burden upon our spiritual contemplation. What burdens do you seek to remove?'

The thief pointed to the brass oil lamps, the silver prayer bells, and the heavy copper cooking cauldrons: 'Those heavy brass and copper vessels, Master! They produce terrible karmic weight!'

'Take them, honest seeker!' proclaimed the Guru. 'Take them, and let our souls be light!'

The thief stuffed the valuable vessels into his canvas sack. Looking around, his eyes fell upon a heavy wooden iron-bound chest in the corner, wherein the Guru stored his silver coins and festival robes.

The thief tried to lift the chest, but it was too heavy for one man: 'Master, this chest is exceptionally heavy with sin! I cannot carry it over the wall alone!'

Guru Paramartha immediately called out: 'Matti! Madayan! Peedan! Wake up, lazy boys! A noble seeker needs assistance in carrying away our worldly sins!'

The five disciples stumbled into the room, rubbing their sleepy eyes.

'What is our duty, Master?' asked Matti.

The Guru instructed: 'Help this honest brother lift this heavy chest upon his shoulders, and escort him politely to the garden gate!'

The five disciples eagerly lifted the heavy iron chest and hoisted it onto the thief's back. Asadan held the thief's torch; Peedan opened the gate, and Mudan bowed low, saying: 'Go in peace, brother, and do not stumble over the stones!'

The delighted thief bowed with a chuckle: 'May your wisdom spread through all the worlds, O Guru!' and vanished into the darkness with the ashram's entire fortune.

Next morning, the village headman arrived to pay respects. Finding the ashram bare of lamps, pots, and the treasure chest, the headman was appalled: 'Master, you have been robbed! Where are your valuables?'

Guru Paramartha smiled with serene, elevated detachment: 'We were not robbed, headman! A nocturnal philosopher visited us and relieved us of all our material entanglements! My disciples carried the chest to the gate with their own hands!'

The headman slapped his forehead in despair: 'You old fool, you gave your life savings to a common highway burglar!'

The Guru turned to his disciples and shook his head with pity: 'Observe, my children, how worldly men misunderstand the higher economics of spiritual liberation!'
moral: A pedantic host who reasons with a robber loses his goods and thanks the thief for his trouble.

title: The River Crossing
summary: Returning from an auspicious pilgrimage to a distant temple, Guru Paramartha and his five faithful disciples arrived at the sandy banks of the broad Palar river. The river was s...
full_text:
Returning from an auspicious pilgrimage to a distant temple, Guru Paramartha and his five faithful disciples arrived at the sandy banks of the broad Palar river. The river was shallow, its crystal-clear water flowing gently over smooth white pebbles, scarcely reaching a man's knees.

Yet as they prepared to wade across, Madayan suddenly seized the Guru's robes, his eyes wide with superstitious terror: 'Halt, revered Master! Do not touch the water! Do you not know that rivers are living, sentient beings, and that this river is currently wide awake and fiercely vigilant?'

The Guru stopped, stroking his beard: 'Is it awake, Madayan? How do we determine whether a river is awake or asleep?'

Madayan expounded his profound theory: 'When a river is awake, Master, its spirit watches for travelers to drag down and swallow! But when a river falls asleep, its spirit closes its eyes, its waters become docile, and travelers may step across without the slightest peril! We must test whether the river is sleeping!'

'How shall we test it?' asked Matti.

Madayan instructed: 'Fetch a blazing firebrand from that roadside campfire. Thrust the fiery brand into the water. If the river is awake, it will shriek and bite; but if it is asleep, it will remain silent!'

Peedan ran to the fire, seized a thick, blazing wooden branch, and ran to the water's edge. With all his might, he thrust the glowing, red-hot brand into the cool river!

The contact of fiery coal with cold water produced a sharp, violent hiss: 'TSSS-SH-SH-SH!' accompanied by a cloud of white steam.

Peedan dropped the brand, leaped three yards backward, and shrieked in horror: 'IT BIT! IT HISSED! THE RIVER IS AWAKE AND ROARING WITH FURY!'

The Guru and his disciples retreated into the shade of a banyan tree, trembling with fear. 'We must wait,' proclaimed the Guru solemnly, 'until the river falls into a deep, peaceful slumber!'

For six long hours under the blazing sun, the six philosophers sat upon the hot sand, watching the water. Whenever a wave lapped against the bank, Madayan whispered: 'Hush! It stirs in its bed! Do not disturb it!'

At noon, an old, weary donkey carrying two heavy bags of salt wandered down the bank. Being thirsty, the donkey stepped boldly into the river, waded into the middle of the current, drank its fill, and walked calmly to the opposite bank without the slightest difficulty.

Watching the donkey cross unharmed, Matti leaped up: 'Look, Master! Look! The river is asleep! The donkey crossed without waking it!'

The Guru nodded with immense gravity: 'The donkey, being a simple beast, crossed softly. But we are men of heavy scholarship! We must cross with extreme stealth, so that our footsteps do not awaken the sleeping monster!'

Guru Paramartha and his five disciples removed their sandals, tied their robes around their necks, and began crawling across the shallow river on their hands and knees, tiptoeing on all fours like stealthy cats, holding their breath in terrified silence!

Whenever water splashed against their chins, they glared at each other, hissing: 'Shhh! Do not wake the river!'

Halfway across, Peedan sneezed: 'ACHOO!'

The disciples shrieked in terror: 'IT WAKES! RUN FOR YOUR LIVES!'

Panicked, they scrambled through the shallows, splashing water in all directions, tumbling over each other, and dragged themselves onto the opposite bank, soaked, muddy, and exhausted, collapsing on the sand.

Turning around, the Guru looked back at the river and proclaimed in triumph: 'We have outsmarted the sleeping river through our supreme stealth! Let all future philosophers study our glorious crossing!'

The village washermen watching from the bank broke into thunderous laughter, while the disciples cheered their master's tactical genius.
moral: Do not invent imaginary perils out of foolish superstition; test the water before you declare the river asleep.

title: The Pot of Ghee
summary: A wealthy merchant whose son had recovered from a fever presented Guru Paramartha with a magnificent gift of gratitude: an enormous, glazed earthen jar filled to the brim with p...
full_text:
A wealthy merchant whose son had recovered from a fever presented Guru Paramartha with a magnificent gift of gratitude: an enormous, glazed earthen jar filled to the brim with pure, fragrant, golden cow's ghee.

The Guru was ecstatic: 'Ah! Pure cow's ghee, sweet as nectar! Matti, carry this precious vessel to our ashram kitchen, and guard it as if it were the nectar of immortality!'

Matti shouldered the heavy jar, but after walking a hundred paces, his arms began to tremble under the forty-pound weight. Setting the jar down on a stone, Matti called to Madayan: 'Brother, this jar is exceedingly heavy, and its bottom is round and unstable. If it slips from my shoulder, our master will have our heads! How shall we transport it safely?'

Madayan pondered with immense philosophical gravity: 'The fundamental law of fluid mechanics dictates that an unstable load must be suspended between two opposing forces! We must tie a strong bamboo pole across the neck of the jar. You will hold the front end on your shoulder, and Peedan will hold the rear end on his shoulder!'

The disciples tied the jar with coir rope to the middle of a long bamboo pole. Matti took the front end, and Peedan took the rear.

As they walked down the road, the swinging motion of the jar caused it to pendulum back and forth: swish, swish.

Peedan, who had shorter legs than Matti, complained: 'Matti! The jar is swinging toward me! Your longer legs are creating an unequal rhythm, and the ghee is sloshing!'

Madayan intervened with scholarly authority: 'To eliminate the pendulum oscillation, both carriers must march with absolute, mechanical synchronization! Whenever Matti takes a stride with his left foot, Peedan must take a stride with his left foot; and when Matti chants "HA!", Peedan must chant "HO!"'

The two disciples began marching: 'LEFT! RIGHT! HA! HO!'

Observing them from behind, Asadan noticed that the glazed jar was slipping slightly along the bamboo pole. He shouted: 'Halt! The jar is sliding toward Peedan's neck! Balance it with a counterweight!'

Mudan, without pausing to reflect, picked up a massive granite boulder weighing thirty pounds from the roadside and tied it to the opposite end of the pole to 'balance' the load!

The sudden, colossal weight bowed the bamboo pole like an archer's bow. The strained bamboo groaned, creaked, and snapped in two with a sound like a gunshot!

Down crashed the glazed earthen jar onto the hard stone road, shattering into a hundred fragments! Forty pounds of golden, aromatic cow's ghee poured across the dust, spreading in a greasy river down the ditch!

The four disciples stared in horror at the yellow puddle.

Peedan began to weep: 'The ghee is lost! The Master will beat us!'

Madayan knelt by the puddle, inspected the oil, and said with brilliant presence of mind: 'Do not despair, brothers! Ghee is oil, and oil rises above water! If we pour water into the ditch, the ghee will float to the surface, and we can scoop it into our mouths!'

They carried water from a nearby pond and dumped it into the ditch, turning the puddle into a thick, disgusting paste of mud, oil, and gravel!

When Guru Paramartha arrived and saw his precious ghee transformed into roadside sludge, he raised his staff in fury. But Madayan explained: 'Revered Master, we proved through practical experimentation that bamboo has an inherent karmic breaking point!'

The Guru lowered his staff, stroked his beard, and sighed: 'Truly, science demands its sacrifices; let us eat dry rice tonight in honor of physics!'
moral: Overcomplicating a simple task with elaborate theories leads straight to the destruction of the prize.

title: The Moon in the Well
summary: On the night of the bright full moon, the sky was a dome of deep indigo, cloudless and tranquil. Guru Paramartha and his disciples sat on the ashram veranda, enjoying the cool n...
full_text:
On the night of the bright full moon, the sky was a dome of deep indigo, cloudless and tranquil. Guru Paramartha and his disciples sat on the ashram veranda, enjoying the cool night breeze.

Feeling thirsty, Matti took a brass bucket and walked to the garden well to draw fresh water. As he leaned over the stone rim and looked down into the dark water, he froze in utter astonishment.

There, shining brightly at the bottom of the deep well, was the round, luminous, silver disc of the full moon, floating serenely upon the water!

Matti did not look up into the sky; he looked only into the well. 'HORROR! CALAMITY!' shrieked the blockhead, dropping his bucket and sprinting back to the veranda. 'Master! Master! The celestial Moon has fallen from the heavens and is drowning in our well!'

The Guru sprang up from his mat, his silver beard bristling with alarm: 'What do you say, Matti? The Moon God is drowning?'

The five disciples and the Guru rushed to the well and peered over the edge.

Sure enough, there lay the glowing silver moon, trembling slightly as ripples stirred the water.

Madayan nodded with grave, cosmic solemnity: 'The celestial orb has lost its heavenly moorings! If the Moon drowns, the universe will be plunged into eternal darkness, tides will cease, and our ashram will be blamed for cosmic homicide! We must rescue the Moon immediately!'

'How shall we fish him out?' asked the Guru.

Asadan suggested: 'We must use an iron hook! We will tie an iron anchor-hook to a strong rope, lower it into the well, snag the Moon by his rim, and haul him back into the sky!'

The disciples fetched a heavy, four-pronged iron grappling hook used for retrieving lost buckets. Tying it securely to a long hemp rope, they lowered it into the depths.

Down sank the heavy iron hook, churning the water and breaking the reflected moon into shimmering silver fragments.

'He struggles!' shouted Peedan. 'The Moon is resisting!'

The hook sank to the bottom and wedged itself firmly beneath a massive, immovable granite slab at the base of the well.

Matti pulled the rope; it did not budge. 'He is hooked!' cheered Matti. 'I have caught the Moon by his collar!'

Guru Paramartha took command: 'All five of you, seize the rope! Pull with all your spiritual might!'

The five disciples gripped the hemp rope in a line, digging their heels into the mud. 'ONE, TWO, THREE, PULL!' they chanted, straining their muscles until their veins bulged.

The heavy iron hook remained firmly wedged beneath the granite slab.

'Pull harder!' shouted the Guru, waving his staff. 'The fate of the cosmos rests upon your shoulders!'

The disciples gave a colossal, superhuman heave. Under the immense strain, the hemp rope snapped near the bottom with a loud crack: SNAP!

With the sudden release of tension, the five disciples tumbled backward in a heap, crashing into Guru Paramartha, sending all six philosophers rolling head-over-heels across the garden, landing in a tangled pile of arms, legs, and bruises!

Lying flat on his back in the grass, bruised and gasping for breath, Guru Paramartha happened to look straight up into the clear night sky.

There, soaring majestically above the coconut palms, was the glorious, shining full moon, completely untouched and radiant!

Pointing his staff toward the heavens, the triumphant Guru shouted with tears of joy: 'REJOICE, MY CHILDREN! REJOICE! Our mighty pull was not in vain! We snapped the rope, but the momentum hurled the Moon back into the sky where he belongs! Behold our handiwork!'

The five bruised disciples looked up, saw the moon in the sky, and broke into ecstatic cheers, dancing around their master, celebrating the night they rescued the universe from eternal darkness!
moral: Mistaking a reflection for reality leads fools to embark on rescue missions that end in bruised bones.

title: The Shadow and the Thief
summary: Following the burglary of their ashram, Guru Paramartha issued a strict decree that his disciples must maintain night vigils to protect their remaining property. Each disciple w...
full_text:
Following the burglary of their ashram, Guru Paramartha issued a strict decree that his disciples must maintain night vigils to protect their remaining property. Each disciple was assigned a two-hour watch on the veranda, armed with a heavy bamboo staff.

One moonlit midnight, it was Peedan's turn to stand sentry. The moon was high and bright, casting long, dark, distinct shadows across the whitewashed courtyard wall.

As Peedan marched back and forth, he suddenly noticed a tall, dark, sinister figure with a long staff mimicking his every movement along the wall! When Peedan stepped forward, the dark figure stepped forward; when Peedan raised his stick, the figure raised its stick; and when Peedan stopped, the intruder stopped!

Peedan's teeth began to chatter with terror: 'A thief! A giant demon thief has entered the courtyard and mocks my martial stance!'

Instead of raising an alarm, Peedan decided to reason with the intruder: 'Halt, shadow thief! Who are you, and what is your business in Guru Paramartha's ashram?'

The shadow, naturally, remained completely silent.

'Insolent scoundrel!' whispered Peedan. 'You refuse to answer? Take this!'

Peedan swung his heavy bamboo staff with all his might at the dark figure on the wall! The stout bamboo struck the solid brickwork of the courtyard wall with a bone-jarring crash. The staff splintered into pieces, and the violent rebound sent sharp vibrations through Peedan's wrists, nearly dislocating his thumbs!

Peedan dropped to his knees, clutching his bruised hands, whimpering in pain: 'The thief possesses armor of solid iron! He has broken my weapon without moving a muscle!'

Hearing the crash, Matti and Madayan rushed onto the veranda: 'What has happened, Peedan?'

'Behold the demon thief!' pointed Peedan, trembling. 'He stands against the wall, armed and silent! I struck him with my staff, and his body is hard as granite!'

Madayan examined the wall. As the three disciples moved together, three dark, joined shadows stretched across the whitewash.

Madayan gasped in horror: 'By the gods! He was alone a moment ago, and now he has summoned two ferocious accomplices! They are an army of darkness! We must perform a strategic retreat!'

The three sentries turned and fled into the Guru's bedchamber, diving beneath the Master's cot, trembling and shivering under the blankets.

When dawn broke and the sun rose, the shadows faded away. Guru Paramartha emerged onto the veranda and inspected the splintered staff and the empty courtyard.

Hearing the disciples' terrified account of the three granite-bodied demons, the Guru stroked his beard and delivered his verdict: 'The demons of the night, my children, were dissolved by the sacred power of our morning prayers! But to ensure they never return, we shall whitewash the entire courtyard with lime, for demons are notoriously allergic to fresh paint!'

And for three days, the disciples painted the walls, proud of their glorious victory over the phantom intruders.
moral: He who fights phantoms and fears his own shadow is defeated before the battle begins.

title: The Donkey and the Guru's Turban
summary: Guru Paramartha possessed a magnificent ceremonial turban made of fine crimson silk, embroidered with gold thread and adorned with a brass crescent, which he wore only when visi...
keywords: the donkey and the guru's turban
full_text:
Guru Paramartha possessed a magnificent ceremonial turban made of fine crimson silk, embroidered with gold thread and adorned with a brass crescent, which he wore only when visiting rajahs and wealthy temple patrons.

One scorching afternoon, the Guru set out on his ancient gray donkey to attend a ceremonial feast in an adjoining village. Because the heat was oppressive, the Guru removed his heavy silk turban, handed it to Matti, and commanded with solemn authority: 'Matti, walk behind the donkey and watch this turban carefully! If anything falls from this beast along the road, pick it up immediately and place it securely in your shoulder bag! Do not lose a single item that drops from this journey!'

Matti bowed with earnest devotion: 'Master, my eyes shall be glued to the donkey's path! Whatever falls to the earth, I shall faithfully collect!'

The procession moved slowly along the dusty country road: the Guru dozing upon the donkey, and Matti marching behind, watching the ground with hawk-like vigilance.

A mile down the road, as the donkey plodded along, the beast lifted its tail and dropped a fresh, steaming heap of round, green manure cakes upon the dust.

Matti stopped, remembered his master's strict command: 'Whatever falls from the beast, pick it up immediately!'

Without hesitation, Matti gathered up the steaming cow-like donkey manure in his hands and stuffed it into his cotton shoulder bag, right alongside the Guru's fine crimson silk turban!

A mile further on, the donkey stumbled over a stone. The jolt caused the Guru's spare leather sandals, which were tied loosely to the saddle, to slip off and drop into the dust.

True to his orders, Matti picked up the dusty sandals and crammed them into the bag, pressing them down upon the manure and the silk turban.

When they reached the host's magnificent mansion, where noble guests and musicians were assembled, Guru Paramartha dismounted with aristocratic dignity. Turning to Matti, the Guru said: 'Fetch my ceremonial turban, Matti, so that I may enter the banquet hall adorned with dignity!'

Matti opened his shoulder bag and pulled out the crimson turban.

To the Guru's utter horror, the once-glorious silk turban was completely flattened, smeared with fresh, green donkey dung, coated with road dust, and smelling like a stable!

The assembled guests recoiled, holding their noses in disgust!

The Guru turned purple with rage: 'Matti! You wretched idiot! What have you done to my magnificent turban?'

Matti looked bewildered and hurt: 'Master, I merely obeyed your sacred command! You strictly ordered: "Whatever falls from this beast, pick it up immediately and put it in your bag!" The manure fell first, so I picked it up; the sandals fell second, so I picked them up; and I stored them all safely with your turban!'

Guru Paramartha was so mortified that he could not attend the banquet. Marching home with his bare, sweaty head, the Guru issued a revised decree: 'Henceforth, Matti, you shall not pick up everything that falls! I will provide you with a written list of approved items that may be collected!'

Madayan nodded in agreement: 'Yes, Master! Administrative protocol requires an itemized inventory of allowable drops!'
moral: Blind and literal obedience without common sense makes a servant the destroyer of what he was sent to guard.

title: The Five Disciples and the Single Bed
summary: During the monsoon season, a torrential downpour flooded the ashram veranda where the five disciples usually slept on their straw mats. Seeking dry shelter, they carried their m...
keywords: the five disciples and the single bed
full_text:
During the monsoon season, a torrential downpour flooded the ashram veranda where the five disciples usually slept on their straw mats. Seeking dry shelter, they carried their mats into a small storage room that contained a single, antique, narrow wooden cot made of four creaky legs and woven coir ropes, designed to accommodate one modest sleeper.

Looking at the narrow cot, Matti said: 'Brothers, the floor is damp mud; we must all sleep upon this dry bed!'

Peedan objected: 'This bed is barely three feet wide and six feet long! How can five grown men sleep upon a single cot?'

Madayan stepped forward with an elaborate mathematical solution: 'The problem is purely geometrical! If five men lie parallel like sardines, they will fall off the edges. Therefore, we must apply the Principle of the Wheel! We will place our five heads together in the exact center of the mattress, forming the hub, and stretch our ten legs outward toward the four corners like spokes!'

The disciples attempted the Wheel arrangement. But because their legs dangled over the edges and their heads collided in the center, Mudan's nose was squashed against Peedan's chin, and Asadan's foot kicked Matti in the ribs.

'This wheel is suffocating!' groaned Mudan. 'My ear is crushed!'

Asadan proposed an alternative: 'Let us sleep in layers! Matti on the bottom; Peedan on Matti; Mudan on Peedan; Madayan on Mudan, and I will sleep gracefully on the top!'

They attempted the Layer arrangement. But the moment the heavy Mudan climbed upon Peedan, Matti at the bottom began gasping for air: 'HELP! I am being crushed like sugarcane in an iron press!'

Madayan then announced the final, perfect scientific solution: 'The Principle of Interlocking Transverse Geometry! We shall lie crosswise across the cot, with our shoulders on the frame and our legs bent like folded grasshoppers! But to ensure no one rolls off, we must tie ourselves together with a single long coir rope!'

The five fools lay across the narrow cot, squished together like bricks in a wall. Matti took a long, thick coir rope and wound it around all five bodies, binding their chests, waists, and knees in one massive, tight, inescapable bundle, knotting the ends securely!

'Now we are secure!' whispered Madayan in triumph. 'No one can fall off!'

They fell asleep.

Around two o'clock in the morning, a large, hairy centipede crawled up the leg of the cot and bit Peedan squarely upon his big toe!

Peedan shrieked in agony: 'AI-YO! A SCORPION HAS BITTEN ME! JUMP, BROTHERS, JUMP!'

Peedan thrashing frantically in the middle of the bundle caused all five bound men to heave simultaneously! The violent, collective lurch shifted the center of gravity beyond the edge of the narrow cot.

The antique wooden bed groaned, its four legs snapped with a splintering crash, and the entire tied bundle of five men tumbled off the cot, crashing heavily onto the mud floor!

Tied tightly together like a sack of potatoes, unable to separate their limbs, the five disciples rolled across the floor in a tangled heap, kicking and screaming in the dark: 'A MONSTER HAS US! UNTIE THE ROPE!'

Guru Paramartha rushed into the room with a lantern, expecting to find robbers, only to discover his five disciples trussed up like market chickens, groaning in the mud.

Cutting the ropes with a kitchen knife, the Guru sighed: 'True unity, my children, is a spiritual quality of the soul; when applied to furniture with ropes, it produces only broken timber!'
moral: Rigid mathematical formulas applied to human sleep result only in bruises and broken beds.

title: The Temple Bell
summary: The regional Shiva temple possessed an ancient, massive bell cast of seven sacred metals, hanging high in the stone gopuram tower. It produced a deep, resonant, melodious chime ...
full_text:
The regional Shiva temple possessed an ancient, massive bell cast of seven sacred metals, hanging high in the stone gopuram tower. It produced a deep, resonant, melodious chime that could be heard across seven villages.

Guru Paramartha and his disciples were visiting the temple during the annual festival. While the priests were conducting rituals inside the sanctum, Matti and Madayan wandered into the bell tower.

Looking up at the gleaming bronze bell, Matti was enchanted: 'Brother Madayan, look at that magnificent bell! If our ashram possessed such a bell, our Master could summon us to philosophy classes from three miles away!'

Madayan nodded with greedy ambition: 'Indeed! Our ashram needs a voice! But how can we carry away a bell that weighs three hundred pounds?'

Matti whispered: 'The rope is loose; if we untie it tonight, we can lower the bell into our cart and roll it away!'

'There is only one obstacle,' cautioned Madayan. 'The moment we touch the clapper, the bell will ring out with a deafening chime, and the temple guards will rush in and beat us to powder!'

Matti stroked his chin, pondering this acoustic dilemma. Suddenly, his face lit up with an extraordinary spark of 'genius':

'I have solved the acoustic problem, Madayan!' proclaimed the blockhead. 'Why does a bell ring? It rings because sound enters the ears of listeners! Therefore, if we plug our ears with thick wads of cotton, we will not hear the chime! And if we cannot hear the chime, the bell cannot be ringing! It is pure philosophy!'

Madayan was dazzled by this logic: 'Brilliant, Matti! Sound cannot exist if the ear is closed!'

That night, at midnight, Matti and Madayan crept into the temple tower. Each disciple took two large balls of raw cotton, soaked them in oil, and stuffed them so deeply and tightly into their ear canals that they could not hear their own breathing!

Believing they were rendered completely acoustically invisible, Matti took a heavy iron hammer and struck the bell's clapper with all his might to loosen the pivot!

'CLAAANG! DONGGGG! CLAAANG!'

The colossal, thunderous chime reverberated across the temple courtyards, rattling the windows of the town and waking three hundred sleeping citizens!

Because their ears were plugged with cotton, Matti and Madayan heard not a whisper. Matti smiled cheerfully at Madayan and struck the bell again: 'CLAAANG! CLAAANG!'

'It works, brother!' shouted Matti (though he could not hear his own voice). 'The bell is completely silent!'

Within two minutes, fifty angry temple guards, priests, and townsmen armed with lanterns, clubs, and ropes burst into the tower!

They surrounded the two thieves, waving their cudgels in furious shouts.

Seeing the shouting guards, Matti pointed to his ears with a triumphant grin: 'You cannot hear us, and we cannot hear you! The bell is silent!'

The guards did not argue about acoustics; they fell upon the two fools with their bamboo cudgels, giving them a thorough thrashing that bypassed their ears and registered directly upon their ribs!

Dragged before the village magistrate, the cotton was pulled from their ears. Guru Paramartha had to pay twenty silver rupees to ransom his acoustic philosophers from the town jail.

Returning to the ashram, the Guru gave a lecture on sound: 'Sound, my children, travels through the air to other ears, even when your own ears are stuffed with cotton! Next time, you must stuff cotton into the ears of the entire village before you strike the bell!'
moral: Closing your own ears does not silence the sound you make; self-deception hides nothing from the world.

title: The Egg and the Chicken
summary: A kind-hearted farmer presented Guru Paramartha with a fine, speckled country hen's egg, suggesting that the ashram might hatch it and raise a rooster to crow for morning prayers.
full_text:
A kind-hearted farmer presented Guru Paramartha with a fine, speckled country hen's egg, suggesting that the ashram might hatch it and raise a rooster to crow for morning prayers.

The Guru placed the egg in a cushioned basket of straw on the veranda and summoned his five disciples: 'Behold this vessel of potential life, my children! Within this shell slumbers a proud, crowing rooster! But a mother hen is lacking; therefore, you five must take turns sitting upon the egg to provide the necessary spiritual warmth for hatching!'

The disciples debated who should sit first.

Matti was chosen. But because Matti weighed one hundred and forty pounds, the moment he sat upon the straw basket, a sickening crunch echoed across the veranda! The egg shattered, and yellow yolk spattered over Matti's loincloth!

The Guru was heartbroken: 'Alas! The rooster was crushed before his comb could sprout!'

Madayan said: 'Master, grieve not! I will purchase a replacement egg from the market, and we will apply a scientific hatching method that requires no clumsy sitting!'

Madayan ran to the bazaar and purchased another speckled egg for two copper coins. Bringing it to the ashram, he revealed his invention: The Rapid Incubator!

'Why do hens take twenty-one long days to hatch an egg?' asked Madayan. 'Because their feathers provide only mild, sluggish warmth! If we provide intense, concentrated, philosophical heat, the chick will hatch within twenty-one minutes!'

Peedan brought a clay brazier filled with glowing red charcoal. Madayan placed a flat iron frying griddle over the coals, smeared it with sesame oil, and placed the fragile speckled egg directly upon the sizzling metal!

'Now watch the miracle of accelerated science!' beamed Madayan.

Within thirty seconds, the egg grew scorching hot. The air within the shell expanded rapidly; the shell browned, smoked, and suddenly—BANG!—exploded like a miniature cannon!

Hot, scalded egg white and sizzling shell fragments spattered across the room, striking Madayan in the cheek and Peedan in the nose!

The disciples shrieked, dancing around the smoke.

Looking at the charred, exploded yolk on the griddle, Guru Paramartha shook his head with profound sorrow: 'The chick possessed an impetuous, fiery temperament; he could not wait for his feathers to grow!'

The ashram cat slipped into the room, licked up the cooked egg fragments from the griddle with great satisfaction, and trotted away, purring contentedly.

The Guru concluded: 'At least the cat has achieved fulfillment; let us rely on the temple bell for morning prayers henceforth!'
moral: Trying to accelerate natural growth through artificial force destroys the life within.

title: The Beard Shaving
summary: Following the donkey ride into the cow manure, Guru Paramartha's magnificent silver beard had lost some of its pristine luster. Several hairs were singed by the exploding egg, a...
full_text:
Following the donkey ride into the cow manure, Guru Paramartha's magnificent silver beard had lost some of its pristine luster. Several hairs were singed by the exploding egg, and the Guru felt that a dignified trimming was urgently required.

The village barber, however, had raised his fee from two coppers to four coppers.

Guru Paramartha was indignant: 'Four copper coins for trimming twenty hairs? Outrageous extortion! Are we not self-sufficient philosophers? Matti, you shall be the ashram barber! Shave my neck and trim my beard with stately precision!'

Matti felt immensely honored: 'Master, my hand shall be as steady as Mount Meru!'

The disciples fetched an old, rusty sheep-shearing razor from the garden shed. Madayan mixed a bowl of cold well-water with laundry soap, producing a stiff, gray lather that smelled of sulfur.

The Guru sat upon the wooden stool, his chin elevated with dignified majesty. Matti lathered his master's face until the Guru looked like a snow-covered mountain.

Matti gripped the rusty razor with both hands, took a deep breath, and brought the blade down against the Guru's throat!

Because the razor was blunt and rusty, it did not slice the hairs; it caught them, pulled them, and scraped the tender skin like a rusty saw!

The Guru gasped, his eyes watering: 'Gently, Matti! You are skinning me like an onion!'

Matti apologized: 'Forgive me, Master! The lather is too thick; I cannot see where the beard ends and your chin begins!'

Peedan intervened: 'Allow me to illuminate the field of operation!'

Peedan lit a large oil torch and held it close to the Guru's face. But as Peedan leaned over to inspect the progress, his elbow bumped Matti's arm.

The sharp jolt caused Matti's hand to slip! The razor sliced off a large chunk of the Guru's left mustache, while the flame of Peedan's torch caught the soapy beard!

'PHUUUUFF!'

A flash of fire flared across the Guru's face! The dry beard burned with a terrifying crackle and a foul stench of singed hair!

The Guru leaped from his stool, screaming like a banshee: 'FIRE! MY BEARD IS BURNING!'

Mudan, reacting with swift presence of mind, grabbed the nearest bucket—which happened to be filled with dirty dye-water from the laundry basin—and hurled the entire contents squarely into Guru Paramartha's face!

The fire was extinguished, but the Guru stood dripping with purple dye, his magnificent silver beard burned to a charred, blackened stubble on the right, completely missing on the left, and his mustache vanished entirely!

The bronze mirror was brought. Looking upon his purple, charred, half-shaved countenance, Guru Paramartha stared in speechlessness for three full minutes.

Madayan nodded with profound artistic appreciation: 'A magnificent transformation, Master! You now possess the austere, terrifying countenance of an ancient Vedic warrior-sage!'

Wiping purple water from his eyebrows, Guru Paramartha croaked: 'Fetch me a shawl to cover my head, and pay the village barber five coppers to never speak of this day!'
moral: Entrusting a delicate blade to inexperienced hands invites bloodshed and comic disfigurement.

title: The Ghost in the Graveyard
summary: Traveling home late at night after attending a religious discourse in a neighboring town, Guru Paramartha and his five disciples had to pass beside the ancient village cremation...
full_text:
Traveling home late at night after attending a religious discourse in a neighboring town, Guru Paramartha and his five disciples had to pass beside the ancient village cremation ground, where banyan trees cast eerie shadows and white limestone memorial stones gleamed in the moonlight.

The disciples huddled close together, trembling at every rustle of dry leaves.

'Master,' whispered Asadan, his voice shaking, 'this burial ground is inhabited by bloodthirsty ghosts, or Pisachas, who hang upside-down from trees and devour unwary travelers!'

The Guru cleared his throat, trying to sound courageous: 'Fear not, children! A true philosopher is fortified by the sacred mantras of truth. No phantom can harm a man of pure intellect!'

At that moment, a sudden gust of wind whistled through the thorn bushes. Directly in the center of the cremation ground, standing atop a mound of earth, was a tall, white, ghostly figure with outstretched arms, swaying rhythmically in the breeze!

Matti fell to the earth: 'A GHOST! A WHITE DEMON WAITS FOR US!'

The disciples turned to flee, but the Guru held them back with his staff: 'Halt! If we run, the ghost will pursue us and strike us down from behind! We must confront the spirit with philosophical logic!'

'Who will address the phantom?' asked Madayan.

The Guru pushed Peedan forward: 'Peedan, you have the loudest voice; step forward three paces and demand his lineage and purpose!'

Peedan, his knees knocking together, took two trembling steps toward the swaying white figure. In a squeaky, terrified voice, he stammered: 'O... O noble spirit of the burial mound! Are you a ghost of the upper air or a demon of the netherworld? Speak, or our Guru will destroy you with Vedic fire!'

The white figure did not speak; it merely swayed its arms in the wind.

Madayan observed: 'He waves his arms! He is summoning his demonic legions from beneath the earth! We must attack him before his army arrives!'

Guru Paramartha commanded: 'Pick up stones, my valiant disciples! Pelt the demon with all your might!'

The five disciples and the Guru gathered heavy granite stones from the roadside. Standing in a line, they launched a furious bombardment: THROW! CLATTER! THWACK!

Dozens of stones flew through the air, striking the white figure. With a hollow crack, the demon collapsed to the ground, its white drapery fluttering in the dust.

'VICTORY!' shouted Matti. 'We have slain the ghost!'

Approaching cautiously with their sticks raised, the disciples poked the fallen monster.

To their astonishment, they found that the 'ghost' was nothing more than an old wooden scarecrow constructed of two crossed sticks, draped in a white cotton bedsheet by the cemetery watchman to frighten stray cattle away from the newly planted jasmine bushes!

Guru Paramartha poked the sheet with his staff and remarked with solemn satisfaction: 'Behold, my children! Even the inanimate scarecrow surrendered before our philosophical bombardment! Let us proceed with victory!'

And the disciples marched home, singing hymns of triumph over the vanquished phantom.
moral: Superstition turns harmless objects into terrifying ghosts; reason dispels the phantoms of the night.

title: The Measuring of the Field
summary: A wealthy landlord donated a strip of barren pasture land on the village boundary to Guru Paramartha's ashram, stipulating that the disciples might claim as much land as could b...
full_text:
A wealthy landlord donated a strip of barren pasture land on the village boundary to Guru Paramartha's ashram, stipulating that the disciples might claim as much land as could be measured by thirty lengths of a bamboo measuring rod.

The Guru was delighted: 'We shall cultivate lentils, sesame, and mustard! Matti, take the measuring rod and mark the boundary stones!'

Matti took a ten-cubit bamboo pole and marched to the field, accompanied by Madayan and Peedan.

Standing at the edge of the road, Matti placed the pole upon the ground: 'One!'

As he prepared to lift the pole for the second measurement, Madayan objected: 'Hold, Matti! How do you lift the pole? If you lift it through the air, you lose the continuity of land contact! The pole must be rolled end-over-end along the soil!'

Matti began rolling the pole end-over-end. But the ground was uneven, covered with thorny bushes and ant-hills. At the fifth roll, the pole rolled down a steep ditch and splashed into a muddy stream!

Peedan fished the pole out, covered in thick, slippery mud.

Matti complained: 'This bamboo pole is rigid and unyielding; it cannot bend around bushes or follow the curves of the boundary!'

Madayan proposed an ingenious substitute: 'We must use an elastic measuring standard that conforms to the natural contours of the earth! Fetch the long, cured leather strap from the donkey's harness!'

The disciples fetched the leather harness strap, which was four cubits long, made of supple, untreated rawhide.

Matti held one end, and Peedan held the other.

'Measure thirty lengths!' commanded Madayan.

Because it was raining, the wet rawhide strap began to stretch. Whenever Matti pulled, the leather stretched two feet; when Peedan pulled harder, it stretched another three feet!

Delighted by the expanding strap, Matti laughed: 'Look, brother! Every time we pull, our ashram gains more land! Pull with all your might!'

The two disciples pulled and strained, stretching the wet leather to twice its original length. By the twentieth measurement, they had stretched the strap across a neighbor's plowed field, over a brick wall, through a farmer's vegetable garden, and right into the village headman's private courtyard!

The headman, who was sitting on his porch eating his morning idlis, saw two muddy fools stretching a slimy leather strap across his veranda, knocking over his potted tulsi plants!

'What are you doing in my house, you idiots?' roared the headman.

Matti smiled proudly: 'We are measuring our ashram's thirty lengths, headman! This veranda now belongs to Guru Paramartha!'

The headman did not consult legal texts; he unhitched his bullock whip and chased the surveyors across three fields, giving them a memorable lesson in cadastral surveying.

Returning to the ashram out of breath, Matti reported: 'Master, we secured thirty lengths, but the headman's bullock whip was longer than our strap!'
moral: Using an elastic standard of measurement produces endless dispute and comic confusion.

title: The Cow and the Tiger Skin
summary: A traveling theatrical troupe had visited the village to perform scenes from the epics, and one of their costumes—a realistic, painted canvas tiger skin with a stuffed head, gla...
keywords: the cow and the tiger skin
full_text:
A traveling theatrical troupe had visited the village to perform scenes from the epics, and one of their costumes—a realistic, painted canvas tiger skin with a stuffed head, glass eyes, and a long striped tail—was discarded behind the temple wall after the performance.

The ashram cow, a gentle, placid white animal named Kamadhenu, was grazing peacefully near the temple. Feeling chilly in the evening breeze, the cow wandered into the discarded properties, tangled her horns in the straps of the tiger skin, and in her clumsy efforts to shake it off, managed to drape the striped canvas securely over her back, with the terrifying tiger head resting right between her horns!

Looking like a monstrous, horned, four-legged striped tiger-beast, the gentle cow ambled down the lane toward the ashram, chewing her cud and mooing softly: 'Moo-oo.'

Matti and Madayan were sweeping the ashram gate when they saw this terrifying apparition strolling down the road.

Matti dropped his broom, his jaw hitting his chest: 'A TIGER! A HORRID HORNED TIGER HAS COME TO EAT US!'

Madayan shrieked in cosmic horror: 'A mutant predator born of the conjunction of Saturn and Mars! He possesses the horns of a bull and the stripes of a tiger! Run for your lives!'

The two disciples sprinted into the ashram, slammed the heavy wooden doors shut, bolted the iron latches, and piled furniture against the entrance!

'What calamity threatens our sanctuary?' demanded Guru Paramartha, emerging from his study.

'A horned tiger is at the gates, Master!' gasped Matti. 'He has already devoured the village and now hungers for holy men!'

Outside, the poor cow, finding the gate locked, bumped her head against the wooden planks: THUD, THUD. She let out a long, plaintive moo: 'Mooooo-oo!'

The Guru frowned in deep contemplation: 'Did you hear that roar? It is an unnatural, deceptive sound designed to lure us into a false sense of domestic security! The beast roars with the voice of a cow to beguile our ears!'

Asadan suggested: 'We must neutralize the predator with defensive weapons! Bring the boiling pepper water!'

Peedan brought a large cauldron of boiling pepper water from the kitchen. Climbing to the flat terrace above the gate, Peedan peered over the parapet. Seeing the striped back of the beast below, he dumped the entire cauldron of hot pepper water over the wall!

The scalding, peppery water splashed over the canvas tiger skin.

The poor cow bellowed in pain and shock, kicked up her heels, shook off the soaked tiger skin, and galloped down the road toward the village pond, leaving the empty painted skin lying in the mud!

Looking down from the terrace, Peedan shouted in triumph: 'I have melted the tiger! The boiling pepper water was so powerful that it dissolved the flesh and bones of the beast on the spot, leaving only his empty skin!'

Guru Paramartha climbed to the terrace and marveled at the miracle: 'Truly, our ashram possesses formidable scientific defenses! We have dissolved a horned tiger into thin air!'

Next morning, the village cowherd brought the scorched, shivering cow back to the ashram, demanding ten rupees for veterinary medicine.

The Guru paid the fine with a heavy heart, recording in his philosophical diary: 'Note: Certain horned tigers possess the supernatural power of transforming into domestic cows after being doused with pepper water.'
moral: Mistaking a harmless creature in disguise for a deadly beast brings self-inflicted panic.
