title: The Sweet and the Bitter
summary: A wealthy merchant of the Chettiar community celebrated his daughter's wedding with unprecedented lavishness. As a mark of respect for the priestly class, he sent a brass platte...
full_text:
A wealthy merchant of the Chettiar community celebrated his daughter's wedding with unprecedented lavishness. As a mark of respect for the priestly class, he sent a brass platter to Guru Paramartha's ashram laden with thirty large, golden, aromatic laddoos, dripping with pure ghee, stuffed with cashews, and flavored with cardamom and saffron.

The Guru was overjoyed: 'Behold the reward of righteous living, my children! Thirty divine laddoos! Exactly five for each of us!'

Madayan, however, raised an ethical and medical objection: 'Master! A fundamental axiom of Ayurvedic medicine states: "Whatever tastes sweet upon the tongue produces bitter phlegm in the belly; while that which tastes bitter upon the tongue produces sweet health in the marrow!" Therefore, to eat sweet laddoos directly is to invite bitter destruction!'

The Guru was troubled: 'How shall we neutralize the sweetness, Madayan?'

Madayan expounded his brilliant solution: 'We must balance the sweet with the bitter! Before eating each laddoo, we must coat it thoroughly with a thick paste of crushed bitter neem leaves and raw gall-nut juice! Thus will the sweet and the bitter achieve philosophical equilibrium!'

Matti ran to the garden, stripped a basket of bitter neem leaves, pounded them into a dark green, foul-smelling paste, and rolled the delicious laddoos in the bitter slime until they looked like balls of swamp mud.

The Guru took the first green, bitter-coated laddoo, placed it in his mouth, and took a bite.

The horrifying bitterness of neem struck his tongue, followed by the cloying sweetness of sugar, creating a taste so vile, nauseating, and repulsive that the Guru's face twisted into an unrecognizable grimace of agony!

He choked, spat, and coughed: 'PHTHOO! PHTHOO! What demon's concoction is this?'

Matti, watching his master spit, said earnestly: 'Master, you must not spit out the medicine! Chew with fortitude!'

Peedan took a whole neem-coated laddoo and swallowed it in a single gulp to demonstrate his philosophical bravery. Within sixty seconds, Peedan's stomach rebelled: he turned pale green, clutched his belly, and began vomiting violently into the flowerbed!

One by one, the disciples who attempted to eat the balanced delicacies were seized with violent stomach cramps, groaning and clutching their bellies on the veranda.

The ashram dog trotted into the courtyard, sniffed the remaining green laddoos, sneezed in disgust, and walked away with his tail down.

Wiping his mouth with a towel, Guru Paramartha delivered his final verdict: 'Our philosophical equation was correct, but our stomachs are made of unphilosophical clay! Next time, we shall eat the sweet laddoos alone, and leave the bitter neem to the goats!'
moral: Consuming delicacies without restraint turns sweetness into bitter physical torment.

title: The Prayer and the Sneeze
summary: Guru Paramartha resolved to conduct an elaborate, auspicious Maha Yajna for peace and prosperity, requiring the recitation of one thousand sacred mantras without interruption.
full_text:
Guru Paramartha resolved to conduct an elaborate, auspicious Maha Yajna for peace and prosperity, requiring the recitation of one thousand sacred mantras without interruption.

Assembling his five disciples around the sacrificial fire pit, the Guru warned with immense solemnity: 'Mark well, children! This ritual requires unbroken spiritual concentration. According to the ancient science of omens, if any soul sneezes during the recitation of a mantra, the entire ritual is instantly contaminated and rendered void, and we must begin counting from number one all over again! Therefore, control your noses with iron discipline!'

The disciples sat cross-legged around the fire, pinching their nostrils between their fingers to guard against sneezing.

The Guru began chanting: 'Mantra one... Mantra two... Mantra three...'

The smoke from the sacred fire, fueled by dry cow dung and camphor, rose in dense, swirling clouds, filling the closed room with pungent, stinging haze.

By the forty-seventh mantra, Matti's nose began to tickle. His eyes watered; his nostrils flared, and his face contorted in desperate agony as he fought to suppress the tickle.

'Mantra forty-eight...' chanted the Guru.

Matti could bear it no longer: 'ACHOOOO!'

The sneeze exploded like a musket shot, blowing ashes across the sacrificial pit.

The Guru stopped, his eyes blazing with fury: 'Matti! You have defiled the ritual! We must start from the beginning!'

They cleared the ashes and began again: 'Mantra one... Mantra two... Mantra three...'

By the seventy-second mantra, Peedan's throat filled with acrid smoke. He pinched his nose, clamped his mouth shut, and held his breath until his cheeks turned purple. But nature was unyielding:

'ACHOO-O-O!'

The Guru threw down his ladle in despair: 'Polluted again! Back to number one!'

By late afternoon, after restarting the ritual nine consecutive times, the disciples were exhausted, their noses swollen red from pinching, and their throats raw from smoke.

Madayan stepped forward with a scientific remedy: 'Master! A sneeze occurs because air enters the nostrils! If we plug our noses with wooden clothes-pegs, sneezing will be physically impossible!'

The disciples fetched five wooden clothes-pegs and clamped them firmly onto their noses, speaking in hilarious, squeaky, nasal voices: 'How we are safe, Master!'

The Guru restarted the ritual for the tenth time.

At mantra eighty-five, Mudan felt an irresistible sneeze building up. Because his nose was clamped with the wooden peg, the tremendous pressure found no exit! His eyes bulged, his ears popped, and the explosive force blew the wooden peg straight off his nose like a missile!

The flying wooden peg flew across the pit and struck Guru Paramartha squarely between his eyebrows with a sharp crack!

The Guru dropped his prayer book, clutched his bruised forehead, and shouted: 'Cursed be the sneeze, and cursed be the pegs! The ritual is concluded; let prosperity find us by other means!'

The disciples removed their pegs, coughing and laughing with relief, having learned that nature cannot be contained by wooden clips.
moral: Allowing trivial superstitions to disrupt sacred focus turns devotion into an endless farce.

title: The Donkey's Wedding
summary: Following the advice of an itinerant astrologer who declared that an auspicious marriage brought prosperity to any household, Guru Paramartha conceived an extraordinary idea: th...
full_text:
Following the advice of an itinerant astrologer who declared that an auspicious marriage brought prosperity to any household, Guru Paramartha conceived an extraordinary idea: the ashram's ancient gray donkey, who had served them faithfully, must be wedded to a suitable bride with full Vedic ceremony!

'A bachelor donkey,' argued the Guru, 'is restless and melancholic. But a married donkey will settle down, bray with dignified restraint, and bring domestic harmony to our stables!'

The disciples embraced the project with wild enthusiasm.

Matti was dispatched to the neighboring village to find a suitable bride. He returned leading a remarkably stubborn, shaggy, brown female donkey belonging to a washerwoman, having rented the animal for two days for half a rupee.

The ashram was decorated with festoons of mango leaves and marigold garlands. Madayan prepared an ornate wedding invitation on palm leaf, which he delivered to the village headman and elders, inviting them to 'The Auspicious Nuptials of Sri Gardabha and Srimati Gardabhi.'

The village folk, anticipating immense entertainment, crowded into the ashram courtyard in their best festival attire.

The groom donkey was bathed, rubbed with turmeric paste, and decorated with red kumkum dots upon his ears. The bride donkey was draped in a yellow cotton sari, with jasmine flowers braided into her mane.

Guru Paramartha sat before the ceremonial fire, reciting marriage hymns with great solemnity.

'Bring forward the sacred Mangalsutra!' commanded the Guru.

Peedan brought a yellow cord carrying a brass medallion. The Guru instructed Matti: 'Tie the sacred cord around the bride's neck on behalf of the groom!'

As Matti approached the bride donkey with the cord, the unfamiliar smell of turmeric, the smoke of the fire, and the loud beating of festival drums terrified the animals.

The groom donkey, suddenly catching the scent of the strange female, lifted his head and unleashed a deafening, piercing bray: 'HEE-HAW! HEE-HAW!'

Startled by the bray, the bride donkey lashed out with both hind hooves with lightning speed! Her iron-hard hooves struck the ceremonial fire pit, scattering glowing embers and hot ashes across the spectators!

The crowd shrieked and scrambled for the gates.

The groom donkey, excited by the commotion, broke his tether, leaped over the fire pit, and chased the bride donkey around the courtyard, knocking over the milk vessels, smashing the brass trays, and trampling the Guru's prayer mats!

Guru Paramartha, attempting to restore order, waved his staff and shouted: 'Halt, bridegroom! Observe the sacred decorum of the ritual!'

The galloping groom donkey did not heed Vedic decorum: he crashed squarely into the Guru's round belly, carrying the venerable preceptor across the yard on his back before pitching him headlong into a thorn bush!

The two donkeys bolted through the open gate, galloping down the road together into the open fields, braying in matrimonial triumph.

As the villagers wept with uncontrollable laughter, the disciples pulled their scratched Guru from the thorn bush.

Madayan brushed twigs from the Guru's beard and observed philosophically: 'Revered Master, the marriage was a complete success! The bride and groom have departed on their honeymoon with extraordinary speed!'

Groaning, the Guru replied: 'Never perform a wedding for a beast who carries his own horn in his throat!'
moral: Projecting human customs onto beasts makes the organizers the laughingstock of the district.

title: The Water Pot with Hole
summary: The ashram's large earthenware water storage pot, which stood in the corner of the kitchen and held twenty gallons of drinking water, developed a tiny, pinhole leak near its bas...
full_text:
The ashram's large earthenware water storage pot, which stood in the corner of the kitchen and held twenty gallons of drinking water, developed a tiny, pinhole leak near its base, from which a steady trickle of water seeped onto the mud floor: drip, drip, drip.

Matti reported the leak to Guru Paramartha: 'Master, our water pot is weeping! If this continues, our kitchen will become a swamp!'

The Guru assembled his disciples to inspect the leak.

Madayan examined the tiny hole through a magnifying glass: 'This is not an ordinary fracture; it is a structural vortex! If we plug it from the outside, the internal hydraulic pressure will force the plug out! If we plug it from the inside, the water will dissolve the sealant!'

Peedan suggested: 'Let us hammer a wooden peg into the hole!'

Peedan fetched an iron hammer and a tapered wooden peg. Placing the peg against the pinhole, he gave it a mighty blow with the hammer: WHACK!

Instead of plugging the hole, the heavy blow cracked the delicate earthenware, enlarging the pinhole into a gaping fracture the size of a fist!

A torrent of water gushed out, soaking Peedan's legs and flooding the kitchen floor!

'Horror!' screamed Peedan. 'The vortex has expanded!'

Mudan, determined to stop the flood, took his own woolen shawl, rolled it into a ball, and shoved it into the fracture. The shawl absorbed the water, swelled, and wedged itself tight, temporarily stopping the gush.

'Victory!' cheered Mudan. 'The breach is sealed!'

Madayan, however, was dissatisfied with this crude solution: 'A wet woolen shawl is unhygienic; it will contaminate the drinking water with woolen fibers and sheep odor! We must apply an impenetrable, waterproof sealant: boiled tree resin mixed with hot pitch and charcoal!'

The disciples boiled a pot of black, bubbling, volatile tree resin on the hearth.

'Now pour the boiling pitch over the hole to seal the fracture forever!' commanded Madayan.

Matti poured the boiling, bubbling pitch directly onto the damp earthenware around the fracture.

The sudden, extreme thermal shock of boiling pitch against cold, wet earthenware was fatal: with a loud, sharp CRACK!, the entire twenty-gallon pot split in two from top to bottom!

The remaining fifteen gallons of water, mixed with boiling black pitch and mud, surged across the kitchen floor in a scalding tidal wave, carrying pots, ladles, and the Guru's wooden sandals out into the courtyard!

Guru Paramartha, who was standing at the kitchen threshold inspecting the operation, was caught in the wave, his feet swept from under him, landing on his back in the black, sticky puddle!

Sitting in the muddy pitch, his robes ruined and his beard speckled with black resin, the Guru looked up at his five dripping disciples.

An honest village potter passing the gate with a basket of new clay pots looked into the courtyard and chuckled: 'A new water pot costs exactly four copper coins, O wise masters!'

The Guru sighed with profound philosophical resignation: 'Go, Matti, give the potter four coppers, and remember: never attempt to cure a leak with boiling pitch when four coppers can purchase a whole new universe!'

The five disciples bowed in admiration, having learned that simplicity is often worth more than the most elaborate engineering.
moral: Do not attempt to patch a leak with complicated theories when a simple clay plug solves the problem.

title: The Pumpkin That Was a Horse's Egg
summary: Following the disastrous loss of the rented donkey, Guru Paramartha announced that renting mounts was beneath their spiritual status: 'A sage must breed his own noble charger fr...
full_text:
Following the disastrous loss of the rented donkey, Guru Paramartha announced that renting mounts was beneath their spiritual status: 'A sage must breed his own noble charger from the egg! Thus will the steed recognize our voices from birth!'

Matti was dispatched to the vegetable market to inquire where horse's eggs might be purchased.

At the market, a sly farmer was selling colossal, round, green ash-gourds and golden pumpkins. Seeing Matti looking around with bewildered curiosity, the farmer called out: 'Ho, scholar! Are you seeking rare treasures? Behold this magnificent, speckled, emerald-green egg laid by a royal Persian warhorse!'

The farmer pointed to a gigantic, forty-pound round green pumpkin resting on straw.

Matti's eyes widened in awe: 'Is it true? A horse's egg? How much does it cost?'

'Because you are disciples of the great Guru Paramartha,' whispered the rogue, 'I will part with this noble embryo for only five silver rupees! Take it home, wrap it in wool, and keep it warm for seven days; a winged royal colt will hatch forth!'

Matti paid the five rupees, lifted the heavy pumpkin onto his head, and staggered home in ecstasy.

Guru Paramartha was ecstatic when he beheld the green marvel: 'What a majestic egg! Notice its glossy rind and substantial weight! Matti, carry it with extreme reverence to the southern grove and let it rest on soft grass while we prepare the nursery!'

Matti carried the pumpkin toward the grove. But as he walked along a steep, rocky ridge overlooking a dense thicket of briars, his foot tripped over a tree root.

The heavy pumpkin slipped from his hands, tumbled over the edge of the cliff, bounced against three boulders, and shattered into twenty wet pieces upon the rocks below!

In that exact thicket below, a wild, long-eared hare had been sleeping peacefully. Startled by the sudden crash of the falling pumpkin, the frightened hare leaped out of the bushes and dashed across the meadow at blinding speed, its long ears flattened against its back!

Looking down from the cliff and seeing the frightened hare sprinting away from the broken pumpkin pieces, Matti shrieked in mingled wonder and despair:

'THE COLT HAS HATCHED! THE COLT HAS HATCHED! CATCH HIM, BROTHERS! HE IS RUNNING AWAY ON HIS HIND LEGS!'

The Guru, Madayan, Peedan, and Asadan came running to the cliff.

Seeing the brown creature bounding across the plain, Guru Paramartha waved his staff: 'RUN, DISCIPLES! CATCH THE ROYAL COLT BEFORE HE FORGETS OUR ASHRAM!'

The five disciples sprinted across the rocky plain, shouting: 'WHOA, COLT! WHOA, ARABIAN STEED!' But the swift hare vanished into the distant scrub in seconds.

Panting, exhausted, and covered in scratches, the disciples returned to their master, weeping over their lost horse.

Guru Paramartha comforted them with profound philosophical grace: 'Grieve not, children. You saw how swift the colt was—he ran forty leagues in three heartbeats! If he was so fast as an infant, think how terrifying he would have been when fully grown! We would have been thrown from his back into the clouds! It is a blessing that the wild beast escaped before our necks were broken!'

The disciples bowed in admiration of their master's foresight, and dined on pumpkin soup for a week.
moral: Greed to possess an impossible marvel makes a fool believe that vegetables lay steeds.

title: The Sleeping River and the Cold Charcoal Test
summary: Six months after their first crossing of the Palar river on their hands and knees, Guru Paramartha and his five disciples had to cross the river once again to attend a naming ce...
full_text:
Six months after their first crossing of the Palar river on their hands and knees, Guru Paramartha and his five disciples had to cross the river once again to attend a naming ceremony.

Remembering their past ordeal, Matti halted at the bank: 'Hold, brothers! We must verify whether the river is sleeping before we risk our lives!'

Madayan nodded with grave scientific authority: 'On our previous journey, we tested the water with a hot firebrand. But fire is an aggressive element that provokes the water to anger! Today, we must use a gentle, peaceful diagnostic instrument: cold charcoal!'

Peedan fetched a piece of black, extinguished wood charcoal from his bag.

'Now,' instructed Madayan, 'place the cold charcoal gently upon the surface of the water. If the river accepts the charcoal in silence without hissing, it is fast asleep; but if it creates ripples, it is plotting mischief!'

Peedan laid the light lump of charcoal upon the gentle current.

The piece of charcoal floated peacefully on the water, drifting downstream without a sound.

'VICTORY!' shouted Madayan. 'The river is in a deep, snoring coma! It did not utter a whisper! Step forward, Master, and cross in peace!'

Guru Paramartha, proud of his disciples' scientific rigor, hoisted his robes above his knees and stepped boldly into the water.

However, during the preceding week, heavy rains in the distant mountain catchment had deepened the river. What had once been knee-deep water was now an eight-foot swirling pool in the main channel!

As the Guru took his fourth stately stride, his feet slipped off the submerged sandbar! He plunged headlong into the deep current with a colossal splash!

'GLUB! GLUB! HELP! I AM DROWNING IN THE SLEEPING RIVER!' gurgled the venerable sage, thrashing his arms and swallowing mouthfuls of muddy water!

Standing on the bank, the five disciples stared in philosophical debate.

Madayan observed: 'Remarkable! The river appears to be having a violent nightmare in its sleep!'

Matti shouted: 'Do not wake it, Master, or it will bite!'

Fortunately, a group of village washermen who were beating clothes on granite slabs heard the commotion. Dropping their laundry, they plunged into the water, caught the sputtering Guru by his beard and waistband, and dragged him onto the sandbar, coughing up water and weeds.

The washerman chief laughed: 'The river was never asleep, old man, but your wits certainly were!'

Sitting on the sand, shivering and coughing, Guru Paramartha reprimanded his disciples: 'Madayan, your cold charcoal test was fundamentally flawed! Charcoal is black, which signifies dark deceit! Next time, we shall test the river with white chalk!'
moral: Repeated reliance on flawed tests deepens the pit of superstition.

title: The Stolen Butter and the Greased Whiskers
summary: A clay pot of freshly churned, sweet white butter had been placed on the kitchen shelf of the ashram, intended for the morning festival offering. When dawn broke, the earthen li...
full_text:
A clay pot of freshly churned, sweet white butter had been placed on the kitchen shelf of the ashram, intended for the morning festival offering. When dawn broke, the earthen lid was found knocked to the floor, and the pot was licked clean to the bottom.

Guru Paramartha was furious: 'A theft has been committed within the sacred precincts of philosophy! Summon the five disciples!'

The disciples lined up on the veranda, each swearing on his life that he had not touched the butter.

Madayan stepped forward to conduct the forensic investigation: 'Master, a thief cannot consume butter without leaving physical evidence! When butter is eaten in the dark, grease inevitably adheres to the lips and whiskers of the culprit! Therefore, we must inspect the whiskers of every resident of the ashram!'

The Guru, however, possessed a magnificent mustache, while Matti had a sparse beard, but Peedan and Asadan were clean-shaven!

'How can we inspect whiskers where no hair grows?' asked Peedan.

Madayan devised an ingenious diagnostic technique: 'The Whisker Replication Test! We will dip a tuft of sheep's wool into melted lamp oil and hold it before each man's mouth. If his breath smells of butter, the wool will curl!'

While Madayan was lecturing on wool curling, the ashram cat, who was the true culprit and had gorged herself on the butter at midnight, strolled past the veranda, purring contentedly, her white whiskers glistening with rich cream!

Matti pointed to the cat: 'Look, brother Madayan! The cat has butter on her whiskers!'

Madayan scoffed with scholarly disdain: 'Do not be absurd, Matti! A cat is an irrational feline quadriped lacking philosophical awareness; she cannot be held accountable under jurisprudence! The thief must be a rational being!'

Mudan, seeking to prove his absolute innocence, took a dollop of leftover rancid oil from the lamp and smeared it thickly over his own lips and chin: 'Look, Master! My face is completely clean of butter—I have only pure lamp oil on my lips!'

Seeing Mudan's shiny, greasy face, Madayan shouted in triumph: 'AHA! THE THIEF STANDS REVEALED BY HIS OWN GREASY SHINE!'

Mudan was seized by Matti and Peedan, tied to the veranda pillar, and sentenced to miss three meals of rice, while the fat ashram cat curled up on Guru Paramartha's lap, purring softly and licking the last traces of butter from her paws.

The Guru stroked the purring cat and sighed: 'Behold the innocent creature, my children; even beasts take comfort in the triumph of justice!'
moral: A foolish investigator who creates artificial evidence convicts the innocent and rewards the thief.

title: The Cow with Her Head in the Brass Pot
summary: The ashram cow, Kamadhenu, was a gentle beast with a chronic habit of sticking her nose into every bucket, basin, and basket left in the courtyard.
full_text:
The ashram cow, Kamadhenu, was a gentle beast with a chronic habit of sticking her nose into every bucket, basin, and basket left in the courtyard.

One morning, the kitchen maid left an ancient, narrow-necked brass pot containing a handful of salted rice flour on the courtyard steps. Smelling the flour, the cow thrust her muzzle deep into the brass vessel. She licked the bottom clean, but when she tried to pull her head out, her flared cheekbones and the curled base of her horns caught on the rolled rim of the brass neck!

Unable to withdraw her head, the poor cow stumbled blindly around the courtyard, shaking the heavy brass pot: CLANG, CLANG, CLANG! She mooed in muffled distress from inside the metal chamber: 'Mooo-oo!'

Matti ran out and shrieked: 'Master! A catastrophe! The brass pot has swallowed our cow's head!'

Guru Paramartha and his disciples gathered around the bumping, blinded animal.

'How shall we extract our cow?' asked the Guru. 'The pot is valuable; it was gifted by the royal jeweler!'

Madayan examined the situation with grave engineering logic: 'We are faced with an immovable perimeter and an irreplaceable asset! If we smash the brass pot with an iron hammer, the metal will split, and we will lose a vessel worth eight silver rupees! Therefore, the brass pot must be preserved at all costs!'

'Then how do we free the cow?' asked Peedan.

Madayan replied with calm, ruthless logic: 'We must separate the cow from the vessel by surgical detachment! Slice off the cow's head with a butcher's cleaver; then we can reach our hands into the neck of the pot, extract the head, and polish the brass vessel until it shines like new!'

The disciples nodded in admiration of this practical economy: 'Brilliant, Madayan! Save the eight-rupee pot!'

Matti was dispatched to fetch the heavy woodcutting axe to decapitate the cow.

Just as Matti raised the heavy axe to strike the poor cow's neck, a village blacksmith who was walking past the gate heard the commotion. Rushing into the courtyard, the blacksmith caught Matti's arm: 'Madmen! What are you doing?'

Madayan explained: 'We are saving our eight-rupee brass pot from this stubborn cow!'

The blacksmith pushed the fools aside. Taking a small iron chisel and a wooden mallet from his leather apron, he tapped the rolled lip of the brass pot at two points, widening the soft metal neck by half an inch. With a gentle twist, he slipped the pot off the cow's head, completely unharmed!

The cow blinked in the sunlight, shook her ears, and trotted to the shed, safe and whole.

Guru Paramartha looked at the freed cow, then at the intact brass pot, and delivered his verdict to the blacksmith: 'You have solved the problem, artisan, but your method was crude and unphilosophical! It lacked the dramatic elegance of surgical detachment!'

The blacksmith pocketed his chisel, shook his head in disbelief, and walked away laughing.
moral: Destroying a life to preserve a cheap vessel is the ultimate triumph of inverted reasoning.

title: The Lost Needle in the Haystack
summary: While mending his cotton prayer shawl in the dim, shadowed corner of the ashram storage room, Guru Paramartha accidentally dropped his long iron sewing needle into a massive, de...
full_text:
While mending his cotton prayer shawl in the dim, shadowed corner of the ashram storage room, Guru Paramartha accidentally dropped his long iron sewing needle into a massive, deep heap of dry hay and straw that had been stacked for the winter.

The tiny needle slipped between the straw stalks and vanished into the darkness.

The Guru called his disciples: 'Children! A precious needle, forged of fine iron, has slipped into this haystack! Find it immediately, for without it, our sacred vestments cannot be mended!'

The five disciples entered the dark storage room. They crawled through the hay, but the room was windowless and pitch-black; they pricked their fingers on straw, sneezed from dust, and found nothing.

Madayan stopped and declared: 'Brothers, this search is fundamentally irrational! How can any man find an iron needle in a pitch-dark room? It violates the epistemology of perception!'

'Where then shall we search?' asked Matti.

Madayan pointed through the door to the bright, sunlit courtyard outside: 'Look! The courtyard is bathed in glorious, brilliant sunlight! Not a shadow obscures the ground! We must search for the needle out in the bright courtyard, where the visibility is perfect!'

The disciples cheered: 'A magnificent deduction! Search where the light is bright!'

The five disciples immediately marched out of the dark storage room, knelt down in the middle of the blazing, sunny courtyard, and began sifting through the clean white sand, searching earnestly for the lost needle!

Guru Paramartha joined them, crawling on his hands and knees, peering through his spectacles at the dust.

For two full hours under the blazing noon sun, the six philosophers combed the clean sand of the courtyard.

A wandering tailor who was passing by paused at the gate, observing the holy men crawling in the dust: 'What are you searching for, revered masters?'

The Guru replied: 'We are searching for our precious iron sewing needle!'

The tailor asked: 'Where did you drop it?'

Matti pointed to the dark storage room across the yard: 'Over there, in the deep haystack inside the dark shed!'

The tailor stared in dumbfounded amusement: 'If you dropped the needle inside the dark shed, why on earth are you searching for it out here in the courtyard?'

Madayan replied with lofty, pitying condescension: 'Ignorant artisan! Can you not see that there is no light inside the dark shed, whereas out here in the courtyard the light is magnificent? Why search in darkness when light is abundantly provided?'

The tailor slapped his thigh in laughter: 'You may search in the sunlight until doomsday, O wise ones, but what was lost in the hay will not sprout from the sand!'

Taking a strong magnet from his sewing kit, the tailor walked into the dark shed, waved it through the hay, retrieved the needle with a click, and handed it to the astonished Guru.

The Guru marveled: 'Truly, the tailor's magic was impressive, but our method was undeniably brighter!'
moral: Searching for lost truth where the light is convenient rather than where it fell ensures failure.

title: The Salt Washed in the River
summary: Following the advice of the village physician, who recommended that the ashram store clean rock salt to purify the digestion, Guru Paramartha dispatched Matti and Peedan to the ...
full_text:
Following the advice of the village physician, who recommended that the ashram store clean rock salt to purify the digestion, Guru Paramartha dispatched Matti and Peedan to the salt pans on the coast to purchase two sacks of raw sea salt.

The disciples loaded two large burlap sacks of coarse, gray rock salt onto the back of their donkey and set out on the return journey.

As they crossed a dusty, unpaved cart track, a passing bullock cart kicked up clouds of fine, red road dust, coating the coarse burlap sacks and dusting the gray salt crystals with grime.

Matti was distressed: 'Peedan, look! The sacred salt of philosophy is covered in filthy road dust! How can we present dirty salt to our venerable Master?'

Peedan pondered the dilemma: 'When clothes are covered in dust, we wash them in the river with clean water! When vegetables are dusty, we rinse them in the stream! Therefore, to purify the salt, we must wash it thoroughly in running water!'

Matti embraced his brother in joy: 'Brilliant deduction! The river is just ahead!'

Reaching the banks of the river, the two disciples untied the burlap sacks. Carrying them to the water's edge, they dragged the sacks into the clear, flowing current.

'Dunk them deep!' commanded Peedan. 'Rinse out all the dust!'

They plunged both sacks into the flowing water, churning and swishing them back and forth with enthusiastic zeal: SWISH, SLOSH, SWISH!

As the fresh river water surged through the coarse burlap, the soluble salt crystals dissolved rapidly into the current. White, salty foam flowed away downstream, while the sacks grew lighter and lighter.

Matti smiled with delight: 'Look, Peedan! The dust was extraordinarily heavy, but the sacred washing is making our load miraculously light! See how easily I can lift this sack now!'

After fifteen minutes of vigorous washing, they hauled the two sacks out of the water and laid them on the grassy bank.

The sacks were completely limp, flat, and hollow.

Peedan opened the mouth of the first sack and peered inside: 'Matti! The dust is gone, but where is the salt?'

Matti reached inside: the sack contained nothing but clean river water and a handful of small, insoluble river pebbles!

'Horror!' screamed Matti. 'The river spirits have stolen our salt!'

Madayan, who arrived with the Guru to meet them, examined the empty wet sacks. Stroking his beard, Madayan expounded: 'The salt did not vanish; it transformed into its ethereal, aquatic avatar! It has sanctified the entire river! Drink the water, brothers, and taste our purified investment!'

They dipped their hands into the river: sure enough, the water tasted faintly salty!

Guru Paramartha nodded with profound satisfaction: 'We have not lost our salt; we have simply seasoned the river for twenty leagues! Our generosity to the fish is boundless!'
moral: Attempting to clean what dissolves in water washes away the entire treasure.

title: The Five Disciples and the Buffalo's Tail
summary: While walking through the marshy outskirts of the village, the five disciples encountered an enormous, black water buffalo wallowing peacefully in a cool mud pit. The beast belo...
full_text:
While walking through the marshy outskirts of the village, the five disciples encountered an enormous, black water buffalo wallowing peacefully in a cool mud pit. The beast belonged to a fierce dairy farmer, but had strayed into the reeds.

Matti, remembering that the ashram needed milk, proposed: 'Brothers, our cow yields only half a pail of milk daily. This majestic water buffalo possesses a colossal frame; if we lead her to our ashram, she will yield four buckets of rich milk every morning!'

Peedan objected: 'She has long, curved, pointed horns, and she is covered in wet mud! She has no halter; how shall we lead her?'

Madayan examined the anatomy of the animal: 'A quadruped is governed by its steering rudder! In a ship, the rudder is at the stern; therefore, in a buffalo, the steering organ is the tail! If we grip her tail firmly, we can steer her straight to the ashram gate!'

The five disciples agreed to this mechanical theory.

Matti crept quietly through the mud behind the wallowing beast. He reached down and seized the buffalo's thick, coarse, mud-encrusted tail with both hands!

Peedan grabbed Matti's waist; Asadan grabbed Peedan; Mudan grabbed Asadan, and Madayan gripped Mudan's shoulders, forming a human tug-of-war team anchored to the buffalo's tail!

'HEAVE!' shouted Madayan. 'Steer her forward!'

The five disciples gave a violent, coordinated pull upon the animal's tail.

The peaceful buffalo, suddenly experiencing five grown men violently wrenching her tail from behind, was seized with outrage!

With a snort of volcanic fury, the beast rose from the mud pit like a dark mountain. Lowering her head, she kicked backward with both her heavy hind hooves, sending a spray of foul swamp mud directly into Matti's face!

Then, with an enraged bellow, the buffalo galloped across the marsh at top speed!

'HOLD ON!' screamed Madayan from the rear. 'DO NOT SURRENDER THE RUDDER!'

The stubborn disciples refused to let go of the tail! Dragged by the galloping beast, they were pulled across the swamp like a string of fish! Through thorny briars, over muddy ridges, through stagnant ditches, and across cow pastures they bumped and slid, screaming in terror as the buffalo dragged them at thirty miles an hour!

Finally, the enraged beast plunged through a massive, thorny cactus hedge into the village pond!

The sharp cactus thorns peeled the disciples off the tail like peas from a pod, sending all five philosophers flying into the deep, green, slimy pond water!

The buffalo shook her tail, snorted triumphantly, and trotted off to her master's barn.

Guru Paramartha, arriving with his staff, saw five muddy, weed-covered heads bobbing in the green pond.

'Have you secured the dairy asset?' inquired the Master.

Spitting duckweed from his mouth, Matti replied: 'Master, the rudder operated with extraordinary power, but the vessel lacked navigational brakes!'
moral: Holding fast to an angry beast's tail is a sure path to muddy humiliation.

title: Catching the Sun in an Earthen Jar
summary: During the chilly winter season, the interior of the ashram study hall was damp, dark, and frigid, while the courtyard outside was bathed in warm, golden, glorious sunlight.
full_text:
During the chilly winter season, the interior of the ashram study hall was damp, dark, and frigid, while the courtyard outside was bathed in warm, golden, glorious sunlight.

Guru Paramartha sat shivering on his wooden cot, his teeth chattering: 'If only we could bring this delightful, warm sunlight inside our dark chamber, we could study the scriptures in comfort throughout the night!'

Madayan leaped up, his eyes sparkling with scientific ambition: 'Revered Master, your wish is the command of physics! Why should sunlight be wasted upon empty courtyards when it can be harvested and stored for domestic use?'

'How can sunlight be stored?' asked the Guru.

Madayan explained his Revolutionary Photonic Capture Technique: 'Sunlight consists of warm, golden celestial rays! If we take five large, clean earthenware storage jars, open their lids in the bright sun, let the jars fill to the brim with sunlight, and then slam the heavy wooden lids shut and seal them with clay, the sunlight will remain trapped inside! Tonight, when the room grows dark, we will unseal the jars, open the lids, and the stored sunlight will pour forth, illuminating the room with midday warmth!'

The Guru was dazzled by this brilliant innovation: 'Magnificent, Madayan! Fetch the jars immediately!'

The disciples brought five massive, sixty-gallon earthen grain jars into the middle of the blazing courtyard. They removed the lids, wiped the interiors with clean silk cloths, and let the jars sit in the scorching sun for four hours.

'Observe!' whispered Madayan, peering into a jar. 'The interior is warm and golden! The jars are full to the brim with sunlight! Slam the lids shut!'

With frantic haste, the disciples slammed the heavy wooden lids onto the five jars, plastered the rims with thick wet clay, and wrapped them in heavy blankets to prevent the 'light from leaking out.'

They carried the five heavy jars into the dark study hall and waited for nightfall.

At midnight, when the room was pitch-black and freezing cold, Guru Paramartha summoned his disciples: 'The hour has arrived! Unseal the photon jars and let the golden daylight flood our sanctuary!'

The disciples broke the clay seals and heaved the heavy lids off all five jars simultaneously!

They stepped back, waiting for the blinding flash of sunlight to illuminate the room.

The room remained in absolute, impenetrable, pitch-black darkness.

Matti reached his hand deep into a jar: 'Madayan, it is completely dark! I cannot see my own fingers!'

Madayan stuck his head into the jar, sniffed the interior, and declared with unshakeable confidence: 'The sunlight was trapped so tightly that it suffocated in the dark and turned into shadow! Next time, we must drill ventilation holes in the lids so the sunlight can breathe!'

The Guru nodded with profound understanding: 'Of course! Even celestial rays require oxygen; fetch the oil lamps!'
moral: Attempting to bottle the daylight only leaves you stumbling in the dark.

title: The Disciples Who Painted the Elephant Green
summary: The regional temple owned a magnificent, gentle royal tusker elephant named Airavata, who was revered by the entire province. During festival processions, the elephant was decor...
full_text:
The regional temple owned a magnificent, gentle royal tusker elephant named Airavata, who was revered by the entire province. During festival processions, the elephant was decorated with painted floral patterns on his forehead and trunk.

Guru Paramartha, observing the elephant grazing near the ashram, remarked: 'The elephant is a noble creature, but his natural color is a dull, depressing, muddy gray. How much more spiritually elevating he would appear if he were painted the auspicious, vibrant green of a fresh parrot's wing!'

Matti embraced the aesthetic challenge: 'Master, we have three large pots of green laundry dye in the shed! Let us sanctify the royal elephant with artistic beauty!'

While the elephant's mahout was asleep beneath a tree after eating a heavy meal of rice and buttermilk, the five disciples crept into the grove carrying three wooden buckets of thick, emerald-green dye and large whitewashing brushes made of coconut fiber.

Approaching the massive beast, Matti whispered: 'Gently, brothers! Begin with his legs, and work upward to his majestic belly!'

They began slapping the wet green dye onto the elephant's hide: SLAP, SLAP, SLOP!

Within fifteen minutes, they had painted the elephant's four legs, his broad flanks, and half his trunk bright emerald green! The beast looked like a colossal walking cabbage.

Presently, Peedan, attempting to paint the elephant's sensitive ears, accidentally poked the rough coconut brush into the elephant's left eye!

The startled beast trumpeted in pain and annoyance! He shook his great head, flapping his ears, spraying green dye across the five disciples!

Then, seeing the three open buckets of green dye sitting upon the grass, the intelligent elephant lowered his long trunk, sucked up two gallons of the thick green liquid into his trunk, and turned around to inspect his decorators.

'Look!' whispered Madayan. 'The elephant is deeply moved by our art; he is bowing his trunk in gratitude!'

Before the words were finished, the elephant unleashed a colossal, pressurized blast of green dye from his trunk, spraying the five disciples and Guru Paramartha (who had just arrived to inspect the work) from head to toe!

The six philosophers were completely coated in thick, sticky, indelible emerald green dye, looking like swamp goblins!

The awakened mahout rushed in, waving his iron ankus, and chased the six green philosophers through the village streets, while the villagers cheered and clapped at the walking green statues!

For two months, the dye refused to wash off, and Guru Paramartha conducted his philosophical lectures looking like an oversized lime, having learned that elephants prefer their natural gray.
moral: Painting nature with artificial colors earns only the beast's retaliatory splash.

title: The Astrologer's Broken Slate
summary: An arrogant, pompous astrologer named Kalanidhi arrived in the village, claiming that he could predict the exact hour of every mortal's birth, death, marriage, and financial rui...
full_text:
An arrogant, pompous astrologer named Kalanidhi arrived in the village, claiming that he could predict the exact hour of every mortal's birth, death, marriage, and financial ruin by calculating planetary transits upon his stone slate.

Guru Paramartha visited the astrologer's tent to discover whether his ashram was destined to receive royal patronage.

The astrologer cast the Guru's horoscope on his black slate, shook his head with grave arrogance, and sneered: 'Alas, venerable Guru! The planetary alignments reveal that your ashram is governed by Saturn and the Donkey! You are destined to remain impoverished, your disciples are born fools, and within seven days, your ashram will be burned to the ground!'

The disciples wept in terror, but Matti, suspicious of this dire prediction, whispered to Madayan: 'Does this man truly foresee the future with absolute certainty?'

'He claims his slate reveals every future event,' replied Madayan.

Matti picked up a heavy, sharp-edged granite stone from the roadside, concealed it in his palm, and approached the astrologer: 'Revered Pandit! You who see the future through the eyes of the stars, tell me: within the next ten seconds, will this stone in my hand fall upon your slate, or will it remain in my palm?'

The astrologer sneered: 'Foolish boy! The planetary motions reveal that the stone will remain peacefully in your palm!'

Before the astrologer finished speaking, Matti brought the heavy stone down squarely upon the astrologer's black slate: SMASH!

The slate shattered into fifty fragments, and the sharp rebound struck the astrologer's knuckles, sending him hopping across the tent, howling in pain: 'My slate! My hands! You rogue!'

Matti smiled politely: 'If your stars could not predict the fate of your own slate three seconds in advance, how can they foresee the fate of our ashram seven days hence?'

Guru Paramartha smiled with immense satisfaction, retrieved his consultation fee, and praised Matti: 'For once, Matti, your empirical demonstration was sharper than the stars!'

The humbled astrologer packed his broken fragments and fled the village before sundown.
moral: An astrologer who cannot foresee the stone falling on his own head cannot predict your tomorrow.

title: The Pot That Gave Birth to Little Cups
summary: An unscrupulous, greedy village moneylender named Dhanapala was notorious for extorting exorbitant interest from impoverished farmers.
full_text:
An unscrupulous, greedy village moneylender named Dhanapala was notorious for extorting exorbitant interest from impoverished farmers.

Guru Paramartha and his disciples visited the moneylender's shop to borrow a large, polished copper cauldron for a festival feast.

The moneylender lent the cauldron, charging an extortionate fee of two silver coins.

The feast concluded, and next morning, Matti returned the copper cauldron to the moneylender's shop. Alongside the large cauldron, Matti handed over two tiny, shiny, miniature copper cups!

The moneylender was surprised: 'What are these two small copper cups, Matti? I lent you only the large cauldron!'

Matti replied with wide-eyed innocence: 'Revered Dhanapala! While your large copper cauldron was in our ashram kitchen last night, a miraculous event occurred: the cauldron went into labor and gave birth to these two healthy baby copper cups! Because they were born of your pot, they belong to you by natural law!'

The greedy moneylender's eyes gleamed: 'The pot gave birth? Truly, a miracle!' Accepting the two free copper cups, he chuckled at the disciples' stupidity.

A week later, Guru Paramartha returned to the moneylender's shop and asked to borrow his largest, most valuable solid silver banquet platter, worth two hundred gold sovereigns.

Thinking: 'If the copper cauldron gave birth to two cups, this massive silver platter will surely give birth to a litter of silver saucers!' the greedy moneylender eagerly handed over his priceless silver tray.

A week passed; two weeks passed, and the silver platter was not returned.

Suspicious and anxious, the moneylender marched to the ashram: 'Guru Paramartha! Where is my magnificent silver banquet platter? Return it immediately!'

Guru Paramartha emerged from his room, wiping tears from his eyes with a black shawl. In a trembling, heartbroken voice, the Guru sighed: 'Alas, brother Dhanapala! Weep with us! A terrible domestic tragedy has struck our ashram!'

'What tragedy?' gasped the moneylender.

The Guru sobbed: 'Last night, your beloved silver platter was taken with a sudden, violent fever during childbirth... and alas! She passed away in the night, and we cremated her upon the ashram hearth!'

The moneylender turned purple with rage: 'Are you mad? How can a silver platter die and be cremated? Silver is metal; metal does not die! Return my property, or I will have you arrested!'

Guru Paramartha replied with serene, unyielding logic:
"If you could believe with a greedy heart that a copper cauldron could give birth,
Why do you doubt when a silver platter returns to the sacred earth?
What is born of metal must also perish, by natural and karmic law;
You accepted the birth of the little cups; now accept the death with awe!"

The moneylender was struck dumb by his own greed. The village council laughed him out of court, while the ashram used the silver for the village poor.
moral: He who believes in impossible births of metal must not complain when the mother pot dies.

title: The Tree That Stole the Guru's Slippers
summary: Guru Paramartha owned a pair of magnificent wooden padukas, or sandals, made of polished teakwood and inlaid with mother-of-pearl buttons.
full_text:
Guru Paramartha owned a pair of magnificent wooden padukas, or sandals, made of polished teakwood and inlaid with mother-of-pearl buttons.

While traveling along a deserted woodland trail on a hot afternoon, the Guru felt weary. Removing his precious wooden sandals, he placed them neatly at the roots of an ancient, sprawling tamarind tree, lay down upon the grass, and fell into a peaceful slumber.

His five disciples sat nearby, dozing in the shade.

While they were all asleep, a troop of mischievous wild monkeys swung through the branches. Seeing the shining mother-of-pearl buttons on the sandals, a large baboon hopped down, grabbed both sandals in his paws, and carried them high into the tree canopy, dropping them into a deep, hollow knot-hole sixty feet above the ground.

When Guru Paramartha awoke and reached for his sandals, the ground was empty!

'My sandals!' cried the Guru. 'Who has committed this theft?'

The disciples searched the ground, but no human footprints were visible.

Madayan examined the trunk of the tamarind tree: 'Master, look! There are no tracks of man or beast! The sandals were placed directly at the roots of this ancient tree! Therefore, the tree itself has swallowed your sandals!'

The Guru frowned with judicial severity: 'Trees possess life, but they must respect property! Summon the tree to court!'

Guru Paramartha sat upon a rock, holding court beneath the boughs: 'O Tamarind Tree! You are accused of grand larceny! Surrender my teakwood sandals this instant, or face the maximum penalty of the law!'

The tree, naturally, merely rustled its leaves in the wind.

'Contempt of court!' declared the Guru. 'Matti, administer fifty lashes of the cane to the accused!'

The five disciples took heavy bamboo switches and began beating the rough bark of the tamarind trunk with furious zeal: THWACK, CRACK, THWACK! 'Surrender the sandals, thief!'

As they battered the trunk, the violent vibrations shook the upper boughs.

Suddenly, a shower of hard, sour tamarind pods, dry twigs, and angry wild hornets rained down upon their heads!

The enraged hornets stung the Guru on his bald crown and attacked the disciples' noses and ears!

Shrieking in agony, the six philosophers fled down the road, pursued by the swarm.

Reaching the river, they plunged into the water to escape the stings.

Poking his swollen nose above the surface, Guru Paramartha declared: 'The criminal tree has resisted lawful arrest with armed accomplices; we shall place its name upon the municipal blacklist!'
moral: Holding an inanimate object accountable for a crime is the hallmark of pedantic folly.

title: The Thief Who Sold Back the Guru's Robe
summary: While the ashram laundry was hanging on the line behind the kitchen, a petty thief reached over the bamboo fence with a long hooked pole and stole Guru Paramartha's finest cerem...
full_text:
While the ashram laundry was hanging on the line behind the kitchen, a petty thief reached over the bamboo fence with a long hooked pole and stole Guru Paramartha's finest ceremonial yellow silk robe, trimmed with crimson borders.

The Guru was in despair: 'That robe was spun from Kanchipuram silk! Without it, I cannot preside over the upcoming full-moon assembly!'

Matti was sent to the town bazaar to search the second-hand clothing stalls.

Coincidentally, the thief had carried the stolen robe to that very bazaar and was displaying it upon a bamboo rack, shouting: 'Come, noble buyers! A celestial robe of pure silk, blessed by the Himalayan masters!'

Matti approached the stall, touched the fabric, and admired the crimson border: 'Trader! This robe is magnificent! It resembles our Guru's robe in every detail!'

The rogue trader smiled with silky flattery: 'Young scholar! This is no ordinary robe; this is an identical twin to the robe worn by the great Guru Paramartha! A king's daughter embroidered this silk! I would not sell it for twenty rupees, but for you, I will surrender it for eight silver coins!'

Matti's eyes shone: 'Eight rupees? What a miraculous coincidence! Our Master lost his robe, and here is an identical replacement!'

Matti ran back to the ashram, fetched eight silver rupees from the emergency box, paid the thief, and carried the robe home in triumph.

Guru Paramartha examined the robe, stroking the silk with tears of joy: 'Look, disciples! Look at the exquisite craftsmanship! It even possesses the exact ink stain on the right sleeve where I spilled my inkwell three days ago! What astonishing synchronicity!'

Madayan nodded with profound cosmic understanding: 'It is the law of celestial twins, Master! When an ink stain is born in our ashram, an identical ink stain manifests in the heavenly realm! We have purchased the cosmic archetype of your lost garment!'

The Guru wore the robe to the assembly, boasting to all the village elders that heaven had duplicated his wardrobe, while the thief sat at the local tavern drinking palm wine on the Guru's eight rupees.
moral: Purchasing back your own stolen goods at double price is the supreme achievement of the gullible.

title: The Iron Pole That Shrank in the Rain
summary: Guru Paramartha wished to erect an auspicious iron flagstaff in the center of the ashram courtyard to fly the temple banner.
full_text:
Guru Paramartha wished to erect an auspicious iron flagstaff in the center of the ashram courtyard to fly the temple banner.

He purchased a straight, solid iron rod measuring exactly twelve cubits in length from the village blacksmith. To verify its height, Matti stood beside it on a sunny morning, measuring it against the courtyard wall: it reached precisely to the third row of roof tiles.

That evening, a torrential monsoon downpour soaked the courtyard, turning the dry soil into deep, soft, soupy mud.

Next morning, after the rain ceased, the Guru ordered the iron pole erected. Matti pushed the heavy iron rod upright into the ground. Because the rod was heavy and the soil was soft mud, the lower four cubits of the iron pole sank deep into the mire!

Matti looked up at the top of the rod: instead of reaching the third row of roof tiles, it barely reached the windowsill!

Matti shrieked in horror: 'Master! Master! A catastrophe of metallurgy! The iron pole has shrunk in the rain!'

Guru Paramartha and his disciples rushed out to inspect the marvel.

Madayan measured the visible pole: 'It was twelve cubits yesterday; it is barely eight cubits today! The cold rainwater has caused the iron molecules to contract by four cubits!'

Peedan nodded in agreement: 'Everyone knows that cold water shrinks woolen shawls; naturally, it shrinks iron rods as well!'

'What is the remedy?' asked the Guru. 'We cannot fly a royal banner from a shrunken stump!'

Madayan proposed an engineering cure: 'We must expand the iron through heat! Fetch two boiling cauldrons of hot water and three bags of hot charcoal! If we pour boiling water over the pole and bake it with charcoal, it will expand back to its original twelve cubits!'

The disciples piled hot charcoal around the base of the pole and poured cauldrons of boiling water over the metal.

Because the water softened the mud even further, the heavy iron rod sank another two cubits deeper into the mire!

Now barely six cubits remained above ground!

Matti wailed: 'The heat was too intense! It shrank it even further!'

The village blacksmith, passing by, saw the six philosophers heating a half-buried pole in the mud. He laughed: 'Idiots! The pole has not shrunk; it has sunk into the mud! Pull it up!'

The blacksmith grabbed the pole and pulled it out of the ground: all twelve cubits emerged, coated in four cubits of thick wet mud!

Guru Paramartha stroked his beard and remarked with dignity: 'The blacksmith speaks from shallow observation; our experiment merely demonstrated that the earth was attempting to swallow our iron!'
moral: Ignoring the mud beneath your feet makes you blame the iron pole for shrinking.

title: The Cold Water Cure for the Fire
summary: While frying sweet banana fritters for the Guru's afternoon tea, Peedan knocked a ladle of hot coconut oil into the open hearth. A sheet of flame flared upward, catching the dry...
full_text:
While frying sweet banana fritters for the Guru's afternoon tea, Peedan knocked a ladle of hot coconut oil into the open hearth. A sheet of flame flared upward, catching the dry palmyra thatch of the kitchen roof!

Smoke billowed into the courtyard, and flames began to crackle along the rafters!

Peedan rushed into the study, shouting: 'FIRE! THE KITCHEN ROOF IS BURNING!'

Guru Paramartha sprang from his cot: 'Fetch water! Extinguish the conflagration immediately!'

Matti ran to the well and drew a large wooden bucket of fresh, crystal-clear water.

As Matti was about to throw the bucket onto the flames, Madayan seized his arms: 'HOLD, MATTI! Do not commit a fatal therapeutic blunder!'

Matti shouted: 'The roof is burning, Madayan! Why do you stop me?'

Madayan explained with intense academic urgency: 'What is the temperature of this water? It is icy cold from the deep well! If you throw freezing cold water onto hot, boiling flames, the extreme thermal contradiction will produce a catastrophic atmospheric explosion! Medical and philosophical treatises dictate that like cures like! The water must be heated to a lukewarm temperature so that it does not shock the fire!'

The disciples stopped. Matti agreed: 'True! We must not shock the fire!'

While the roof crackled and flames leaped higher into the sky, the disciples placed three buckets of water on an outdoor brazier to heat the water to 'lukewarm'!

Peedan kept dipping his finger into the buckets: 'Not yet, brother! It is still too cold! Wait five minutes more!'

Meanwhile, the fire devoured the palmyra rafters, leaped across the ridgepole, and burned the kitchen roof down to the bare brick walls!

Just as the last charred beam collapsed into the ashes with a cloud of sparks, Peedan cheered: 'The water is lukewarm! Throw it now!'

Matti threw the bucket of lukewarm water onto the smoldering pile of charred ruins, extinguishing a single dying ember!

Madayan beamed with satisfaction: 'Observe, Master! The lukewarm water extinguished the ember without the slightest thermal shock!'

Looking upon the smoldering, roofless kitchen, Guru Paramartha sighed: 'The scientific victory is complete, but we shall have to eat cold rice under the open sky for a month!'
moral: Debating the temperature of water while the roof burns reduces the house to ashes.

title: The Measuring of the Well with a Thread
summary: The village council was preparing to clean and deepen the public community well, and asked Guru Paramartha, as the most learned man in the district, to calculate the exact depth...
full_text:
The village council was preparing to clean and deepen the public community well, and asked Guru Paramartha, as the most learned man in the district, to calculate the exact depth of the water from the stone rim to the bottom.

The Guru accepted the civic honor with pride: 'A task worthy of our mathematical acumen! Madayan, fetch the measuring cord!'

Madayan brought a ball of thin cotton sewing thread.

Standing on the stone coping of the well, Matti tied a small brass button to the end of the thread and lowered it into the dark depths.

Down sank the thread until the button touched the water with a soft plop!

Matti marked the thread at the stone rim with a knot: 'The measurement is secured, Master!'

'Now,' said the Guru, 'we must translate this vertical thread into cubits of length so that we can report to the council.'

Madayan objected: 'How can you measure a wet thread in cubits? If you pull the thread out of the well, it will stretch, shrink, or tangle! The measurement must be conducted in situ!'

'How can we measure it in situ?' asked Peedan.

Madayan expounded his Brilliant Horizontal Projection Method: 'The depth of a well is simply the height of a cylinder turned upside down! Therefore, if we measure the circumference of the well rim on dry land, multiply it by the number of stones, and walk forty paces toward the east, the length of the thread will reveal itself on the ground!'

Matti pulled the thread up and laid it out across the dusty road leading to the village temple.

A passing herd of goats trampled across the thread, breaking it into five tangled pieces.

A stray village puppy grabbed one fragment and ran down the lane, while the wind blew another piece into a thorn bush.

Matti picked up the remaining two-inch piece of thread and measured it against his thumb: 'Master, according to my calculation, the well is exactly two inches deep!'

The Guru was astonished: 'Two inches deep? But yesterday, the cowherd said his bull fell into the well and sank fifteen feet!'

Madayan replied with philosophical certainty: 'The cowherd was deceived by optical refraction! Science has proved that the well is two inches deep; if a bull sank, it was because the bull was unusually heavy!'

The Guru presented the official report to the village council: 'Honorable elders, your well is two inches deep; three buckets of dirt will fill it to the brim!'

The village council stared at the report, burst into roaring laughter, and hired a professional well-digger, having learned that Guru Paramartha's measurements were best taken with a grain of salt.
moral: Measuring depth horizontally on dry land leaves you no wiser about the water below.

title: The Disciples Who Guarded the Wooden Gate
summary: Guru Paramartha was invited to attend a grand spiritual symposium in the provincial capital. Before departing, he called his most trusted disciple, Matti, and gave him strict, s...
full_text:
Guru Paramartha was invited to attend a grand spiritual symposium in the provincial capital. Before departing, he called his most trusted disciple, Matti, and gave him strict, sacred instructions:

'Matti, I leave the ashram in your sole care. Our most valuable possession is the ancient, hand-carved teakwood gate at the entrance of our courtyard, carved by master artisans of Tanjore! Watch this gate with your very life! Do not leave it for a single second! Guard the gate above all things!'

Matti bowed to the ground: 'Master, my eyes shall never leave the gate!'

The Guru departed.

On the second night, a traveling fair set up booths in the adjoining village, featuring shadow puppets, fireworks, and free distribution of sweet jalebis.

Hearing the music and drums in the distance, Matti's heart burned with longing to see the puppets and taste the sweets. But he remembered his master's strict command: 'Do not leave the gate for a single second!'

Matti sat before the gate, agonizing over the dilemma.

Suddenly, a stroke of brilliant literalism struck his simple brain: 'The Master commanded me never to leave the gate! But he did not forbid me to take the gate with me!'

Taking a heavy iron crowbar from the shed, Matti pried the two heavy teakwood gate leaves off their iron hinges!

Hoisting one heavy wooden door onto his left shoulder and the other onto his right, Matti marched down the road toward the carnival, carrying the ashram gate with him!

At the carnival, crowds stared in amazement as a young man marched past the sweet stalls carrying two colossal, carved wooden doors upon his shoulders, enjoying the puppet show while resting his chin upon the timber!

Meanwhile, back at the ashram, two opportunistic thieves passed by. Seeing the entrance wide open with neither gate nor sentry, they walked inside, ransacked the rooms at their leisure, loaded three bullock carts with brass vessels, carpets, grain sacks, and the Guru's books, and drove away into the night!

When Guru Paramartha returned next morning, he found his ashram stripped bare to the walls, empty of furniture, pots, and food!

As the Guru wept in despair, Matti marched cheerfully through the archway, carrying the two carved teakwood doors upon his shoulders:

'Master! Rejoice! I obeyed your sacred command to the letter! I never left the gate for a single second! Behold your precious gate, safe and sound!'

Guru Paramartha looked at the two doors, then at the empty, plundered house, and collapsed onto the ground in speechless despair.

Madayan consoled the Guru: 'Master, the thieves took only perishable worldly goods, but Matti has preserved the sacred entrance! While the entrance remains, another house can always be built behind it!'
moral: Guarding the gate while the house is carried away is the crown of literal obedience.

title: The Shadow That Bit the Disciple's Heel
summary: Walking along a sandy country road under the late afternoon sun, the shadows of Guru Paramartha and his disciples stretched long and dark behind them.
full_text:
Walking along a sandy country road under the late afternoon sun, the shadows of Guru Paramartha and his disciples stretched long and dark behind them.

Asadan happened to look down at his feet. Because the low sun was behind him, his own long, dark shadow stretched across the sand, and whenever he raised his heel, the shadow's heel followed him with absolute precision.

Asadan halted, his eyes wide with suspicion: 'Brothers! A dark, thin demon is pursuing my footsteps! Whenever I step forward, he snaps at my heels!'

Peedan examined the shadow: 'Look! He has long legs and a flat head! He is a subterranean parasite seeking to swallow your footprints!'

Asadan took a stride; the shadow followed.

'He bites!' shrieked Asadan, feeling an imaginary sting on his heel. 'He has bitten my Achilles tendon!'

Madayan stepped forward with a combat strategy: 'The demon is attached to your feet! If you run, he runs with you! Therefore, you must ambush him with a crushing frontal assault!'

Asadan raised his heavy bamboo staff and struck backward with all his might at the dark shape on the sand: THWACK!

He struck his own shin!

Asadan screamed in agony, hopping on one foot: 'AI-YO! The demon struck back with an iron rod!'

Mudan, determined to rescue his brother, took a heavy iron hoe and shouted: 'I will sever the demon's neck!'

Mudan brought the iron hoe down upon the shadow right beside Asadan's foot!

The sharp iron blade missed the shadow (which remained perfectly flat) and sliced clean through Asadan's leather sandal, cutting his big toe!

Blood spurted onto the sand, and Asadan collapsed, howling in genuine pain!

Seeing the blood, Madayan shouted in triumph: 'Look! The demon bleeds! We have wounded him mortally!'

Guru Paramartha arrived and inspected the wounded toe: 'Asadan, you have fought a valiant duel with your own projection! But look into the sky: the sun is setting behind the hills!'

As the sun dipped beneath the horizon, the long shadow dissolved into the twilight.

'VICTORY!' cheered the disciples. 'The demon has dissolved!'

Bandaging his bleeding toe, Asadan was carried home on a litter, proud of having survived a mortal duel with his own shadow.
moral: Fearing an illusion leads a man to harm his own flesh to destroy a phantom.

title: The Stolen Mustard Seeds and the Ants
summary: A wealthy patron presented Guru Paramartha with a small cloth bag containing five hundred tiny, golden mustard seeds of an exceptionally rare, aromatic Himalayan variety, used f...
full_text:
A wealthy patron presented Guru Paramartha with a small cloth bag containing five hundred tiny, golden mustard seeds of an exceptionally rare, aromatic Himalayan variety, used for temple offerings.

While Matti was carrying the bag to the altar, the bottom seam unravelled, and thirty tiny mustard seeds spilled onto the mud floor of the ashram veranda, scattering among the dust.

Matti was in despair: 'Master! Thirty sacred mustard seeds have fallen into the dust! If we sweep them with a broom, they will be crushed; if we leave them, the ashram mice will eat them!'

The Guru stroked his beard: 'Every seed is sacred! Recover all thirty seeds without losing one!'

The disciples knelt on the floor, attempting to pick up the tiny seeds with their fingers. But their fingers were large and clumsy, and the tiny seeds slipped into the fine cracks between the floorboards.

Madayan devised an extraordinary biological retrieval plan: 'The Ant Labor Cooperative!'

'Explain your plan, Madayan,' said the Guru.

Madayan expounded: 'Ants are professional gatherers of seeds! Their mandibles are microscopically precise! If we invite a colony of red ants onto the floor, they will gather all thirty mustard seeds and carry them to their anthill! Then we can simply dig up the anthill and collect our seeds!'

Matti ran to the garden, broke off a branch from a mango tree covered with thousands of vicious, stinging red tree-ants, and shook the branch over the veranda floor!

Thousands of furious, stinging red ants rained down upon the floorboards!

Instead of gathering the mustard seeds, the enraged ants swarmed over the bare feet, ankles, and legs of Guru Paramartha and his disciples!

Within seconds, hundreds of fiery, agonizing stings bit into the holy men's flesh!

The Guru shrieked, hopping like a madman: 'AI-YO! THE WORKERS ARE ON STRIKE! THEY ARE EATING MY ANKLES!'

The disciples danced around the veranda, slapping their legs and howling in pain: 'FIRE! FIRE ON OUR LEGS!'

Running to the garden well, they poured buckets of cold water over their legs to wash away the stinging ants.

Sitting on the grass, covered in painful, burning red welts, Guru Paramartha looked at his swollen feet.

The thirty tiny mustard seeds remained peacefully in the cracks of the floorboards, completely ignored.

The Guru sighed with profound resignation: 'The ant labor force was uncooperative; let the floorboards keep the mustard seeds as rent!'
moral: Fretting over microscopic losses wastes the hours needed to secure the harvest.

title: The Great Debate with the Village Barber
summary: Guru Paramartha was immensely proud of his debating skills, believing that no scholar in South India could withstand his formidable Sanskrit syllogisms.
full_text:
Guru Paramartha was immensely proud of his debating skills, believing that no scholar in South India could withstand his formidable Sanskrit syllogisms.

One afternoon, sitting under the village banyan tree where the village elders gathered, the Guru fell into an argument with the sharp-witted village barber, a shrewd, uneducated man named Kandasamy.

The Guru declared: 'Kandasamy, you understand only the hair on men's chins, while I understand the metaphysical essence of the cosmos! Name any proposition, and I will prove its opposite through irresistible philosophical logic!'

The barber smiled, stroking his razor: 'Very well, revered Master! Let us have a formal debate before the village elders! Here is my proposition: "A razor is an instrument used to shave beards, and hair grows upon human skin!" Can you disprove that?'

The village elders crowded around to watch the contest.

Guru Paramartha rose, cleared his throat with immense gravity, and unleashed his grand dialectic:

'Hearken, O elders! The barber's proposition is founded upon vulgar optical delusion! According to the sacred doctrine of Non-Duality, hair does not truly exist; it is merely an illusion produced by the interaction of air and ether upon the surface of perception! Furthermore, the razor has no inherent "shaving" essence; it is merely cold iron! Therefore, to claim that a razor shaves hair is as absurd as claiming that a shadow eats mangoes! Ergo, the beard is never shaved, the hair was never grown, and the barber's trade is an ontological impossibility!'

The disciples cheered: 'A masterstroke! The barber is annihilated!'

The barber did not recite Sanskrit verses. He bowed respectfully to the Guru, reached into his leather apron, pulled out a small brass bowl of warm soapy water, and dabbed a thick lather of soap across Guru Paramartha's right eyebrow!

Before the Guru could react, the barber took his sharp razor and with a single, lightning-fast flick of his wrist, shaved off the Guru's right eyebrow clean to the bone!

Holding up the tuft of gray eyebrow hair upon the blade, the barber held it before the Guru's nose:

'Revered Master! If hair does not exist, what is this gray tuft on my blade? And if your eyebrow was never shaved, why does the right side of your forehead feel so cold and naked?'

The assembled village elders and farmers burst into a thunderous roar of laughter!

Guru Paramartha reached up, felt his smooth, bald eyebrow bone, and turned crimson with embarrassment!

Unable to refute the empirical evidence upon his forehead, the defeated philosopher pulled his shawl over his head and hurried back to the ashram, followed by his bewildered disciples.

Madayan whispered to Matti: 'The barber employed an uncivilized, non-scriptural counter-argument; but the absence of the eyebrow is undeniable!'
moral: Pompous jargon collapses like a house of cards before simple, earthy common sense.

title: The Broken Coconut and the Sage's Tooth
summary: Following a temple festival, Guru Paramartha received an auspicious offering: a colossal, dry, rock-hard coconut whose brown husk had been stripped, leaving a thick, impenetrabl...
full_text:
Following a temple festival, Guru Paramartha received an auspicious offering: a colossal, dry, rock-hard coconut whose brown husk had been stripped, leaving a thick, impenetrable shell as hard as tempered iron.

The Guru sat on the veranda, salivating at the thought of sweet, white coconut meat: 'Matti, break this coconut on the stone doorstep!'

Matti was about to smash the coconut against the stone, when Madayan intervened:

'Hold, Matti! A sacred coconut offered to the gods must not be struck against base stones; it contaminates the offering! It must be breached with dignity!'

'How shall we breach it with dignity?' asked Matti.

Madayan expounded his Jaw-Strength Calibration Theory: 'Human teeth are composed of pure ivory enamel! Ivory is harder than coconut fiber! In ancient times, the rishis cracked coconuts with their teeth to demonstrate spiritual tapas!'

Guru Paramartha stroked his beard, proud of his remaining five teeth: 'True! I possess the tooth of an ascetic! Give me the coconut!'

The Guru placed the hard, brown shell between his jaws, clamped his two upper molars and three lower incisors against the rock-hard shell, and bit down with all his spiritual might!

A sickening, loud CRUNCH! echoed across the veranda!

It was not the coconut shell that cracked.

Guru Paramartha's front tooth snapped in half with excruciating agony! A sharp stab of pain shot through his jaw, and a fountain of blood welled into his mouth!

The Guru dropped the unbroken coconut onto the floor, clutching his bleeding mouth, screaming in agony: 'MY TOOTH! MY WISDOM TOOTH HAS SHATTERED!'

Peedan shrieked in horror: 'The coconut has retaliated! It has broken our Master's jaw!'

Madayan examined the broken tooth upon the floor with scientific curiosity: 'Remarkable! The coconut shell exhibited an unexpected tensile resistance of the fourth degree! The tooth was merely sacrificed to verify the hardness of the husk!'

The village ironsmith was summoned with a pair of iron pliers to extract the broken root.

Sitting with a swollen cheek, wrapped in hot salt bags, Guru Paramartha looked at the unbroken coconut sitting peacefully on the shelf.

Matti took a heavy iron hammer and with a single blow—WHACK!—split the coconut into two neat halves, exposing the sweet white meat.

The Guru looked at the hammer, then at his swollen jaw, and sighed: 'The hammer is unphilosophical, Matti, but it has fewer nerve endings than my mouth!'
moral: Attempting to crack a hard shell with human bone ends in the dentist's chair.

title: The Blindfolded Philanthropist
summary: A wealthy merchant died, bequeathing a chest of copper and silver coins to Guru Paramartha's ashram with the condition that it be distributed to the most deserving, modest poor ...
full_text:
A wealthy merchant died, bequeathing a chest of copper and silver coins to Guru Paramartha's ashram with the condition that it be distributed to the most deserving, modest poor of the district.

The Guru summoned his disciples: 'We must distribute this treasure with absolute impartiality! According to the sacred scripture: "Let not your right eye see what your left hand gives!" Therefore, to avoid the sin of favoritism, I will distribute the coins while wearing a thick silk blindfold over both eyes!'

The disciples tied three layers of black silk tightly over the Guru's eyes.

The Guru sat upon a stone bench outside the ashram gate with the open chest of coins before him, holding a brass scoop in his hand.

'Announce to the poor that the blindfolded distribution has commenced!' commanded the Guru.

Matti shouted to the road: 'Come, noble poor! Our Guru gives with closed eyes!'

Instead of the modest village poor, three notorious village rascals and pickpockets heard the call. Seeing the old Guru blindfolded with a chest of coins, they smiled with delight.

The first rascal approached, disguised his voice in a squeaky whisper: 'Charity, Master!'

The Guru scooped a handful of silver coins and dropped them into the rascal's cloth: 'May your poverty be healed, son!'

The rascal stepped back, changed his voice to a deep, raspy croak, stepped forward again: 'Charity for an old lame grandmother, Master!'

The Guru dropped another scoop of silver: 'Blessings on your age, grandmother!'

The rascal ran behind a bush, altered his voice to a nasal whine, stepped forward a third time: 'Charity for a blind orphan, Master!'

The Guru scooped more coins: 'Blessings on your youth, orphan!'

For two hours, the same three rascals took turns changing their voices—croaking, wheezing, squeaking, and coughing—collecting sixty scoops of silver and copper coins, filling three heavy gunny sacks!

Meanwhile, an honest, impoverished widow with three hungry children stood timidly at the back of the crowd, too modest to push forward.

When the chest was scraped to the bottom, the Guru removed his blindfold, smiling with saintly satisfaction: 'Behold, my children! We have relieved the distress of sixty distinct, suffering souls without the slightest favoritism!'

At that moment, the widow approached, weeping: 'Master, the three village rascals have taken all the silver, and my starving children have received not a single copper!'

The Guru blinked in dismay: 'Where are the sixty suffering souls?'

Matti pointed down the road: 'There they go, Master! The three rascals are carrying three heavy sacks to the tavern!'

Madayan consoled the Guru: 'Master, your eyes were closed, which preserved your spiritual purity! If the rascals had sixty voices, they suffered from sixty distinct vocal afflictions!'

The Guru emptied his own personal lunch bag, handed his bread to the widow, and vowed: 'Henceforth, we shall open both eyes wide when charity is in our hands!'
moral: Giving charity with closed eyes ensures that rogues take the silver while the needy starve.
