title: The Miracle Mustard Oil
summary: While boiling herbs in the kitchen, Madayan accidentally mixed mustard oil, crushed red pepper, crushed garlic, and vinegar into a dark, pungent, foul-smelling concoction.
full_text:
While boiling herbs in the kitchen, Madayan accidentally mixed mustard oil, crushed red pepper, crushed garlic, and vinegar into a dark, pungent, foul-smelling concoction.

Instead of throwing it out, Madayan presented the bottle to Guru Paramartha: 'Master! I have accidentally discovered the legendary Maha-Siddha Tailam—The Universal Miracle Oil! It cures fevers, baldness, toothache, snakebite, and poverty with a single application!'

The Guru was impressed: 'We shall demonstrate its miraculous power to the village!'

That afternoon, the village headman's favorite hunting dog was limping from a thorn in its paw.

The Guru announced: 'Bring the hound to the ashram! Our Miracle Oil will heal the beast in seconds!'

The villagers gathered to watch the miracle.

Madayan took a generous spoonful of the fiery mustard-pepper-garlic mixture and rubbed it vigorously into the dog's wounded paw, and then—for good measure—smeared a dab onto the dog's nose!

The concentrated pepper and mustard struck the dog's tender paw and sensitive nostrils with the fury of liquid fire!

The poor hound let out an ear-splitting yelp: 'YOWWWW-WWL!'

His eyes watering, sneezing frantically, the enraged dog sprang into the air, snapped his jaws, and bit Madayan squarely on the thigh!

Then, running in wild circles, the dog knocked over the Guru's stool, sent the bottle of Miracle Oil flying into the crowd, and bolted down the street like a whirlwind, howling in torment!

Madayan hopped on one foot, clutching his bleeding thigh: 'The medicine works with extraordinary speed! The dog is no longer limping; he is running at thirty leagues an hour!'

The headman shook his fist: 'You poisoned my dog, you charlatan! If my hound does not recover, I will make you drink the rest of your miracle oil!'

Guru Paramartha retreated to the veranda, stroking his beard with dignity: 'The dog lacked spiritual receptivity; his canine constitution was too primitive for the higher vibrations of mustard!'
moral: Boasting of miraculous cures for ailments you cannot diagnose leads to public ridicule.

title: The Feast in the Dark
summary: A pious disciple invited Guru Paramartha and his five disciples to a magnificent evening feast in his country home. Platters of fragrant ghee rice, spicy vegetable curries, cris...
full_text:
A pious disciple invited Guru Paramartha and his five disciples to a magnificent evening feast in his country home. Platters of fragrant ghee rice, spicy vegetable curries, crispy appalams, sweet payasam, and ripe plantains were laid out upon clean banana leaves spread on the floor.

As the guests sat cross-legged before their platters, the solitary oil lamp in the corner flickered and died, plunging the windowless dining hall into pitch-black darkness.

The host apologized: 'Forgive me, revered masters! I will run to the kitchen and fetch another lamp!'

Madayan called out: 'Do not hurry, noble host! A true philosopher transcends the sensory illusion of sight! As the ancient verse declares: "The mouth knows the way to the belly even in the dark!" We shall eat in philosophical darkness!'

The six philosophers began eating in the pitch-black room.

Because they could not see their hands, chaos immediately ensued.

Matti reached out for a crispy appalam, but grasped Peedan's hairy knee, dipping it into the hot curry!

'AI-YO!' yelled Peedan. 'Matti is eating my leg!'

Peedan reached for a sweet plantain, but shoved it squarely into Asadan's open ear!

'HELP!' shrieked Asadan. 'A snake has entered my ear canal!'

Mudan, determined to secure his share of the sweet payasam pudding, scooped two handfuls of hot liquid and flung them toward where he thought his face was, splashing the sweet sticky pudding directly across Guru Paramartha's beard!

The Guru choked and sputtered: 'Who pours payasam upon my chin? Order! Observe philosophical decorum!'

Matti, swinging his hand to find his water cup, struck Madayan squarely in the nose with his elbow!

Thinking he was being attacked by bandits, Madayan picked up his brass drinking vessel and hurled it across the room: CLANG! The brass pot struck Guru Paramartha's shoulder!

The dark room erupted into a wild, hysterical brawl: men slipping on ghee rice, splashing curry, shoving plantains into nostrils, and shouting in terror: 'THIEVES! DEMONS! MY PAYASAM!'

When the host returned carrying two bright oil lanterns, he stopped in paralyzed horror at the threshold.

The dining hall was an unrecognizable battlefield of culinary devastation!

Rice was plastered across the whitewashed walls; curry dripped from the ceiling; the Guru sat covered in yellow payasam with a plantain stuck in his beard; Matti had a banana leaf draped over his head like a helmet, and Peedan was wrestling with Asadan on the floor over a crushed appalam!

Guru Paramartha wiped curry from his eye, looked at the lanterns, and remarked with dignified calm: 'A delightful banquet, noble host; but we have verified through empirical testing that the mouth occasionally misplaces its navigational bearings in the dark!'
moral: Dining in pitch darkness out of false modesty ensures that food goes into the ear instead of the mouth.

title: The Guru's Cold and the Steam Blanket
summary: Following the feast in the dark and the dip in the pond, Guru Paramartha caught a severe head cold. He lay upon his cot, sneezing, coughing, and groaning: 'My chest is congested...
full_text:
Following the feast in the dark and the dip in the pond, Guru Paramartha caught a severe head cold. He lay upon his cot, sneezing, coughing, and groaning: 'My chest is congested, my head throbs like a drum, and my nose runs like a mountain spring!'

The five disciples gathered around their ailing preceptor with immense concern.

Madayan consulted his mental encyclopedia of medicine: 'The disease is a classic imbalance of cold phlegm! To expel the cold, we must apply the Ayurvedic Steam Blanket of Intensive Sudation!'

'How is it performed?' asked Matti.

Madayan instructed: 'We will boil four large cauldrons of water mixed with eucalyptus leaves, turmeric, and black pepper. We will place the boiling cauldrons beneath the Guru's cot, drape ten heavy woolen blankets over the cot, sealing every opening, and let the hot steam penetrate his pores for two full hours!'

The disciples boiled the pepper-eucalyptus water until thick, scalding steam billowed from the cauldrons.

They slid the boiling cauldrons directly under the Guru's woven rope cot. Then, piling ten heavy, coarse woolen horse blankets over the Guru, they tucked the edges tightly beneath the mattress, placing heavy granite grinding stones on the corners so that 'not a single drop of therapeutic steam could escape!'

The scalding steam rose through the rope weave of the cot.

Within two minutes, the temperature beneath the blankets reached that of a pottery kiln!

Guru Paramartha began to roast!

He kicked and screamed from beneath the mountain of blankets: 'LET ME OUT! I AM BOILING! I AM BEING STEAMED LIKE AN IDLI!'

Standing outside the blankets, Madayan nodded with satisfaction: 'Listen to the master chant! The healing sweat is expelling the demons of disease! Keep the stones pressed down!'

Matti held the blankets tight: 'Endure with fortitude, Master! One hour and fifty minutes remain!'

Beneath the blankets, the Guru's face turned crimson; sweat poured from his beard in rivers; he felt his eyebrows melting! Desperate to save his life, the Guru gathered all his remaining strength, arched his back like a wild mustang, and heaved upward with all his might!

The ten heavy blankets, the grinding stones, and Matti were thrown across the room!

The Guru burst from the cot like an erupting geyser, red as a boiled lobster, wearing only his loincloth, dripping with hot water, and dashed out into the courtyard, leaping headlong into the cold water storage tank with a loud SIZZLE!

The steam hissed from his hot skin as he plunged into the cold water.

Surfacing among the water lilies, shivering and gasping, the Guru shouted: 'You fools! You tried to boil your own master alive!'

Madayan observed with scholarly triumph: 'Notice, brothers: the Master has forgotten his cough! He is shouting with a voice like a temple trumpet! The Steam Blanket has cured his cold completely!'

Floating in the cold tank, the Guru groaned in agreement: 'The cold is indeed gone, Madayan; but only because you boiled away half my skin!'
moral: Boiling a patient to cure a sneeze produces a cooked philosopher instead of health.

title: The Mirror and the Double Guru
summary: A wealthy pilgrim from the royal port of Madras presented Guru Paramartha with a rare and costly European looking-glass, framed in carved rosewood and polished to silver perfect...
full_text:
A wealthy pilgrim from the royal port of Madras presented Guru Paramartha with a rare and costly European looking-glass, framed in carved rosewood and polished to silver perfection. The Guru, who had lived his entire life seeing his reflection only in muddy well-water or tarnished bronze plates, held the glass before his face.

Looking into the mirror, the Guru gasped in astonishment: staring back at him was an elderly, silver-bearded man with a solemn belly, wearing an identical yellow shawl!

Guru Paramartha bowed with courtly grace: 'Greetings, venerable brother! Welcome to our humble hermitage! From which sacred mountain do you arrive?'

The reflection, naturally, bowed silently in return, moving its lips without sound.

The Guru frowned: 'He mimics my bow, yet he maintains haughty silence! Matti, come here! Another spiritual preceptor has entered our room and refuses to speak!'

Matti approached and peeked over the Guru's shoulder. In the mirror appeared Matti's own bewildered face beside the Guru's.

Matti shrieked in terror: 'Master! Not only has a rival Guru invaded our sanctuary, but he has brought a replica of me as his disciple! Look at his stupid blockhead face!'

Madayan was summoned to analyze the phenomenon. Pacing the floor with fingers on his brow, the Dunce expounded his Dual Dimensional Hypothesis:

'This glass frame is not an ordinary piece of furniture; it is a portal to the Parallel World of Pratibimba! In that alternate universe dwells an identical ashram with an identical Guru and disciples! But because they live inside the glass, they are plotting to crawl out tonight and usurp our beds, our rice, and our monastery!'

'What must be done to prevent this hostile invasion?' asked Guru Paramartha, trembling with alarm.

Madayan instructed: 'We must neutralize their sensory organs! We will paint over the glass with thick, black lamp-soot mixed with castor oil! Once the alternate Guru is blinded, he will be unable to find the portal!'

Peedan brought a bowl of black soot and smeared it thickly across the silver glass until not a speck of reflection remained.

Wiping his sooty fingers, Guru Paramartha smiled with deep relief: 'A brilliant defensive victory, Madayan! The rival Guru is now trapped in pitch-black darkness, while we dwell peacefully in the light of truth!'

The disciples bowed in admiration of their master's tactical genius, and hung the blackened glass in the shed to scare away rats.
moral: Failing to recognize your own reflection leads you to accuse the mirror of harboring a rival.

title: The Cow That Flew over the Palmyra Tree
summary: One evening, a traveling bard was reciting verses from the Puranas under the village banyan tree, singing poetically of celestial flying cows that soared across the skies in the...
full_text:
One evening, a traveling bard was reciting verses from the Puranas under the village banyan tree, singing poetically of celestial flying cows that soared across the skies in the golden age of truth.

Matti and Peedan listened with wide eyes and open mouths.

Next morning, while grazing the ashram cow Kamadhenu near a grove of towering palmyra trees, a flock of white egrets suddenly took flight from behind the palm fronds, beating their wings and soaring above the treetops.

At that exact second, the cow walked behind a dense bamboo thicket out of Matti's sight.

Matti looked up, saw the white egrets in the clouds, looked down, saw the empty grass, and shrieked in hysterical wonder: 'PEEDAN! LOOK UP! LOOK UP! OUR COW KAMADHENU HAS TAKEN WING! SHE IS FLYING OVER THE PALMYRA TREES!'

Peedan squinted into the bright sky: 'I see white forms soaring above the leaves! She has attained the celestial siddhi of levitation!'

The two disciples sprinted back to the ashram, shouting: 'Master! A miracle! Kamadhenu has flown into the upper atmosphere!'

Guru Paramartha rushed into the courtyard, took off his spectacles, and stared up into the clouds.

Madayan immediately calculated the theological implications: 'If our cow has become an aeronautical deity, her milk will henceforth possess the power of flight! Anyone who drinks her buttermilk will float up to heaven!'

The Guru commanded: 'Prepare the sacred welcoming altar! When she descends from the stratosphere, she must be received with conch shells and camphor!'

The five disciples and the Guru assembled in the garden, blowing conch shells, beating brass gongs, and waving incense burners toward the sky, shouting: 'Descend, O flying mother! Land upon your sacred straw!'

For three hours, the six philosophers danced in a circle, gazing into the empty clouds.

Presently, the gentle white cow emerged calmly from behind the bamboo thicket, chewing a clump of dry grass, and ambled slowly into the courtyard, looking with placid curiosity at her dancing masters.

Matti gasped in awe: 'Look! She has landed with absolute, silent aerodynamic perfection!'

Guru Paramartha stroked the cow's nose with deep reverence: 'Welcome back to earth, celestial traveler! How was the climate above the clouds?'

The cow let out a long, unphilosophical moo: 'Moooo-oo.'

The village cowherd, leaning over the fence, laughed until his sides ached: 'She was behind the bamboo eating grass all morning, you old fools!'

The Guru frowned with scholarly pity: 'The cowherd understands only the four legs on the ground; he cannot comprehend the secret aerial journeys of the spirit!'
moral: Believing preposterous rumors without verification makes you the butt of village mockery.

title: The Stolen Moonbeam and the Lockbox
summary: On a warm summer evening, a brilliant shaft of silver moonlight entered the open window of Guru Paramartha's private bedchamber, illuminating a polished brass plate on the table...
full_text:
On a warm summer evening, a brilliant shaft of silver moonlight entered the open window of Guru Paramartha's private bedchamber, illuminating a polished brass plate on the table with extraordinary, jewel-like brightness.

The Guru called his disciples: 'Behold this wondrous phenomenon, children! The celestial Moon has deposited a concentrated beam of solid silver upon our brass plate! Silver is expensive in the town market; let us secure this celestial asset before the clouds steal it away!'

Matti ran to fetch the ashram heavy iron cash-box, fitted with three brass hasps and a massive iron padlock.

'How shall we transfer the beam into the box?' asked Peedan.

Madayan directed the operation: 'Place the open iron box directly beneath the beam of light! When the moonbeam pours into the box, slam the iron lid shut, turn the key three times, and lock the silver light inside!'

Matti carefully positioned the iron box. The white moonbeam shone brightly into the open chest, illuminating the velvet lining.

'NOW!' yelled Madayan.

Matti slammed the heavy iron lid shut with a thunderous CLANG!, drove the iron bolts into the sockets, and turned the key three times!

'The moonbeam is imprisoned!' cheered Matti. 'We possess a permanent reservoir of liquid silver!'

The disciples hid the heavy iron box beneath the Guru's cot, guarding it with bamboo staffs throughout the night.

Next morning, when the sun was shining brightly, the Guru summoned the village goldsmith to evaluate their new celestial treasure.

'Goldsmith,' said the Guru proudly, 'prepare your scales! We have captured a pure beam of concentrated lunar silver!'

The disciples hauled the heavy iron box into the center of the room. Guru Paramartha unlocked the three heavy padlocks with solemn ceremony and threw back the lid!

The goldsmith peered inside.

The box was completely empty, containing nothing but dry air and stale dust.

The goldsmith chuckled: 'There is nothing here, Master!'

Matti blinked in dismay: 'Where did the silver go?'

Madayan examined the keyhole through his magnifying glass and delivered his diagnosis: 'The moonbeam was exceptionally slender and ethereal; during the night, it liquefied and escaped through the keyhole!'

Guru Paramartha nodded in agreement: 'Next time, Madayan, we must plug the keyhole with beeswax before we lock the box!'

The goldsmith bowed with a smirk: 'Indeed, Master; and don't forget to tie the sun to your flagpole as well!'
moral: Locking an iron key upon empty air will never capture the radiance of the sky.

title: The Oil Lamp That Drank Milk
summary: Guru Paramartha was preparing for the festival of Deepavali, the festival of lights. The ashram possessed an ancient, ornate seven-tiered brass standing lamp, designed to hold f...
full_text:
Guru Paramartha was preparing for the festival of Deepavali, the festival of lights. The ashram possessed an ancient, ornate seven-tiered brass standing lamp, designed to hold forty-nine oil wicks.

Matti was sent to the storehouse to fetch five bottles of sesame oil to fill the lamp.

Returning with empty hands, Matti wept: 'Alas, Master! The storehouse is empty; the rats tipped over the oil jars, and not a single drop of sesame oil remains in the ashram!'

The Guru was distressed: 'A festival of lights without a lamp is an inauspicious catastrophe! What other liquids do we possess?'

Peedan reported: 'The dairy farmer has just delivered four large pails of rich, fresh, unpasteurized buffalo milk!'

Madayan immediately formulated his Sacred Dairy Combustion Theory: 'Why do we burn base vegetable oils in the presence of the gods? Milk is the sacred essence of the cow! Butter originates from milk; ghee originates from butter; therefore, milk possesses the latent, concentrated fire of pure ghee! If we fill the brass lamp with fresh buffalo milk, it will burn with a pure, white, heavenly, celestial flame that smells of sandalwood!'

The Guru was enraptured: 'A sublime theological discovery! Fill the forty-nine reservoirs with buffalo milk!'

The disciples filled all forty-nine tiers of the brass lamp to the brim with rich, white buffalo milk. They soaked cotton wicks in the milk, placed them in the spouts, and prepared to light them.

Guru Paramartha took a flaming match and applied it to the first wick.

The match hissed against the cold, wet milk and went out.

He struck a second match; it sputtered and died.

Madayan intervened: 'The milk requires pre-heating! Bring the kitchen blowpipe and fan the embers!'

The disciples blew on the wicks with bamboo blowpipes, holding burning camphor blocks against the wet cotton.

After ten minutes of frantic blowing, the wicks did not ignite with a white celestial flame; instead, the milk in the brass bowls began to curdle, scorch, and burn against the hot metal!

A thick, acrid, suffocating cloud of black smoke billowed through the temple hall, carrying the foul, sickening stench of burnt milk, scorched cheese, and charred cotton!

The disciples began coughing and choking: 'COUGH! COUGH! MY EYES! IT SMELLS LIKE A BURNING DAIRY!'

Guru Paramartha fled into the courtyard, coughing violently, his white robes stained with black soot.

The temple priest who had arrived for the ceremony stopped at the gate, sniffing the air in horror: 'What abomination are you burning? Has a cow caught fire in your sanctuary?'

Wiping soot from his tears, Guru Paramartha declared: 'The buffalo milk was spiritually impure; it had not undergone the necessary meditation to release its latent fire!'

The priest brought two bottles of cheap sesame oil, lit the lamps, and the festival proceeded, while the disciples scrubbed scorched cheese from the brass lamp till midnight.
moral: Feeding butterfat to a lamp wick produces foul smoke instead of holy illumination.

title: The Five Disciples and the Honey Pot
summary: A wealthy forest warden presented Guru Paramartha with a small, precious earthenware jar filled with pure, golden wild forest honey, gathered from the highest cliffs of the West...
full_text:
A wealthy forest warden presented Guru Paramartha with a small, precious earthenware jar filled with pure, golden wild forest honey, gathered from the highest cliffs of the Western Ghats.

Knowing the sweet-toothed weaknesses of his five disciples, the Guru placed the jar high on a wooden beam in his private study. Summoning Matti, Madayan, Peedan, Asadan, and Mudan, the Guru pointed to the jar and warned with terrifying gravity:

'Mark well, children! Within that earthen pot lies a deadly, concentrated magical poison known as Kalakuta! If any mortal so much as dips the tip of his little finger into that pot and touches his tongue, he will swell up like a poisoned toad, roll across the floor, and die in agonizing convulsions within three minutes! Therefore, touch it not under penalty of instant death!'

The disciples bowed in trembling terror, swearing never to look upon the pot.

That afternoon, Guru Paramartha went to the village to deliver a lecture on renunciation.

Left alone in the ashram, Matti sat looking up at the high earthen jar. The sweet, irresistible fragrance of wild mountain honey drifted down through the room.

Matti licked his lips: 'Brothers... can a deadly poison truly smell as sweet as wild mountain honey?'

Madayan reasoned: 'It is a known fact that certain celestial poisons mimic the fragrance of ambrosia to entice the unwary! But as philosophers, is it not our duty to investigate the empirical properties of toxicity?'

Peedan brought a ladder. Matti climbed up, took down the jar, and removed the cloth seal.

A golden, thick, luscious drop clung to the rim.

Matti dipped his finger, touched it to his tongue, and closed his eyes, preparing to die.

Three seconds passed; thirty seconds passed. Instead of swelling like a toad, Matti's face lit up with heavenly ecstasy: 'BROTHERS! THIS IS NOT POISON! THIS IS AMBROSIA FROM THE GODS!'

The other four disciples rushed forward with wooden spoons. Within five minutes of frantic, ecstatic gorging, the five philosophers scraped the jar clean to the very bottom, licking every drop!

Looking at the empty pot, sudden, cold panic seized Matti's heart: 'The pot is empty! When the Master returns and discovers his "poison" gone, he will realize we have discovered his deceit and beat us with his staff!'

Madayan smiled with criminal genius: 'Do not panic! I have devised an unshakeable defense: The Dog Intrusion Theory! We will shatter the Guru's favorite clay inkwell on the floor, break his bamboo pen, and leave the empty honey pot beside the wreckage. When he returns, we will say: "Master! A vicious stray dog broke into the study, smashed your inkwell, ate your deadly poison, and ran into the woods to die!"'

Peedan smashed the inkwell; Asadan broke the bamboo pen, and they threw the empty pot on the floor.

At that moment, Peedan noticed that sticky honey was dripping from Asadan's fingers and beard. 'Wipe your face, Asadan!'

Asadan grabbed a handful of fluffy white cotton waste from the pillow basket and wiped his sticky face and beard!

The sticky honey caused the fluffy white cotton to adhere firmly to Asadan's chin, nose, cheeks, and eyebrows! He looked like an exotic, bearded, white-feathered owl!

When Guru Paramartha returned, he found his broken inkwell, his shattered pen, and the empty honey jar.

'What catastrophe has occurred here?' roared the Guru.

Madayan stepped forward, reciting his prepared speech: 'Alas, Master! A wild dog broke in, smashed your inkwell, and ate your deadly poison!'

The Guru looked down, then looked up at Asadan, who was standing at attention with fluffy white cotton feathers stuck to his sticky beard, blinking like a stunned rooster.

The Guru picked up his bamboo staff: 'And pray, Madayan, what species of wild dog is this that has sprouted white feathers and smells of wild honey?'

Before Madayan could formulate a metaphysical defense, the Guru's bamboo staff descended upon the five guilty backs: THWACK, THWACK, THWACK!

Rubbing their sore shoulders, the disciples washed the sticky feathers from Asadan's face, having learned that honey cannot be hidden under cotton.
moral: Guilt covered in feathers reveals the thief more clearly than any witness.

title: The Donkey That Sat in the Palanquin
summary: A wealthy merchant of the town, having completed his pilgrimage, donated an old, discarded wooden palanquin to Guru Paramartha's ashram. The palanquin was carved of teak, lined ...
full_text:
A wealthy merchant of the town, having completed his pilgrimage, donated an old, discarded wooden palanquin to Guru Paramartha's ashram. The palanquin was carved of teak, lined with worn red velvet cushions, and carried on a long, curved bamboo shoulder-pole designed for four bearers.

Guru Paramartha was ecstatic: 'At last, a conveyance worthy of our supreme spiritual stature! Matti, Madayan, Peedan, and Asadan, you four shall be the bearers of the palanquin; Mudan will carry the umbrella, and I will ride inside like an emperor!'

The Guru attempted to enter. But because of his majestic, expanding belly and his heavy wooden sandals, he could not squeeze through the narrow doorway without getting stuck!

Puffing and panting, Matti pushed from behind, while Madayan pulled from inside. The Guru groaned: 'Hold! My ribs are being compressed! A philosopher must ride in comfort, not as a prisoner in an iron cage!'

The Guru climbed out, disappointed.

Matti then looked at the ashram gray donkey standing in the corner: 'Master, if you cannot ride, why should this magnificent palanquin sit idle? Our noble donkey carries our heavy luggage daily; let us honor the faithful beast by giving him a royal ride in the palanquin!'

The disciples cheered: 'A magnificent gesture of inter-species compassion!'

They hoisted the bewildered, kicking gray donkey into the palanquin! They tied his four legs loosely with silk scarves so he would not fall out, placed a floral garland around his neck, and arranged his long ears over the red velvet cushions.

The donkey looked out of the palanquin window, blinking with profound confusion.

Matti and Madayan took the front pole on their shoulders; Peedan and Asadan took the rear pole.

'LIFT!' shouted Matti.

With immense groaning and straining, the four disciples hoisted the heavy wooden palanquin containing the three-hundred-pound donkey onto their shoulders!

Guru Paramartha walked ahead, waving his staff like a herald, while Mudan carried the silk umbrella over the donkey's head: 'Clear the road for the Royal Steed of Guru Paramartha's Ashram!'

The village folk stopped, stared in speechlessness, and then burst into hysterical, uncontrollable laughter! Crowds followed the procession, clapping and whistling: 'Look at the donkey in the palanquin carried by four fools!'

The noise of the whistling crowd, the flapping umbrella, and the swinging motion terrified the donkey.

The beast struggled against his silk bonds, kicked violently inside the narrow wooden cabin, and let out an ear-splitting, vibrating bray: 'HEE-HAW! HEE-HAW!'

The violent kicking shifted the center of gravity.

Peedan stumbled over a stone in the road. Asadan lost his footing; Matti slipped in the dust, and the heavy wooden palanquin crashed onto the stone pavement with a splintering crash!

The wooden roof collapsed; the bamboo pole snapped, and the donkey scrambled out of the wreckage, kicking Peedan in the shin and galloping down the road, leaving four bruised disciples groaning beneath the broken timbers!

Guru Paramartha picked up his spectacles from the dust and remarked with grave philosophical insight: 'We have learned today that an ass prefers the dust of the road to the velvet of the court; nobility cannot be imposed upon long ears!'
moral: Elevating a beast of burden into a seat of honor brings the vehicle down in ruins.

title: The Broken Plow and the Blacksmith's Tongs
summary: The ashram garden had to be plowed before the monsoon rains to sow seeds of sesame and lentils. The wooden share of the ashram hand-plow had rotted, so Guru Paramartha sent Matt...
full_text:
The ashram garden had to be plowed before the monsoon rains to sow seeds of sesame and lentils. The wooden share of the ashram hand-plow had rotted, so Guru Paramartha sent Matti to the village blacksmith to borrow an iron tool to cultivate the soil.

The blacksmith was busy forging horse-shoes over his roaring bellows.

Matti shouted above the din of the hammer: 'Blacksmith! We need an iron instrument to break the earth for our garden!'

The busy blacksmith pointed to a pair of heavy, four-foot iron tongs leaning against the wall, intended for gripping red-hot ingots: 'Take those heavy iron tongs and bring them back tomorrow!'

Matti shouldered the heavy iron tongs, believing they were an advanced, double-bladed cultivating machine.

Returning to the ashram, Matti showed the tongs to Madayan: 'Look, brother! The blacksmith has provided us with a miraculous, two-legged iron plow!'

Madayan examined the hinge: 'Notice the mechanical pivot! This instrument operates through scissor-like hydraulic pressure! Matti, you will hold the left handle; Peedan will hold the right handle, and you will open and shut the iron jaws to bite the earth!'

The two disciples took the tongs to the garden.

The soil was hard, baked clay, dry as stone.

Matti opened the jaws; Peedan slammed them shut into the hard earth: CLANG!

The blunt, rounded tips of the blacksmith's tongs bounced off the hard clay, sending painful vibrations through their arms, without making a scratch on the soil!

'The earth is stubborn!' cried Peedan. 'We must use leverage!'

Peedan jumped onto one handle of the tongs, while Matti stood on the other, jumping up and down to force the iron jaws into the ground.

Under their combined weight, the iron hinge groaned, bent, and the central rivet sheared off with a sharp SNAP!

The two handles flew apart, sending both disciples tumbling into the thorny brinjal bushes!

Now they possessed two separate, twisted iron bars.

Matti wept: 'The blacksmith's tool is broken! He will demand ten silver rupees!'

Madayan examined the bent bars and formulated a solution: 'The tool was not broken; it has multiplied! One tool has become two! We will return both halves to the blacksmith and explain that we have doubled his inventory through philosophical fission!'

When they returned the two twisted pieces to the blacksmith, the burly artisan did not appreciate philosophical fission: he picked up his leather apron and chased the disciples out of the smithy with a hot iron poker!

Guru Paramartha paid for a new rivet, recording in his diary: 'Note: Blacksmiths possess fiery temperaments and lack appreciation for structural division.'
moral: Borrowing an instrument without understanding its use ruins both the tool and the field.

title: The River That Stole the Sandalwood Paste
summary: A wealthy devotee presented Guru Paramartha with an exquisite, small silver cup filled with pure, fragrant sandalwood paste, prepared from the heartwood of ancient trees of Myso...
full_text:
A wealthy devotee presented Guru Paramartha with an exquisite, small silver cup filled with pure, fragrant sandalwood paste, prepared from the heartwood of ancient trees of Mysore, reserved for anointing holy men before prayers.

The Guru valued the paste dearly. While traveling to a temple assembly across the river, the Guru handed the silver cup to Matti, commanding: 'Matti, carry this sacred paste across the river with the utmost reverence; do not let a drop be lost!'

As they waded through the shallow river, the current swirled around Matti's knees.

Matti looked down into the clear water and thought: 'The river is a sacred goddess! Is it not our duty to offer worship to the water before we cross?'

Matti dipped his finger into the silver cup, scooped a large dollop of the fragrant sandalwood paste, and dropped it into the swirling river: 'Accept this offering, O sacred Goddess Ganga!'

The yellow paste dissolved into the current and was swept away in seconds.

Matti scooped another dollop: 'Accept this for the fish, O Goddess!'

Swish! The second dollop vanished.

Matti scooped a third, a fourth, and a fifth, until the silver cup was scraped completely clean!

Reaching the opposite bank, Guru Paramartha sat upon a flat stone, prepared to perform his morning prayers: 'Matti, bring the silver cup, and anoint my brow with the fragrant sandalwood paste!'

Matti presented the cup. It was empty and shiny clean.

The Guru stared in horror: 'Matti! Where is the sacred sandalwood paste?'

Matti beamed with saintly piety: 'Master, I performed a supreme act of devotion! I offered the entire cup of paste to the sacred river goddess as we crossed!'

The Guru was speechless: 'You offered my twenty-rupee sandalwood paste to the river?'

Madayan nodded with profound theological approval: 'A magnificent gesture, Master! The river goddess has received our offering, and in return, she has perfumed the entire aquatic ecosystem! Smell the water!'

Guru Paramartha bent down, scooped a handful of river water, and sniffed it. It smelled of mud, decaying weeds, and wet fish.

The Guru splashed the muddy water into Madayan's face: 'Does that smell like Mysore sandalwood to your philosophical nose, Madayan?'

Wiping muddy water from his eyes, Madayan replied: 'Master, the spiritual perfume is perceptible only to the subtle senses!'

The Guru sighed, picked up a handful of yellow river mud, and smeared it across his forehead: 'Let us pray with mud, my children; at least mud does not cost twenty silver rupees!'
moral: Pouring perfumed treasure into a running current leaves you smelling only of muddy water.

title: The Disciples Who Counted the Stars
summary: On a clear, cloudless midnight, the celestial dome was ablaze with millions of glittering, diamond-like stars. Guru Paramartha sat on the ashram veranda, contemplating the vastn...
full_text:
On a clear, cloudless midnight, the celestial dome was ablaze with millions of glittering, diamond-like stars. Guru Paramartha sat on the ashram veranda, contemplating the vastness of creation.

The Guru mused aloud: 'Astronomers claim that the stars are innumerable. But surely a disciplined, methodical mind can calculate their exact number through systematic enumeration!'

Matti and Madayan immediately volunteered: 'Master, we shall count the celestial host tonight!'

Madayan divided the sky into four sectors: 'Matti will count the Northern quadrant; Peedan will count the Southern; Asadan will count the Eastern, and I will count the Zenith!'

The four disciples lay flat on their backs upon the gravel courtyard, pointing their fingers toward the sky, and began counting aloud:

'One... two... three... four... twenty-seven... ninety-four...'

After ten minutes, a brilliant shooting star streaked across the sky, leaving a glowing white tail before vanishing.

Matti shrieked in distress: 'Hold, brothers! A star has fallen from the northern quadrant! Deduct one from the total!'

Madayan argued: 'No, it did not fall from the sky; it was transferred into the eastern quadrant! Add one to Asadan's column!'

Asadan complained: 'I lost my place! Was I at two hundred and fourteen, or four hundred and twelve?'

At that moment, a swarm of hungry mosquitoes descended upon the four disciples lying motionless upon their backs. The insects buzzed around their ears and bit their noses, foreheads, and necks.

Peedan slapped his cheek: SLAP! 'Matti, did you count that star near the Great Bear?'

Matti turned his head to look, lost his point of focus, and groaned: 'Alas! I blinked, and the stars shifted their positions! They are moving!'

Madayan declared: 'The stars are engaged in a cosmic conspiracy to confuse our mathematical audit! Whenever we count twenty, three more twinkle to mock our calculations!'

Mudan, who was sitting near the well, brought out a small bowl of dry black pepper seeds: 'Brothers! Why count through the air? For every star you see, drop one pepper seed into this clay bowl! When morning comes, we will weigh the bowl and calculate the stars by weight!'

The disciples began tossing pepper seeds into the bowl in the dark: 'There is one! There is another!'

Half the pepper seeds missed the bowl, bouncing across the courtyard gravel.

By dawn, the four disciples were freezing cold, their necks stiff as stone, their faces covered in red mosquito bites, and the clay bowl contained exactly forty-seven pepper seeds and three dead beetles.

Guru Paramartha emerged from his room and inspected the bowl: 'How many stars illuminate the heavens, my scholars?'

Madayan bowed with grave scientific precision: 'Master, according to our empirical seed-calibration method, the universe contains exactly forty-seven stars, three beetles, and six million mosquitoes!'

Rubbing his sore neck, the Guru nodded: 'A satisfactory astronomical census; let us retire and sleep!'
moral: Counting the infinite stars of heaven with clumsy fingers yields only a stiff neck.

title: The Shadow of the Temple Gopuram
summary: The regional temple possessed a magnificent, ancient granite gopuram tower that soared one hundred and twenty cubits into the sky, adorned with thousands of carved figures of ce...
full_text:
The regional temple possessed a magnificent, ancient granite gopuram tower that soared one hundred and twenty cubits into the sky, adorned with thousands of carved figures of celestial dancers, lions, and deities.

The village council was debating the exact height of the tower to order new copper flagpoles, but no carpenter was brave enough to climb to the dizzying pinnacle with a measuring cord.

Guru Paramartha offered his services: 'A philosopher does not risk his neck upon heights; he measures the tower through its projected shadow upon the earth!'

The village elders praised his wisdom and promised ten silver rupees for the measurement.

At seven o'clock in the morning, when the sun was low on the eastern horizon, the temple gopuram cast an enormous, colossal, elongated shadow that stretched three hundred paces across the western fields, over a fence, and into a farmer's cabbage patch.

Matti and Madayan arrived with a bamboo measuring pole.

Matti began measuring the shadow from the base of the tower: 'One pole... two poles... ten poles...'

Because the sun was rising steadily in the sky, the shadow was shrinking every minute!

By the time Matti reached the cabbage patch, the tip of the shadow had retreated fifty paces toward the temple!

Matti shouted in bewilderment: 'Madayan! The shadow is retreating! It is running backward toward the tower!'

Madayan checked his calculations: 'The tower is shrinking! As the morning heat increases, the granite stones are contracting into the earth! Measure faster before the tower disappears completely!'

The two disciples ran back and forth across the fields, chasing the shrinking shadow like boys chasing butterflies!

By noon, the sun was directly overhead. The shadow shrank to a tiny, two-foot pool of shade huddled directly beneath the eaves of the foundation.

Matti stood beside the foundation, measured the two-foot shadow with his hand, and reported in triumph: 'Master! The tower is exactly two cubits high!'

Guru Paramartha delivered his official report to the village council: 'Honorable elders, your colossal temple tower is exactly two cubits in height; an ordinary goat can step over it with ease!'

The village elders stared at the soaring, one-hundred-and-twenty-cubit stone tower, then at the Guru's report, and burst into roaring laughter!

The chief elder said: 'If our tower is two cubits high, O wise Guru, why do your eyes water when you look up at the top?'

The Guru replied with unruffled dignity: 'Optical refraction, elder; the tower is small, but the air above it is remarkably magnified!'
moral: Chasing a shifting shadow to measure a permanent tower leaves you wandering in the fields.

title: The Stolen Mangoes and the Blindfold Test
summary: A basket of six prime, luscious, ripe Alphonso mangoes, presented to Guru Paramartha by a visiting prince, was left upon the dining table for the evening feast.
full_text:
A basket of six prime, luscious, ripe Alphonso mangoes, presented to Guru Paramartha by a visiting prince, was left upon the dining table for the evening feast.

When the Guru entered the dining room at dusk, only five mangoes remained in the basket. One magnificent golden fruit had vanished.

The Guru called his five disciples into the room, his brow furrowed with judicial wrath: 'A theft has been committed! One of you has devoured the royal fruit! Confess, or the wrath of heaven shall descend upon the culprit!'

The five disciples fell to their knees, each loudly proclaiming his absolute innocence.

Madayan stepped forward to conduct a trial by divine ordeal: 'Master, human witnesses are frail and deceitful! We must conduct the Trial of the Sacred Scent! Mango leaves a powerful, lingering perfume upon the fingers of the eater! If you blindfold yourself and smell the fingers of each disciple, your divine olfactory sense will instantly detect the criminal!'

The Guru agreed: 'Bind my eyes with silk!'

They tied a thick silk blindfold over the Guru's eyes.

Guru Paramartha held out his nose: 'Present your fingers, disciples!'

Matti presented his fingers: the Guru sniffed: 'Pure!'
Peedan presented his fingers: 'Pure!'
Asadan presented his fingers: 'Pure!'

Now it was Madayan's turn. Madayan was the true thief who had stolen and eaten the mango an hour earlier, and his fingers smelled richly of sweet mango juice!

Knowing he would be exposed, Madayan did not present his own fingers. Instead, he reached behind him, grabbed the paw of the sleeping ashram dog, and held the dog's dusty paw right under the Guru's nose!

The Guru sniffed the dog's paw: 'Faugh! This smells of dry dirt and road dust! Pure!'

Then Madayan took Matti's clean left hand and held it under the Guru's nose a second time: 'Pure!'

The Guru removed his blindfold, blinking in confusion: 'All five pairs of fingers are completely innocent! How can this be?'

Madayan smiled with triumphant philosophical deduction: 'The mystery is solved, Master! None of your disciples took the fruit! The missing mango was eaten by an invisible, disembodied wandering spirit who hungered for vitamins! The spirit took the fruit, leaving our ashram blessed!'

Guru Paramartha nodded with deep reverent satisfaction: 'Truly, our ashram is favored by celestial visitors! Let us divide the remaining five mangoes among our honest disciples!'

And Madayan, having eaten one whole mango in secret, received his second mango with pious humility.
moral: A blindfolded trial where the accused controls the evidence acquits the thief every time.

title: The Ghost Who Swept the Veranda
summary: For three consecutive mornings, when Guru Paramartha and his disciples awoke at dawn, they found the broad ashram veranda miraculously clean: the dust had been swept into neat h...
full_text:
For three consecutive mornings, when Guru Paramartha and his disciples awoke at dawn, they found the broad ashram veranda miraculously clean: the dust had been swept into neat heaps; the flagstones were sprinkled with fresh water, and beautiful, intricate geometric kolam designs of white rice flour were drawn upon the threshold!

The disciples were terrified.

Matti shrieked: 'A ghost! A nocturnal demon is haunting our veranda!'

Madayan examined the white rice flour designs with profound occult analysis: 'Notice the geometric precision of these lines! No mortal broom could sweep with such symmetrical harmony! We are being served by a Brahmarakshasa—a learned ghost of a deceased scholar who is performing penance by sweeping our hermitage!'

The Guru was deeply flattered: 'A scholar-ghost recognizes my preeminence! He sweeps for us by night to earn spiritual merit!'

Peedan asked: 'How should we reward the benevolent ghost?'

Madayan instructed: 'A Brahmarakshasa feeds upon milk, puffed rice, and jaggery! We must leave a large brass bowl filled with sweet milk and honey upon the veranda tonight as an offering to our spectral servant!'

That evening, the disciples placed a large bowl of sweet milk and honey on the swept veranda and locked their doors, peeking through the window shutters in terrified anticipation.

At midnight, the gentle, elderly widow who lived in the adjoining cottage—who had lost her son years ago and out of pure neighborly kindness had been sweeping the holy men's veranda at night while they slept—crept into the courtyard carrying her broom.

Seeing the large brass bowl of sweet milk and honey on the step, the poor, hungry widow smiled with gratitude: 'How kind of the holy Guru to leave refreshment for an old neighbor!'

She sat on the step, drank the sweet milk, ate the honey, swept the veranda with her broom, drew a lovely lotus kolam, and walked home in peace.

Inside the dark room, Peedan peeked through the shutter. Seeing a white-clad figure sitting on the step drinking the milk, Peedan whispered in awe: 'Look! The ghost is drinking our offering! See her white spectral drapery!'

Next morning, finding the bowl licked clean and the veranda swept, Guru Paramartha delivered a profound lecture to the village:

'Our ashram has established diplomatic relations with the spirit world! A celestial ghost sweeps our floors and drinks our milk every midnight!'

The village elders nodded in awe, while the old widow smiled quietly at her spinning wheel, continuing to sweep the veranda and drink her midnight milk in peace.
moral: Attributing an unexpected benefit to ghosts prevents you from thanking the real servant.

title: The Guru's Wooden Leg
summary: After sitting cross-legged for four hours in deep meditation on a cold marble slab, Guru Paramartha attempted to rise. Because his right leg had fallen completely asleep from re...
full_text:
After sitting cross-legged for four hours in deep meditation on a cold marble slab, Guru Paramartha attempted to rise. Because his right leg had fallen completely asleep from restricted circulation, his foot was numb, prickly, and unresponsive.

When he stepped upon the floor, his right knee buckled, and he collapsed onto his cot with a mournful groan: 'Alas, my children! My right leg has turned to solid stone! It has lost all sensation, warmth, and vitality! I have become a cripple!'

The disciples rushed to his bedside in weeping panic.

Matti pinched the Guru's right foot: 'Do you feel this, Master?'

Because of the numbness, the Guru felt nothing: 'Nothing! Not a whisper of sensation! The limb is dead!'

Madayan diagnosed the condition with terrifying certainty: 'Petrification of the Fibula! The bone has calcified into granite! If a petrified limb remains attached to the living body, the stone infection will spread upward into the belly, turn the heart into marble, and petrify the entire philosopher!'

'What is the surgical remedy?' wept Peedan.

Madayan declared: 'Amputation! We must saw off the dead stone leg and fit our Master with an elegant, polished wooden leg carved of seasoned rosewood!'

The disciples fetched the large woodcutting saw from the carpenter's shed. Matti held the Guru's shoulders; Peedan held his left leg, and Madayan raised the saw over the numb right knee!

Just as the iron saw teeth brushed against the Guru's skin, the sharp sensation of cold steel triggered a sudden return of circulation!

A wave of intense, tingling 'pins and needles' surged through the Guru's nerves!

With an involuntary, violent reflex, the Guru's right leg kicked out like an iron spring!

His foot struck Madayan squarely in the stomach, sending the amateur surgeon flying across the room into a basket of laundry!

The Guru leaped to his feet, hopping on both legs: 'AI-YO! PINS AND NEEDLES! MY LEG IS ALIVE!'

Madayan struggled out of the laundry basket, rubbing his sore belly, and cheered in triumph:

'A MIRACLE! THE PROSPECT OF MY SURGERY WAS SO MEDICALLY POTENT THAT IT TERRIFIED THE PETRIFIED BONE BACK TO LIFE! MY MENTAL THERAPY HAS CURED THE MASTER!'

The disciples danced in joy, praising Madayan's psychological medicine, while Guru Paramartha walked thirty laps around the courtyard to ensure both legs were made of flesh.
moral: Treating an imaginary malady with drastic remedies cripples the healthy limb.

title: The Miracle Cow Dung and the Silver Coin
summary: A wandering charlatan alchemist visited the ashram, demonstrating a trick: by dropping a shiny silver rupee into a lump of fresh cow dung and muttering strange syllables, he ret...
full_text:
A wandering charlatan alchemist visited the ashram, demonstrating a trick: by dropping a shiny silver rupee into a lump of fresh cow dung and muttering strange syllables, he retrieved two shiny coins (having concealed the second coin in his palm).

He whispered to Guru Paramartha: 'Master, the dung of your sacred white cow Kamadhenu possesses latent alchemical properties! If you bury silver coins in her manure piles for three days during the full moon, the dung will gestate and double the silver!'

The alchemist departed, leaving the seed of greed planted in the Guru's mind.

Guru Paramartha called Matti: 'Matti, our ashram emergency fund contains twenty silver rupees! Collect twenty fresh piles of cow dung from Kamadhenu, insert one silver coin into the center of each pile, and guard the mounds for three days!'

Matti collected twenty fresh, steaming piles of cow dung, arranged them in neat rows in the backyard, and pressed a shiny silver coin into the heart of each heap.

The five disciples stood guard day and night with sticks, chasing away crows and chickens.

On the third morning, the Guru and his disciples assembled to harvest their doubled fortune.

'Dig into the alchemical mounds!' commanded the Guru. 'We should find forty silver rupees!'

The disciples plunged their bare hands into the dried, crusty manure piles, searching through the dung with eager fingers.

They searched the first pile: empty!
They searched the second pile: empty!
They searched all twenty piles, coating their arms, fingers, and clothes in filthy manure: not a single silver coin was found in any pile!

Matti wailed: 'The silver has vanished! Where are our forty coins?'

Madayan examined the trampled ground and discovered footprints leading from the garden fence: 'Master! A tragedy of reverse alchemy! The manure piles did not double the silver; they dissolved the silver into ethereal vapor!'

At that moment, the village sweepers passed the fence, jingling twenty silver coins in their pockets, laughing merrily. They had watched Matti bury the coins three nights earlier and had dug them up thirty minutes after the disciples fell asleep!

The Guru stood amidst the trampled manure piles, his hands filthy, his robes soiled, and his treasury empty.

Guru Paramartha delivered his philosophical conclusion: 'We have proved through empirical research that cow dung is exceptionally fertile for vegetables, but completely infertile for silver!'

The disciples spent the afternoon at the river with five bars of soap, scrubbing the alchemical failure from their hands.
moral: Searching for gold in manure piles leaves you with dirty hands and empty pockets.

title: The Feast of the Seven Pickles
summary: A wealthy patron sent a festival gift of seven glazed earthenware jars to the ashram, each containing a different variety of fiery, spicy South Indian pickle: lime pickle, mango...
full_text:
A wealthy patron sent a festival gift of seven glazed earthenware jars to the ashram, each containing a different variety of fiery, spicy South Indian pickle: lime pickle, mango pickle, ginger pickle, garlic pickle, citron pickle, green chili pickle, and fiery red avakaya pickle!

The jars were lined up on the kitchen shelf, glistening with red mustard oil and chili powder.

Guru Paramartha was ecstatic: 'Seven jars of divine digestive stimulants! Each represents one of the seven sacred planets!'

Madayan proposed a Philosophical Degustation Ceremony: 'Master, common people eat pickles with rice, which dilutes their celestial potency! To absorb the pure astral energy of the seven planets, we must taste each pickle in concentrated, pure spoonfuls, without a single grain of rice to weaken the impact!'

The Guru agreed: 'A noble scientific method! Bring the spoons!'

The Guru and his five disciples sat in a circle.

Matti took a large tablespoon of fiery red avakaya pickle and shoved it into his mouth.

Within two seconds, Matti's eyes bugged out of his head! His face turned the color of a ripe beet; tears gushed from his eyes, and his mouth began smoking like a chimney: 'GAHHH! WATER! MY TONGUE IS ON FIRE!'

Madayan scoffed: 'Matti lacks spiritual stamina! Observe how a philosopher absorbs the ginger pickle!'

Madayan took a heaping spoonful of spicy ginger pickle.

The intense, burning ginger and chili hit his throat like molten lead! Madayan choked, gagged, fell backward, and began slapping the floor with both hands, unable to breathe!

Peedan tasted the garlic; Asadan tasted the chili; Mudan tasted the citron!

Within sixty seconds, all five disciples were rolling on the floor, weeping, choking, gasping for breath, their mouths burning like volcanic craters!

Guru Paramartha, unwilling to be outdone by his disciples, took a large wooden ladle, dipped it into the green chili jar, and swallowed a massive mouthful!

The explosion in the Guru's throat was catastrophic!

He leaped three feet into the air, dropped his staff, clutched his throat with both hands, and let out a sound like a wounded steam boiler: 'HUUUU-SHHHH! FIRE! WATER! MY BELLY IS BURNING!'

The six philosophers rushed in wild panic to the garden well, fighting over the bucket! They drank gallons of water, plunged their heads into the trough, and stuffed handfuls of raw wet mud into their burning mouths to cool the flames!

For three days, the ashram was silent: six philosophers sat on their mats, unable to speak, their tongues swollen, their stomachs rumbling, living on cold curd rice.

The Guru recorded his medical evaluation: 'Note: The seven planets are remarkably hostile to the human esophagus when taken without yogurt.'
moral: Indulging in fiery pickles without rice burns the tongue and sets fire to the stomach.

title: The Water Pot That Whistled
summary: Guru Paramartha purchased a new, polished copper kettle fitted with a tight lid and a slender, curved pouring spout, designed for boiling herbal tea.
full_text:
Guru Paramartha purchased a new, polished copper kettle fitted with a tight lid and a slender, curved pouring spout, designed for boiling herbal tea.

One morning, Peedan filled the kettle with water, clamped the tight lid shut, and placed it upon a blazing hearth fire of tamarind wood.

As the water reached a rolling boil, the expanding steam built up high pressure inside the sealed copper chamber. Finding only the narrow, curved spout as an exit, the hot steam rushed through the nozzle with a high-pitched, piercing, musical whistle:

'WHEEEEE-EE-EE-EET!'

Peedan, who was peeling ginger, froze in terror!

The whistling grew louder and shriller: 'WHEEEEE-EET!'

Peedan dropped his knife, sprinted into the study hall, and dove behind the Guru's cot: 'MASTER! A DEMON HAS ENTERED THE COPPER POT! HE IS WHISTLING A WAR CHANT ON THE HEARTH!'

Guru Paramartha and his disciples crept into the kitchen, armed with iron fire tongs and wooden cudgels.

The kettle sat on the blazing coals, trembling slightly, whistling with ear-splitting intensity: 'WHEEEEEE-EET!'

Madayan analyzed the sound with grave occult expertise: 'That is the unmistakable whistling call of a Pisacha of the Air! He is using the copper kettle as an acoustic resonator to summon a storm upon our ashram!'

The Guru ordered: 'Smite the whistling demon before his storm breaks!'

Matti raised a heavy iron pestle, rushed forward, and struck the whistling kettle with all his might: SMASH!

The heavy blow crushed the copper kettle into a flat, deformed pancake! The trapped boiling water and scalding steam erupted sideways in a violent blast, spraying hot water over Matti's bare chest and legs!

Matti screamed, dropping his pestle and hopping across the room: 'THE DEMON BIT ME WITH SCALDING TEETH!'

The kettle was flattened, ruined, and silent.

Madayan pointed to the silent, dented copper lump with immense satisfaction: 'Observe, Master! The demon has been silenced! The pestle crushed his whistling throat!'

Guru Paramartha praised Matti's heroism, paid the blacksmith for a new pot, and spent the evening applying cooling aloe vera paste to Matti's scalded chest, proud of their triumph over the whistling tea kettle.
moral: Mistaking escaping steam for a whistling demon leads you to smash your own kettle.

title: The Stolen Slippers and the Muddy Trail
summary: Guru Paramartha owned a pair of new leather sandals, stitched by the village cobbler with red thread. One evening, after washing his feet at the well, he left them on the front ...
full_text:
Guru Paramartha owned a pair of new leather sandals, stitched by the village cobbler with red thread. One evening, after washing his feet at the well, he left them on the front veranda.

Next morning, the sandals were missing.

The Guru called his disciples: 'My red-stitched sandals have been stolen! Search the ground for the footprints of the thief!'

Matti and Madayan knelt in the soft dust outside the veranda. In the damp soil was a clear, distinct trail of human footprints: broad heel, five toes, heading away from the veranda steps.

'Aha!' shouted Madayan. 'The thief has left an undeniable trail of physical evidence! Follow the footprints!'

The five disciples and the Guru began following the trail.

The footprints led off the veranda, walked around the well, circled the mango tree, walked along the bamboo fence, turned through the vegetable garden, and led straight back to the veranda steps!

Matti was perplexed: 'The thief walked in a circle!'

Madayan examined the prints with forensic brilliance: 'Notice the depth of the heel impression! The thief was a heavy man with a slight limp in his right foot! When he reached the steps, he circled the tree a second time!'

The disciples followed the circular trail a second time: around the well, past the mango tree, through the fence, and back to the steps!

For forty-five minutes, the six philosophers marched in a circle around their own garden, following the footprints!

Finally, Peedan stopped and looked at Guru Paramartha's feet.

The Guru's feet were dusty and had a slight limp on the right side.

Peedan whispered: 'Master... place your foot in that footprint on the sand!'

The Guru placed his right foot into the track: it fit with absolute, microscopic perfection! Every toe, every line of the heel matched identically!

Madayan gasped in horror: 'BY THE GODS! THE THIEF WAS A SHAPE-SHIFTER WHO POSSESSED FEET IDENTICAL TO OUR MASTER'S! HE WAS THE GURU'S SPIRITUAL DOPPELGANGER!'

Matti, however, happened to look beneath the wooden cot on the veranda. There, pushed into the dark corner by the ashram cat, were the red-stitched sandals, completely safe and untouched!

The Guru had forgotten that he had walked around the garden in his bare feet the previous evening before going to bed!

Looking at the sandals, then at the circular tracks in the mud, Guru Paramartha cleared his throat with dignified gravity: 'A magnificent exercise in perimeter surveillance, my children! We have verified that our ashram security is impenetrable from all directions!'
moral: Following a circular trail of footprints leads you to arrest your own feet.

title: The Guru's New Spectacles
summary: An itinerant traveling merchant from the Dutch port of Cochin sold Guru Paramartha a pair of 'marvelous European reading spectacles' fitted with thick, powerful convex lenses fr...
full_text:
An itinerant traveling merchant from the Dutch port of Cochin sold Guru Paramartha a pair of 'marvelous European reading spectacles' fitted with thick, powerful convex lenses framed in brass.

The merchant claimed: 'These lenses reveal the hidden spiritual dimensions of reality!'

The Guru put on the spectacles.

Because the lenses were designed for extreme farsightedness, the entire world warped into a dizzying, distorted blur! Close objects appeared twenty times their size, while distant trees looked upside down!

The Guru took three staggering steps and bumped into a wooden post: 'OH! The post has expanded to the size of a mountain!'

Matti approached to assist him. Looking at Matti through the thick lenses, the Guru screamed in terror:

'HORROR! Matti, you have grown six feet wide! Your nose is the size of an elephant's trunk, and your ears are flapping like sails! An evil curse has mutated your flesh!'

Matti touched his face in panic: 'Master! Am I truly a monster?'

Madayan inspected the Guru's spectacles: 'Master, you are viewing the universe through the Lens of Cosmic Magnitude! To adjust your equilibrium, we must alter the environment to match your enlarged perception!'

The Guru tried to walk into the garden. Looking down at a tiny puddle of rainwater barely three inches wide, the distorted lenses magnified it into a raging, hundred-foot abyssal lake!

The Guru stopped at the edge of the puddle, trembling: 'Halt! We have reached the shores of the Pacific Ocean! Fetch a boat, or we will drown!'

Matti looked at the tiny three-inch puddle on the gravel: 'Master, it is barely three inches of water! Step across!'

The Guru shouted: 'Fool! Do you dare to challenge my optical perception? The water is thirty leagues deep!'

Asadan brought a twelve-foot bamboo ladder and laid it across the tiny three-inch puddle.

Guru Paramartha crawled across the ladder on his hands and knees with agonizing slowness, his knuckles white with terror, while the disciples cheered his heroic oceanic crossing!

When he reached the other side, the ashram cat trotted past and stepped right through the puddle, the water barely wetting its paws.

The Guru stared through his spectacles: 'Look at the giant feline sea monster walking upon the waves!'

At that moment, the village schoolmaster arrived. Seeing the Guru crawling across a ladder over a puddle, the schoolmaster gently took the brass spectacles from the Guru's face and looked through them: 'Good heavens! These are magnifying glasses for inspecting gemstones, not spectacles for walking!'

Without the spectacles, the world snapped back to normal. The Guru saw the three-inch puddle, the wooden post, and his normal disciples.

The Guru sighed, handed the spectacles to the schoolmaster, and remarked: 'The European lenses were fascinating, but truth is much easier to navigate without Dutch magnification!'
moral: Looking through distorted lenses makes the whole world appear upside down.

title: The Elephant That Slipped on the Soap
summary: Following their laundry day, Peedan left a large, slimy, wet bar of country laundry soap—made of beef tallow, caustic soda, and coconut oil—sitting right in the middle of the na...
full_text:
Following their laundry day, Peedan left a large, slimy, wet bar of country laundry soap—made of beef tallow, caustic soda, and coconut oil—sitting right in the middle of the narrow stone bridge that crossed the irrigation canal outside the ashram gate.

Ten minutes later, the royal temple elephant Airavata, carrying his mahout on his neck, came ambling across the stone bridge on his way to the river bath.

The massive, eight-ton beast placed his right front foot squarely onto the slimy bar of wet laundry soap!

The soap squirted out from beneath his foot like a watermelon seed!

The elephant's massive foot shot forward; his huge legs splayed sideways; his hind quarters slipped, and with a deafening, earth-shaking crash, the colossal beast sat down hard upon his rump on the stone bridge, nearly pitching the mahout into the canal!

The bridge groaned; the water splashed, and the stunned elephant sat in the middle of the bridge, trumpeting in bewildered embarrassment!

Seeing the mountain of a beast sitting like a dog on the bridge, Matti and Madayan rushed out.

Matti clapped his hands: 'Look, brother! The temple elephant has enrolled as a student! He is sitting cross-legged upon the bridge to meditate!'

The furious mahout scrambled down, waving his iron ankus: 'Meditation, you fool? He slipped on a bar of soap left by your ashram! Help me get this mountain onto his feet!'

The disciples attempted to hoist the eight-ton beast. Matti pulled the elephant's tail; Peedan lifted a leg; Madayan pushed from behind, shouting: 'ONE, TWO, THREE, HEAVE!'

The eight-ton elephant did not budge an inch.

Madayan devised an engineering solution: 'The Friction Restoration Technique! We must spread three bags of dry red chili powder beneath his hind legs to provide traction!'

The disciples scattered fiery chili powder beneath the sitting elephant's tail.

The pungent chili powder drifted into the elephant's sensitive tail and hindquarters.

The elephant let out an enraged, trumpet of volcanic fury! He scrambled to his feet in a single bound, swung his trunk, and chased the five disciples across the fields, spraying water and mud from the canal over the ashram walls!

The disciples dove into the haystack, hiding until the mahout led the irritated colossus away.

Guru Paramartha surveyed the trampled garden and delivered his verdict: 'Soap, my children, is designed for the linen of mortals, not for the promenade of pachyderms!'
moral: A tiny slippery surface can fell a colossus; do not leave soap where giants tread.

title: The Disciples Who Buried the Sun
summary: During a total solar eclipse, the afternoon sky darkened to eerie twilight. The birds fell silent in the trees; the air grew chill, and the stars appeared in the middle of the a...
full_text:
During a total solar eclipse, the afternoon sky darkened to eerie twilight. The birds fell silent in the trees; the air grew chill, and the stars appeared in the middle of the afternoon.

Guru Paramartha and his disciples gathered in the courtyard in absolute panic.

Matti wept: 'The Sun God has been slain by the demon Rahu! Darkness has conquered the earth!'

Madayan examined the darkened sky through a smoking shard of glass: 'The Sun has expired! His celestial body has fallen into the western hills! If the deceased solar orb is not buried with proper funerary rites, his ghost will haunt the cosmos and plunge us into eternal frost!'

The Guru nodded with profound liturgical solemnity: 'We must perform the funeral rites of the Sun God! Matti, dig a symbolic grave in the center of the courtyard!'

The disciples dug a deep pit in the middle of the courtyard.

They placed a round, golden brass plate inside the pit to represent the deceased Sun. They covered it with white silk, scattered marigold petals, and poured libations of milk into the hole.

Guru Paramartha stood over the pit, chanting ancient funeral mantras: 'O glorious Sun! You shone upon the good and the evil; now rest in peace within our courtyard!'

They shoveled the mud back into the pit, patting down the earth and planting a sacred tulsi shrub atop the mound.

The eclipse concluded; the moon moved past the solar disc, and brilliant, blazing sunlight flooded the earth once again!

The disciples looked up at the blazing sun shining in the sky, then down at the fresh grave in the courtyard.

Matti was paralyzed with terror: 'MASTER! THE SUN HAS RISEN FROM THE DEAD! HE IS WALKING OUT OF HIS GRAVE!'

Madayan gasped in awe: 'A celestial ghost! That is not the real Sun; that is the solar phantom, returning to inspect his own funeral!'

The disciples ran into the study, locked the doors, and peeked through the blinds, trembling in terror at the 'ghostly sun' shining outside!

They remained locked in the dark room for three days, surviving on dry biscuits, refusing to look upon the 'spectral light.'

On the fourth morning, a cheerful vegetable vendor knocked at the gate, delivering fresh radishes. Seeing the holy men peering through the shutters like frightened owls, the vendor laughed: 'Why are you hiding from the glorious morning sun?'

Guru Paramartha whispered: 'Is that the real Sun or his ghost?'

The vendor laughed till tears rolled down his cheeks: 'The eclipse ended four days ago, you old scholars! The Sun never died!'

The Guru emerged, blinking in the bright light, and remarked with dignified composure: 'Our funerary mantras were so spiritually potent that they resurrected the solar deity in four days! Praise be to our liturgy!'
moral: Fearing the sunset as a permanent burial of light reveals ignorance of the morning dawn.

title: The Bell That Wouldn't Ring
summary: Following the incident with the temple bell, Guru Paramartha purchased a small, bronze prayer bell to summon his disciples to morning prayers at five o'clock.
full_text:
Following the incident with the temple bell, Guru Paramartha purchased a small, bronze prayer bell to summon his disciples to morning prayers at five o'clock.

The Guru instructed Matti: 'Matti, ring this bell every morning at five o'clock sharp, but ensure you ring it gently so that it does not disturb my delicate morning slumber!'

Matti took the bell and pondered the problem: 'How can I ring a loud bronze bell to awaken the disciples, without disturbing the Master who sleeps in the very next room?'

Madayan provided the acoustic solution: 'The Soft-Strike Clapper Modification! Wrap the brass clapper in ten layers of thick sheep's wool, coat the outside of the bronze bell with soft cow dung, and strike it upon a feather pillow! Thus will the chime be soft as a whisper!'

Matti wrapped the clapper in ten layers of wool, plastered the bell with cow dung, and placed it upon a feather pillow.

Next morning, at five o'clock, Matti sat beside the Guru's bed and began ringing the bell with all his might:

He shook the handle vigorously. The wool-wrapped clapper struck the dung-coated bronze upon the feather pillow:

THUMP... THUFF... THUFF...

The sound was as quiet as a moth fluttering its wings against silk.

Matti rang for forty-five minutes, sweating with exertion.

Guru Paramartha slept peacefully until nine o'clock. When he finally awoke, the sun was high in the sky.

The Guru sat up, furious: 'Matti! Why did you not ring the prayer bell at five o'clock? We have missed our morning prayers!'

Matti held up the bell, exhausted: 'Master! I rang the bell for forty-five minutes without stopping! My arm is aching!'

The Guru took the bell, saw the wool, the cow dung, and the pillow, and shook his head in speechless dismay: 'Matti, a bell that makes no sound is not a bell; it is a bronze dumbbell!'

Matti beamed: 'Yes, Master; but observe how peacefully you slept!'
moral: Wrapping a hammer in wool to muffle the blow ensures that the bell remains silent.

title: The Magic Mustard Seed of Invisibility
summary: A clever wandering street conjurer visited the village fair, selling 'Magical Himalayan Mustard Seeds of Invisibility' for four copper coins each.
full_text:
A clever wandering street conjurer visited the village fair, selling 'Magical Himalayan Mustard Seeds of Invisibility' for four copper coins each.

He told Matti: 'Place this sacred seed beneath your tongue, and you will become completely invisible to all mortal eyes! You can walk through royal palaces and take whatever you desire!'

Matti paid four coppers, placed the black seed beneath his tongue, and walked back to the ashram.

Entering the room where Guru Paramartha was reading, Matti stood before his master, completely silent, smiling with smug, invisible superiority.

The Guru looked up from his book: 'Matti, why are you standing there grinning like a village idiot? Go fetch my tea!'

Matti was stunned: 'Master! Can you see me?'

The Guru snapped: 'Of course I can see you! You are six feet tall, broad as a bullock, and wearing a dirty yellow dhoti! Are you mad?'

Matti concluded: 'The seed requires activation through a mantra!'

Madayan helped Matti activate the seed with three hours of chanting.

Matti then resolved to test his invisibility in the village bazaar. Placing the seed firmly beneath his tongue, he walked boldly into the shop of the town's most muscular, short-tempered sweetmeat vendor.

Believing he was completely invisible, Matti reached out his hand and scooped five large, dripping, golden jalebis right from the cooling tray, stuffing two into his mouth!

The vendor, standing two feet away, stared in dumbfounded disbelief as a grown man walked up to his stall in broad daylight, grabbed his jalebis, and began chewing them with a triumphant grin!

The vendor did not ask philosophical questions. He picked up his heavy wooden sugar-crushing pestle and brought it down across Matti's back with a deafening CRACK: THWACK!

Matti shrieked in shock, dropping the jalebis: 'AI-YO! WHY DO YOU BEAT ME?'

The vendor roared: 'Because you are stealing my sweets, you brazen thief!'

Matti spat out the mustard seed: 'Wait! Can you see me?'

The vendor brought the pestle down across Matti's ribs: 'I can see you clearly enough to break your bones, you rogue!'

Matti sprinted through the bazaar, pursued by the vendor, taking three more blows before diving through the ashram gate.

Collapsing before Guru Paramartha, rubbing his bruised back, Matti wept: 'The invisibility seed was counterfeit, Master!'

The Guru sighed: 'The seed was real, Matti; but your body was unfortunately too solid for the magic!'
moral: Believing you are invisible when you walk in broad daylight invites the rod of truth.

title: The Donkey's Horoscope
summary: Following the donkey's failed wedding and flight, the ancient beast was found grazing in a neighboring ditch and returned to the ashram.
full_text:
Following the donkey's failed wedding and flight, the ancient beast was found grazing in a neighboring ditch and returned to the ashram.

Guru Paramartha was troubled by the animal's erratic behavior: 'The donkey must have been born under an inauspicious planetary conjunction! We must cast his horoscope to determine his auspicious days for carrying laundry!'

The Guru sent Madayan to the village astrologer with a basket of rice and two silver coins to cast the donkey's horoscope.

The astrologer, who enjoyed humor, asked: 'What was the exact hour and minute of the beast's birth?'

Madayan replied: 'He was born seven years ago on a Tuesday, at the exact moment when the village roosters crowed and an old woman sneezed in the next street!'

The astrologer drew complex geometric diagrams upon his slate, moved cowrie shells, and declared:

'The donkey was born under the sign of Taurus the Bull, with Saturn in the house of braying! His chart reveals that on Mondays, he must not carry red bundles; on Wednesdays, he must face east while eating grass, and on Fridays, he must be addressed with honorific titles, or he will kick his handlers into the canal!'

Madayan returned to the ashram with the written palm-leaf horoscope.

The Guru read the document with awe: 'Henceforth, on Fridays, the beast must be addressed as Sri Sri Gardabha Swami!'

On the following Friday, Matti approached the donkey with a heavy bundle of laundry: 'Revered Sri Sri Gardabha Swami, deign to accept this humble bundle upon your sacred back!'

The donkey, seeing the heavy load, flattened his ears, kicked backward with both hooves, and struck Matti in the knee, knocking him into the well-trough!

Madayan consulted the palm leaf: 'Ah! Look at the planetary transits! The moon entered an eclipse house five minutes ago! Sri Sri Gardabha Swami was astrologically provoked!'

The Guru nodded with profound respect: 'A beast of such astrological sensitivity must not be burdened with laundry; let Matti carry the bundle on his head today!'

And Matti carried fifty pounds of wet clothes to the river on his head, while the donkey grazed peacefully under the shade of the mango tree, braying at the stars.
moral: Consulting the stars for an ass produces predictions suited only for a stable.

title: The Broken Rice Pot and the Hungry Cat
summary: A large pot of fragrant, golden sweet pongal rice, cooked with jaggery, cashews, and ghee, was cooling on the kitchen counter for the Guru's evening meal.
full_text:
A large pot of fragrant, golden sweet pongal rice, cooked with jaggery, cashews, and ghee, was cooling on the kitchen counter for the Guru's evening meal.

A hungry stray village dog was seen pacing outside the kitchen window.

Guru Paramartha called Peedan: 'Peedan, guard that pot of sweet pongal from the stray dog! Do not let a single canine whisker enter the kitchen!'

Peedan stood guard at the door armed with a broom.

Presently, the sleek, fat ashram cat strolled into the kitchen, jumped onto the counter, and began licking the sweet pongal from the rim of the pot.

Peedan watched the cat with peaceful indifference.

Matti entered and gasped: 'Peedan! The cat is eating the Master's pongal!'

Peedan replied with calm, literal self-defense: 'The Master strictly commanded me: "Guard the pot from the stray dog!" He said not a word about the cat! The cat is a feline; she has a constitutional right to eat!'

The cat, encouraged by this legal protection, plunged her head deep into the pot, eating the cashews and jaggery.

Matti shouted: 'Chase her away, Peedan!'

Peedan waved his broom gently: 'Shoo, sister cat!'

Startled by the broom, the cat leaped out of the pot, caught her claws in the woven coir mat beneath the vessel, and dragged the heavy clay pot off the counter!

The pot tumbled off the ledge, struck the hard stone floor, and shattered into twenty pieces!

Ten pounds of hot, golden, sweet pongal rice spilled across the mud floor, mingling with dirt, broken clay shards, and cat hairs!

The stray dog outside the window saw the disaster, slipped under the bamboo gate, and together with the cat, feasted merrily upon the spilled rice on the floor!

Guru Paramartha entered the kitchen, surveyed the shattered clay and the feasting animals, and raised his staff in speechless grief.

Peedan smiled with pride: 'Master, celebrate my fidelity! The stray dog did not touch the pot while it was on the counter; he ate only from the floor after the cat broke it!'

The Guru lowered his staff, stroked his beard, and delivered his verdict: 'Peedan, you are an impeccable lawyer, but a catastrophic cook! We shall dine on dry bread tonight in honor of your jurisprudence!'
moral: Guarding the milk from the dog by giving it to the cat saves nothing for the master.
