title: The River That Forgot Its Own Name
summary: Arriving at the banks of a winding, scenic river during their travels, Guru Paramartha and his disciples sat on the grassy bank to rest.
full_text:
Arriving at the banks of a winding, scenic river during their travels, Guru Paramartha and his disciples sat on the grassy bank to rest.

The Guru looked at the water and asked: 'What is the sacred name of this flowing stream, Madayan?'

Madayan consulted his mental atlas: 'Some maps call it the Cheyyar; other traditions call it the Palar, while ancient scriptures name it the Vegavati!'

Matti stroked his chin: 'If the maps give conflicting names, how does the river know which name to answer to?'

Madayan expounded his Theory of Nominal Amnesia: 'A river is in perpetual flux! The water flowing past our feet this second was in the mountains ten miles away an hour ago! Because the water never stays in one place, the river suffers from chronic memory loss! It has forgotten its own name!'

The Guru nodded with profound concern: 'A tragic metaphysical condition! A river without an identity cannot flow with spiritual stability! We must remind the river of its sacred name!'

'How shall we remind it?' asked Peedan.

Madayan instructed: 'We must assemble along the bank and shout its true name in unison into the current three hundred times! When the water hears its name repeated with philosophical authority, its memory will return!'

The five disciples and Guru Paramartha lined up along the water's edge, cupped their hands around their mouths, and began shouting with all their might into the river:

'YOUR NAME IS PALAR! HEARKEN, O WATER! YOU ARE THE PALAR! P-A-L-A-R!'

For two hours, under the hot sun, the six philosophers shouted at the river: 'PALAR! PALAR! PALAR!'

A passing village ferryman rowing his wooden boat halted his oars, staring in utter amazement at the shouting holy men: 'Why are you screaming at the river, masters?'

Guru Paramartha replied with dignity: 'We are reminding the river of its forgotten name!'

The ferryman chuckled: 'The river cares nothing for names, old man! Whether you call it Palar or mud, it flows to the sea, carries my boat, and waters the rice fields! Step aboard if you want to cross, and stop barking at the water!'

The Guru turned to his disciples and observed: 'The ferryman represents the base, unlettered utilitarian view of geography; but our linguistic baptism has elevated the current!'

They boarded the boat, crossed to the other side, and marched onward, proud of having restored the river's memory.
moral: Debating the philosophical name of a river does not prevent the water from wetting your feet.

title: The Guru's Funeral While Still Alive
summary: After eating three bowls of cold curd rice seasoned with mustard seeds, Guru Paramartha fell into an unusually deep, heavy afternoon slumber on his veranda cot. His breathing wa...
full_text:
After eating three bowls of cold curd rice seasoned with mustard seeds, Guru Paramartha fell into an unusually deep, heavy afternoon slumber on his veranda cot. His breathing was so slow and shallow that his belly scarcely moved, and his limbs felt cold to the touch.

Matti approached to awaken him for evening prayers: 'Master! Master!'

The Guru did not stir.

Matti pinched his ear; the Guru merely snored softly.

Matti shrieked in hysterical grief: 'AI-YO! DISASTER! OUR MASTER HAS DEPARTED FOR THE OTHER WORLD! HE IS NO MORE!'

The five disciples gathered around the cot, beating their chests and wailing in chorus: 'OH, OUR REVERED PRECEPTOR! THE SUN OF PHILOSOPHY HAS SET!'

Madayan examined the Guru's cold toes and consulted an ancient palm-leaf manuscript: 'According to the treatise on clinical expiration: "When the limbs are cold as clay and the eyes remain shut against loud weeping, the soul has dissolved its connection to the physical vessel!" The Master is officially, philosophically deceased! We must conduct the funeral procession before the stars turn inauspicious!'

The disciples built a bamboo funeral bier, laid the sleeping Guru upon it, tied him securely with straw cords, and covered him with white cotton cloths, showering his beard with yellow marigold petals.

Lifting the heavy bier upon their shoulders, the five disciples marched toward the village cremation ground, chanting mournfully: 'GOVINDA! GOVINDA! THE MASTER HAS EMBARKED UPON HIS CELESTIAL JOURNEY!'

The bumpy, swinging motion of the bier, the loud shouting of the disciples, and the afternoon breeze gradually awakened Guru Paramartha from his deep sleep.

He opened his eyes, smelled the marigolds, felt the straw ropes binding his arms, and saw the treetops swinging past above his head!

Sitting up on the bier, the bewildered Guru shouted: 'WHAT IS THIS? WHERE ARE YOU CARRYING ME?'

Matti, marching at the front, looked back over his shoulder and shrieked in terror: 'MASTER! DO NOT SPEAK! YOU ARE DECEASED! THE SCRIPTURE SAYS YOU ARE DEAD!'

The Guru roared: 'You fool! I am alive! Untie these ropes and put me down!'

Madayan reprimanded his master with scholarly severity: 'Revered Master, it is unseemly for a great philosopher to dispute his own medical diagnosis! You exhibited every clinical symptom of mortality! A ghost who speaks on his own funeral bier creates dreadful civic confusion! Lie down and accept your dissolution with dignity!'

The Guru struggled against the straw ropes, shouting: 'I AM NOT A GHOST! I AM HUNGRY! I WANT RICE!'

As they passed the village pond, where several washermen were beating laundry, the Guru shouted to them: 'HELP! MY OWN DISCIPLES ARE CARRYING ME TO THE CREMATION FIRE!'

The washermen dropped their clothes, ran to the road, and stopped the procession.

The chief washerman cut the straw ropes with his knife: 'He is breathing, shouting, and red-faced! He is completely alive, you madmen!'

Guru Paramartha scrambled off the bier, seized a heavy bamboo stick from the litter, and chased his five disciples across the fields, shouting: 'I will demonstrate how alive I am upon your shoulders!'

Madayan, running for his life, called back: 'A magnificent physiological resurrection, Master! Our funeral procession was therapeutic!'
moral: Believing a medical formula over living breath conducts a funeral for the breathing.

title: The Stolen Mustard Greens and the Crow's Nest
summary: The ashram kitchen garden possessed a tender, lush bed of green mustard leaves, cultivated carefully by Matti for the Guru's herbal broth.
full_text:
The ashram kitchen garden possessed a tender, lush bed of green mustard leaves, cultivated carefully by Matti for the Guru's herbal broth.

Every morning, Matti discovered that twenty prime leaves had been neatly snipped off and carried away.

Matti reported the crime to Madayan: 'A thief is plundering our mustard patch!'

Madayan inspected the garden soil. Because the ground was dry, no clear footprints were visible, but high in the branches of the nearby neem tree, a pair of black crows were busy building a large nest of twigs.

Madayan pointed upward with forensic certainty: 'Look at those aerial architects! Crows are notorious thieves of shiny objects and green foliage! They are stealing our mustard leaves to cushion their nest!'

Matti was indignant: 'We must recover our stolen greens from their tree!'

Madayan devised an Aerial Eviction Plan: 'We will climb the tree, confiscate the nest, and retrieve our mustard greens!'

Matti took a long bamboo pole and began climbing the rough bark of the neem tree.

As Matti approached the high bough, the two parent crows, defending their home, began shrieking alarm calls: 'CAW! CAW! CAW!'

Within two minutes, thirty angry woodland crows darkened the sky! They dive-bombed Matti, pecking at his bald crown, pulling his hair, and scratching his ears with their sharp talons!

Matti shrieked in terror, lost his footing on the slippery branch, and tumbled twenty feet down into the middle of the thorny brinjal patch below!

While Matti groaned among the thorns, bleeding from crow scratches, the ashram cow Kamadhenu reached her head over the low garden fence and calmly chewed off thirty more tender mustard leaves right before their eyes!

Peedan gasped: 'Look! The cow was the thief all along!'

Madayan shook his head in philosophical pity: 'The cow was merely an accessory after the fact; the crows were the intellectual masterminds!'

The Guru applied turmeric paste to Matti's scratches, recording in his diary: 'Note: Avian architects defend their aerial real estate with formidable air-to-ground tactics.'
moral: Blaming aerial birds for garden theft leaves the real thief feasting in your kitchen.

title: The Mirror in the Well - Second Investigation
summary: Six months after the rescue of the Moon from the well, Guru Paramartha stood by the garden well at noon. Looking down into the dark water, the bright midday sun illuminated the ...
full_text:
Six months after the rescue of the Moon from the well, Guru Paramartha stood by the garden well at noon. Looking down into the dark water, the bright midday sun illuminated the surface, reflecting his own face with crystal clarity.

The Guru stared: 'Look! Another venerable, silver-bearded sage lives at the bottom of our well! He wears a yellow shawl and watches me with profound spiritual curiosity!'

The Guru summoned his disciples: 'Children, a holy ascetic has taken up residence in our aquatic depths! We must converse with him on the nature of reality!'

Matti leaned over the rim and shouted down the stone shaft: 'REVERED SAGE OF THE DEPTHS! GREETINGS FROM GURU PARAMARTHA!'

The deep, echo-chamber of the circular masonry wall immediately echoed back with hollow resonance: 'GREETINGS FROM GURU PARAMARTHA!'

Matti gasped in awe: 'He answers! He speaks our master's name with profound reverence!'

Madayan shouted down: 'WHAT IS YOUR PHILOSOPHICAL DOCTRINE?'

The well echoed: 'PHILOSOPHICAL DOCTRINE!'

Madayan turned to the Guru with shining eyes: 'He belongs to the Echo School of Veda! He repeats the divine Word!'

The Guru decided to test his hospitality: 'Are you thirsty, holy brother? Shall we lower a pitcher of buttermilk?'

The well echoed: 'BUTTERMILK!'

Peedan lowered a large clay pitcher filled with sweet buttermilk down the well on a rope.

When the pitcher reached the surface, Peedan jerked the cord to offer it. The heavy clay pot struck the rocky wall, shattered to pieces, and twenty pints of white buttermilk poured into the water, clouding the well like milk!

The reflection of the Guru dissolved in the white liquid.

Matti peered down and cheered: 'He drank it! He drank the entire pitcher of buttermilk in a single gulp, and turned the entire lake white with spiritual bliss!'

Guru Paramartha nodded in deep satisfaction: 'A thirsty scholar indeed! May his meditation in our well be blessed!'

And for three days, the ashram drank white buttermilk-water, rejoicing in the presence of their aquatic colleague.
moral: A reflection remains an illusion, whether it wears silver or yellow silk.

title: The Five Disciples and the Elephant's Trunk
summary: While visiting the temple festival in Madurai, the five disciples stood near the tethered royal elephant, admiring its colossal limbs, broad ears, and long, flexible trunk.
full_text:
While visiting the temple festival in Madurai, the five disciples stood near the tethered royal elephant, admiring its colossal limbs, broad ears, and long, flexible trunk.

Matti, who loved anatomical debate, asked: 'Brothers, is the trunk of an elephant a hand, an arm, a nose, or a fifth leg?'

Madayan expounded his Multi-Functional Organ Theory: 'According to Vedic zoology, the trunk is an elastic human arm grafted onto a pachyderm! Because it possesses finger-like lobes at the tip, it is capable of signing documents, picking flowers, and embracing friends!'

Peedan was fascinated: 'Can an elephant shake hands in friendship?'

'Of course!' declared Madayan. 'A handshake is the universal gesture of brotherhood! Matti, step forward and shake the elephant's hand!'

Matti approached the massive beast. Standing before the curling trunk, Matti smiled with courtly warmth, extended his right hand, and said: 'Greetings, noble pachyderm brother! I offer you the hand of friendship from Guru Paramartha's ashram!'

The elephant, however, had spent the morning eating ripe, sticky jaggery balls, and its trunk was coated in sweet sugar residue. Smelling salt on Matti's fingers and mistaking his hand for a sugarcane stalk, the elephant wrapped its powerful, muscular trunk around Matti's wrist, curled it tight, and lifted the terrified disciple four feet into the air!

Matti dangled above the ground, screaming in panic: 'AI-YO! HE SHAKES TOO HARD! HE HAS CAUGHT MY ARM IN AN IRON PYTHON!'

Madayan shouted instructions from a safe distance: 'Return the greeting, Matti! Squeeze back with brotherhood!'

Matti wept: 'I cannot squeeze back! He is lifting me toward his mouth!'

Peedan rushed forward and tried to tickle the elephant's knee; Asadan waved his palm leaf, and Mudan pulled Matti's legs!

Annoyed by the noisy crowd dangling from his trunk, the elephant casually swung his trunk sideways and hurled Matti across the temple yard!

Matti flew through the air and landed squarely in the middle of a vendor's cart loaded with soft, ripe, mushy jackfruits!

Yellow fruit pulp, sticky seeds, and sweet syrup exploded across Matti's face and clothes, cushioning his fall completely!

The five disciples rushed over, pulled Matti from the mush, and wiped fruit from his ears.

Madayan nodded with profound medical satisfaction: 'A magnificent diplomatic success! The elephant shook your hand, lifted you in honor, and deposited you in an abundance of sweet fruits!'

Spitting jackfruit seeds from his mouth, Matti groaned: 'Next time, Madayan, you may shake hands with the elephant's tail instead!'
moral: Mistaking a nose for a hand leads you into the giant's powerful grip.

title: The Scribe Who Wrote on Water
summary: The ashram was out of dried palm leaves, the customary material for inscribing sacred texts with an iron stylus.
full_text:
The ashram was out of dried palm leaves, the customary material for inscribing sacred texts with an iron stylus.

Guru Paramartha, inspired by a sudden flash of philosophical insight, summoned his scribe, Madayan: 'Madayan, an immortal thought has entered my mind regarding the transient nature of the cosmos! Fetch a stylus and record my words immediately before the inspiration evaporates!'

Madayan searched the shed, but no palm leaves remained.

The Guru became frantic: 'The thought is slipping from my memory! We must record it upon some receptive surface!'

Madayan pointed to the stone basin of clear water in the courtyard: 'Master! Water is the most receptive element in creation! It yields to the lightest touch without resistance! Inscribe your divine thought upon the water!'

The Guru agreed: 'A sublime idea! Fluid thoughts require a fluid medium!'

Madayan took a sharp iron stylus, dipped it into the water basin, and leaned over the surface.

The Guru began dictating: 'Chapter One: The Universe is an Illusion born of Maya...'

Madayan moved the iron point through the water with intense, rapid strokes: writing letters, words, and flourishes upon the surface!

The stylus churned the water, creating tiny ripples that smoothed out into flat calm the instant the point moved on.

Madayan wrote for forty-five minutes, sweating with scholarly zeal, filling 'six pages of water' with the Guru's discourse.

At last, the Guru paused: 'Now, Madayan, read back what you have inscribed, so that I may verify the syntax!'

Madayan looked down into the water basin.

The water was crystal clear, flat as glass, reflecting only Madayan's own sweating forehead. Not a single letter, mark, or scratch remained visible!

Madayan stared in dismay: 'Master! The ink has vanished! The letters have dissolved!'

Peedan examined the basin: 'Did you use indelible water-ink, Madayan?'

Madayan delivered his profound metaphysical evaluation: 'The water was so profoundly enlightened by the Master's discourse that it internalized the philosophy into its molecular essence! The words are no longer on the surface; they have achieved liberation in the depths!'

The Guru nodded in awe: 'Drink the water, disciples, and absorb the philosophy directly into your bloodstreams!'

The five disciples dipped brass cups into the basin, drank the water with reverent gulps, and sat on the veranda, feeling intensely enlightened.
moral: Inscribing records upon flowing water ensures that history vanishes with the current.

title: The Donkey's Lost Shadow
summary: On a scorching summer day, when the sun reached its absolute zenith in the heavens, Guru Paramartha and his disciples were traveling across an open, treeless plain with their fa...
full_text:
On a scorching summer day, when the sun reached its absolute zenith in the heavens, Guru Paramartha and his disciples were traveling across an open, treeless plain with their faithful gray donkey.

The heat was oppressive, and the sun beat straight down from the middle of the sky.

Matti happened to look beneath the donkey's belly. Because the sun was directly overhead, the donkey's shadow was compressed into a tiny, four-inch patch directly beneath its hooves, completely hidden by its body!

Matti shrieked in horror: 'MASTER! A DEMONIC CALAMITY! OUR NOBLE DONKEY HAS LOST HIS SHADOW!'

The Guru and disciples halted. They walked around the beast: from the left, no shadow; from the right, no shadow; from behind, no shadow!

Madayan turned pale with astrological dread: 'In occult treatises, when a living creature loses its shadow, it signifies that its soul has been stolen by the Lord of Death! Within three hours, the beast will turn into a zombie and bite our throats!'

The Guru was terrified: 'How can the shadow be restored to its rightful owner?'

Madayan expounded his Shadow Reattachment Ceremony: 'We must supply the beast with an artificial shadow until his natural shadow returns from the other world! We will drape five black woolen blankets over his back, tie them beneath his belly, and hang black umbrellas from his ears!'

The disciples draped five heavy, suffocating black horse blankets over the poor donkey, tied them with ropes, and opened two black umbrellas, tying them to the animal's halter.

The temperature beneath the five black blankets under the blazing noon sun reached boiling point!

The suffocating, sweating donkey stood for three minutes, his eyes rolling in frantic distress.

Then, with an enraged, desperate bray of rebellion, the beast kicked out with all four hooves, bucked like a mad bull, threw off the black blankets, trampled the umbrellas to splinters, and bolted across the plain toward a shady banyan tree half a mile away!

Standing beneath the spreading banyan boughs, where cool shade covered the earth, the donkey stopped, panting contentedly.

The disciples ran across the field, arriving out of breath.

Looking beneath the tree, Matti saw a massive, cool, dark shadow spreading twenty yards around the beast!

Matti cheered in ecstatic triumph: 'A MIRACLE! THE SHADOW HAS RETURNED! AND IT HAS GROWN TWENTY TIMES LARGER THAN BEFORE!'

Guru Paramartha stroked the donkey's nose with deep reverence: 'Our blankets have cured his soul; behold the magnificent expansion of his shadow!'
moral: Looking for an animal's shadow at high noon makes you believe the beast has lost its soul.

title: The Broken Earthen Pot and the Silver Spoon
summary: A clay cooking pot containing black bean soup had burnt on the kitchen hearth, and the dried bean crust was stuck like rock-hard cement to the bottom of the pot.
full_text:
A clay cooking pot containing black bean soup had burnt on the kitchen hearth, and the dried bean crust was stuck like rock-hard cement to the bottom of the pot.

Matti tried to scrape it with a wooden stick, but the wood splintered.

Guru Paramartha remembered his sole family heirloom: an antique, delicate silver spoon with a carved peacock handle, inherited from his grandfather.

The Guru handed the spoon to Matti: 'Take this solid silver instrument, Matti; its metal is noble and unyielding! Scrape the burnt crust from the clay pot!'

Matti took the delicate silver spoon, placed the tip beneath the rock-hard burnt crust, and applied his full weight to the handle to pry the crust loose!

The fragile, soft silver of the antique spoon bent like a banana!

Matti pressed harder: with a sharp SNAP!, the carved peacock handle sheared off, and the silver bowl broke in two!

Matti wailed: 'The silver spoon has broken! Our Master's heirloom is ruined!'

Madayan examined the broken silver pieces and the cheap, two-copper clay pot:

'Grieve not, Matti! The problem is purely mechanical! The silver was too soft for the task! To repair the silver spoon, we must fuse the metal together with the burnt bean crust!'

Madayan placed the broken silver pieces back into the clay pot, added water, and boiled the pot over a roaring fire for two hours, believing the silver would melt and weld itself!

Under the intense heat of the dry hearth, the cheap earthen pot cracked, broke in two, and dumped boiling water, bean sludge, and the broken silver spoon into the burning coals!

When the ashes were sifted, they retrieved two twisted, blackened, melted lumps of silver and a heap of broken clay sherds.

Guru Paramartha surveyed the wreckage with philosophical detachment: 'We have learned today that silver and clay possess incompatible karmic destinies; let us eat boiled bananas henceforth!'
moral: Using a delicate silver spoon as a pry bar breaks the silver to save the mud.

title: The Disciples Who Guarded the Firewood
summary: Winter approached, and Guru Paramartha purchased an enormous cartload of dried tamarind firewood for five silver rupees, stacking it neatly in the backyard to last through the r...
full_text:
Winter approached, and Guru Paramartha purchased an enormous cartload of dried tamarind firewood for five silver rupees, stacking it neatly in the backyard to last through the rainy season.

Hearing that village thieves were stealing firewood by night, the Guru assigned Asadan and Mudan to guard the woodpile: 'Watch this firewood with your lives! Do not let a single stick be taken by cold thieves!'

The two disciples stood sentry beside the woodpile, armed with bamboo sticks.

By two o'clock in the morning, a freezing northern wind swept across the plain. The temperature dropped, and a heavy frost coated the grass.

Asadan's teeth chattered: 'Mudan! I am freezing to death! My fingers are numb, and my feet have turned to ice! If we freeze, who will guard the firewood?'

Mudan shivered: 'True, brother! A dead guard cannot protect property! We must warm ourselves!'

Asadan looked at the colossal stack of dry tamarind wood beside them: 'Look! Here are fifty bundles of dry firewood! Why should we freeze when warmth is at our fingertips? Let us pull out ten sticks and light a small, comforting campfire!'

They pulled ten thick logs from the pile, lit them with an ember, and warmed their frozen hands over the cheerful blaze.

After an hour, the fire burned low.

'Add five more logs!' said Mudan.

By four o'clock, the wind grew fiercer. 'Add ten more logs!' said Asadan.

To maintain their 'vigilant warmth,' the two disciples continuously fed logs from the pile into their roaring campfire. Log after log, bundle after bundle was thrown onto the blaze!

By sunrise, the two guards were sitting before a magnificent, roaring mountain of glowing embers, warm, comfortable, and sweating pleasantly!

Guru Paramartha walked into the backyard to inspect the woodpile.

He stopped in utter disbelief.

The colossal cartload of tamarind firewood was completely gone! In its place sat a mountain of white ashes, while Asadan and Mudan sat happily toasting sweet potatoes over the coals!

'WHERE IS MY FIREWOOD?' roared the Guru.

Asadan smiled with triumphant fidelity: 'Master, rejoice! Not a single stick was stolen by thieves! We burned every single log ourselves to keep warm so we could guard the pile with vigilance!'

The Guru dropped his staff, clutched his temples, and wept for his five silver rupees, while Madayan praised the guards' unshakeable devotion to duty.
moral: Burning the firewood to keep warm while guarding the wood leaves an empty stack at dawn.

title: The Sacred Mango of Immortality
summary: A wandering beggar with matted hair told Matti a secret legend: 'In the royal orchard grows an ancient tree that produces the Amrita-Phala—The Mango of Immortality! Whoever eats...
full_text:
A wandering beggar with matted hair told Matti a secret legend: 'In the royal orchard grows an ancient tree that produces the Amrita-Phala—The Mango of Immortality! Whoever eats of it shall never grow old, nor suffer disease, nor die!'

Matti's heart burned with devotion: 'I must secure this fruit for our beloved Guru!'

Matti crept into the royal orchard at dusk. Beneath an old, gnarled tree, he found a solitary mango lying in the mud. It was black, shriveled, covered in white mold, and smelled of fermenting vinegar—having fallen from the tree weeks earlier and rotted in the ditch.

Matti picked it up with awe: 'Notice its ancient, blackened rind! Only a fruit of extreme antiquity could possess such concentrated spiritual potency!'

Matti wrapped the rotten mango in a clean silk handkerchief and carried it to the ashram.

Presenting it to Guru Paramartha, Matti proclaimed: 'Master! I have secured the Amrita-Phala! Eat this sacred fruit, and you shall live for ten thousand years!'

The Guru unwrapped the silk. A foul, sour stench of rotting fruit filled the room. The mango was soft, black, and leaking brown liquid.

The Guru hesitated: 'Matti... it smells remarkably decayed!'

Madayan intervened with philosophical authority: 'True immortality transcends conventional olfactory aesthetics! To the mortal nose, the nectar of liberation appears rotten, because mortality cannot comprehend eternal life! Eat it with faith, Master!'

The Guru held his nose, opened his mouth, and swallowed a large bite of the rotten, fermenting fruit!

The foul, acidic slime hit his stomach like poison!

Within ten minutes, Guru Paramartha turned pale green. Violent, explosive stomach cramps seized his belly; he dropped to the floor, rolling in agony, vomiting and clutching his abdomen!

The disciples panicked: 'THE NECTAR IS EXPELING HIS MORTALITY WITH VIOLENCE!'

The village physician was summoned in haste. The physician administered castor oil, bitter ginger decoctions, and salt water, purging the Guru's stomach until midnight.

Lying pale and exhausted upon his cot, Guru Paramartha whispered in a weak, trembling voice: 'Matti...'

'Yes, Master?' wept Matti.

'If you ever bring me another fruit of immortality,' wheezed the Guru, 'I will feed it to you first, and watch you live for ten thousand years from my veranda!'
moral: Chasing a mythical fruit of immortality leads you to eat rotten fruit from the ditch.

title: The Guru's Cold and the Chili Paste
summary: Guru Paramartha woke with a stiff neck and a slight cough.
full_text:
Guru Paramartha woke with a stiff neck and a slight cough.

Madayan, eager to demonstrate his medical knowledge, declared: 'A stiff neck is caused by trapped vata wind in the cervical vertebrae! To dissolve the wind, we must apply the Fiery Mustard-Chili Thermal Poultice!'

Madayan pounded ten fiery red chilies, two ounces of black mustard seeds, four cloves of garlic, and raw ginger into a thick, crimson, burning paste.

He smeared the burning paste thickly across Guru Paramartha's neck and shoulders, wrapping it tightly with a hot wool scarf.

Within sixty seconds, the fiery capsaicin penetrated the Guru's pores!

A sensation of scorching, blistering, unbearable fire erupted across the Guru's neck!

He shrieked, tearing at the scarf: 'AI-YO! REMOVE IT! I AM BURNING! SKIN ME ALIVE!'

Madayan held his hands: 'Endure, Master! The fire of disease is fighting the fire of medicine!'

The Guru broke free, dashed into the courtyard, and threw himself into the stone water trough, splashing cold water over his burning neck!

The paste washed off, leaving his neck bright crimson, blistered, and swollen!

The Guru sat in the trough, his teeth chattering from the cold water, his neck burning like fire, glaring at his disciples.

Madayan remarked with scholarly satisfaction: 'Notice, Master: you have completely forgotten your stiff neck! You are moving your head with remarkable agility in the water! The poultice has succeeded!'

The Guru splashed a bucket of water into Madayan's face, concluding his medical treatment for the day.
moral: Applying fiery paste to sensitive skin cures nothing and sets the patient ablaze.

title: The Astrologer's Lost Ring
summary: Another wandering fortune-teller arrived at the ashram, wearing rings on every finger, boasting that he could find hidden underground water, buried gold, and lost cattle through...
full_text:
Another wandering fortune-teller arrived at the ashram, wearing rings on every finger, boasting that he could find hidden underground water, buried gold, and lost cattle through divine divination.

While eating lunch on the veranda, the astrologer removed a heavy brass ring set with a red glass stone and placed it on the windowsill.

When lunch ended, the ring was gone.

The astrologer turned upon the disciples: 'One of you has stolen my magical gemstone ring! Confess, or I will curse your ashram with barrenness!'

The Guru was distressed: 'No disciple of mine is a thief! But you are a diviner of hidden treasures; use your astrological arts to locate your ring!'

The astrologer drew circles in the dirt with a stick, muttered charms, and pointed to Matti: 'The planets reveal that the ring is hidden inside this disciple's waistcloth!'

Matti was stripped and searched: no ring was found.

The astrologer pointed to Peedan: 'It is inside his sandals!'

The sandals were shaken: no ring was found.

The astrologer pointed to the ashram well: 'It has been thrown into the deep water!'

Matti was preparing to dive into the cold well with a rope, when the ashram cat jumped down from the windowsill. Beneath the cat's tail, wedged between two books on the shelf, the brass ring gleamed in the sunlight!

The cat had merely pushed it behind a manuscript while chasing a moth!

Guru Paramartha picked up the ring and handed it to the astrologer:

'Here is your ring, O seer of the cosmos! It was on the windowsill where you left it! If your stars could not distinguish between a cat's tail and my disciple's waistcloth, your divination is as hollow as an empty coconut!'

The embarrassed astrologer pocketed his ring and hurried away without his lunch.
moral: A charlatan who claims to see the stars cannot locate his own ring under his nose.

title: The Great Cow Race of Madurai
summary: During the annual cattle fair in Madurai, a race was announced with a grand prize of fifty silver rupees for the fastest domestic beast.
full_text:
During the annual cattle fair in Madurai, a race was announced with a grand prize of fifty silver rupees for the fastest domestic beast.

Guru Paramartha and his disciples entered their gentle white cow, Kamadhenu.

'Our cow,' declared the Guru, 'is nourished on sacred mantras! Her spiritual energy will outstrip the swiftest steeds!'

On the day of the race, thoroughbred horses, swift bullocks, and racing camels lined up at the starting rope.

In the middle of the line stood Kamadhenu, chewing her cud peacefully, with a garland of marigolds around her horns, while Matti sat upon her back holding a bamboo switch.

The starter beat the drum: BOOM! 'GO!'

The horses galloped like the wind; the racing bullocks thundered down the track, kicking up clouds of dust!

Kamadhenu did not gallop; she did not trot.

She took three slow, dignified strides forward, stopped in the middle of the track, lowered her head, and began peacefully grazing on a patch of lush green clover growing beside the fence!

Matti shouted: 'GALLOP, KAMADHENU! FOR THE HONOR OF PHILOSOPHY, RUN!'

He tapped her with the switch.

The cow swished her tail, blinked her gentle brown eyes, and continued chewing her clover with rhythmic contentment.

The crowd in the grandstand roared with laughter!

The horses crossed the finish line half a mile away, while Kamadhenu finished her patch of clover, lay down on the track, and fell asleep in the warm sun!

Matti walked back to the Guru: 'Master, she refused to run!'

Guru Paramartha smiled with sublime philosophical detachment: 'Kamadhenu demonstrated the supreme wisdom of Non-Attachment! While worldly horses exhausted their breath for fifty perishable silver coins, our cow chose peace, clover, and meditation! She is the true spiritual victor of the race!'

The disciples bowed in awe of their cow's enlightenment.
moral: Attempting to race a placid milk cow against horses earns only laughter from the stands.

title: The Stolen Ghee and the Ant Colony
summary: A bowl of fragrant, sweet ghee had been churned, and Guru Paramartha wished to protect it from stray mice.
full_text:
A bowl of fragrant, sweet ghee had been churned, and Guru Paramartha wished to protect it from stray mice.

Madayan devised an organic security system: 'Mice are terrified of stinging red ants! If we smear the outside of the bowl with honey, a protective guard of five hundred red ants will encircle the rim and bite any mouse that approaches!'

Matti smeared the outside of the bowl with honey and placed it near an anthill.

Within twenty minutes, five thousand red ants swarmed over the bowl.

They did not stay on the outside; they marched over the rim, plunged directly into the sweet, warm ghee, and formed a solid, dark, writhing layer of drowned ants upon the golden surface!

When the Guru came to eat his evening bread, the ghee was black with dead ants!

Matti reported proudly: 'Master, the defensive perimeter was established with complete success! Not a single mouse touched the bowl!'

The Guru looked at the bowl of black ants: 'Indeed, Matti; but how are we to eat the ghee?'

Madayan suggested: 'Filter the ghee through your teeth, Master! Teeth are the natural sieves of the body!'

The Guru dumped the bowl into the garden, fed the ants to the chickens, and dined on dry rice.
moral: Protecting your butter by inviting insects leaves you with butter full of ants.

title: The Temple Flagpole and the Tailor's Thread
summary: The village temple needed to hoist a fifty-foot cedar flagpole into its stone socket. The heavy hemp ropes had rotted, and the elders debated how to lift the timber.
full_text:
The village temple needed to hoist a fifty-foot cedar flagpole into its stone socket. The heavy hemp ropes had rotted, and the elders debated how to lift the timber.

Guru Paramartha offered the services of his disciples: 'A heavy rope is clumsy; modern engineering uses fine, multi-filament tensile cords!'

Madayan purchased fifty spools of thin cotton sewing thread from the village tailor. He twisted the threads together into a thin string: 'This composite cord possesses infinite tensile cohesion!'

They tied the thin cotton string around the fifty-foot cedar flagpole.

Matti, Peedan, Asadan, and Mudan gripped the string and heaved: 'ONE, TWO, THREE, PULL!'

The thin cotton thread snapped with a soft ping!

The four disciples tumbled backward into the temple ditch, landing in a pile of mud, while the heavy cedar flagpole rolled sideways, crushing the village council's wicker chairs!

The village headman shouted: 'Get out of here with your sewing thread, you fools!'

Guru Paramartha remarked with dignity: 'The thread was flawless, but the cedar was unspiritually heavy!'
moral: Hoisting a heavy timber with cotton thread snaps the cord and flattens the crew.

title: The Disciples Who Tried to Dry the Mud
summary: Following a heavy rain, the ashram courtyard was covered in deep, sticky red mud.
full_text:
Following a heavy rain, the ashram courtyard was covered in deep, sticky red mud.

Guru Paramartha wished to walk to the study hall, but refused to soil his sandals.

Madayan summoned the disciples: 'We must accelerate the evaporation of the moisture! Fetch five large palm-leaf hand fans!'

The five disciples knelt in the deep mud, fanning the wet earth with all their might: FLAP, FLAP, FLAP!

The vigorous fanning created violent gusts of air. The air did not dry the mud; instead, it picked up droplets of wet red slime and sprayed them across their faces, eyes, and white shawls!

Within ten minutes, all five disciples were coated in red mud like clay statues!

Guru Paramartha peered from the veranda: 'Is the earth dry, my children?'

Matti wiped mud from his nose: 'The earth remains moist, Master, but our faces have absorbed the mud completely!'

The Guru sighed, stepped onto wooden planks laid by the washerman, and walked across, leaving his fanners to wash in the pond.
moral: Fanning wet mud with palm leaves only spatters your own face with slime.

title: The Bell That Awoke the Village Tiger
summary: A rumor spread that a wild leopard had been seen in the forest outskirts.
full_text:
A rumor spread that a wild leopard had been seen in the forest outskirts.

Guru Paramartha instructed Peedan: 'Predators are terrified of sacred sounds! If you hear a rustle in the bushes tonight, beat the brass gong with all your might!'

At midnight, a stray goat rustled in the garden bushes.

Peedan seized the brass gong and an iron rod, beating it like thunder: CLANG! CLANG! CLANG!

The deafening noise awakened the entire village. It also awakened the local watchdogs, who began barking in chorus.

The real leopard, resting peacefully in the forest three miles away, was intrigued by the commotion. Attracted by the noise, the predator walked into the village to investigate!

Seeing the spotted beast stroll past the gate, Peedan dropped his gong, dove beneath his cot, and prayed: 'The gong was too melodious; it invited the guest instead of driving him away!'

The leopard caught a chicken from the coop and trotted back to the hills.

The Guru concluded: 'Next time, Peedan, we shall use silent meditation; it has fewer acoustic repercussions.'
moral: Ringing bells to frighten predators only summons them to the feast.

title: The Magic Coconut of Knowledge
summary: A wandering trickster sold Mudan a small, dried coconut for two silver coins, whispering: 'This is the Saraswati-Phala! Inscribe the alphabet upon the shell, grind it to powder,...
full_text:
A wandering trickster sold Mudan a small, dried coconut for two silver coins, whispering: 'This is the Saraswati-Phala! Inscribe the alphabet upon the shell, grind it to powder, and drink it with milk; all the wisdom of the Vedas will instantly enter your brain!'

Mudan bought the coconut, ground the rock-hard shell into coarse, jagged brown gravel, and stirred it into a glass of hot milk.

He swallowed the mixture in three gulps!

Within an hour, the sharp, jagged coconut shell fragments began tearing through his stomach and intestines!

Mudan rolled on the floor, groaning in agony: 'MY STOMACH! THE VEDAS ARE BATTERING MY RIBS!'

The village physician administered purgatives and herbal oils, saving the fool's life.

When Mudan recovered, the Guru questioned him: 'Mudan, did the sacred knowledge manifest in your understanding?'

Mudan groaned: 'Master, I learned only one great truth: coconut shells belong on trees, not in bellies!'

The Guru nodded: 'A profound realization; knowledge has indeed commenced.'
moral: Swallowing coconut shells will not plant wisdom in an empty head.

title: The Guru's Wooden Shoes and the Wet Mud
summary: Guru Paramartha had a pair of tall wooden padukas crafted, resting upon wooden pegs six inches high, designed to keep his feet above ordinary puddles.
full_text:
Guru Paramartha had a pair of tall wooden padukas crafted, resting upon wooden pegs six inches high, designed to keep his feet above ordinary puddles.

One rainy morning, he set out to inspect the vegetable garden, proudly walking upon his six-inch stilts.

He reached the garden. The soil was deep, clayey, sticky swamp mud.

The Guru took one stately step into the mud.

The thin wooden pegs sank straight down into the clay like nails driven into butter!

The Guru tried to lift his foot: the vacuum of the sticky mud held the wooden pegs fast! He pulled; his foot slipped out of the strap, and the Guru plunged knee-deep into the cold red mud!

There stood the venerable preceptor: one bare foot deep in the mire, the other perched upon a stilt, wobbling like a crane in a hurricane!

'MATTI! PEEDAN! EXTRACT ME!' roared the Guru.

Matti pulled the Guru's left arm; Peedan pulled his right. Under their combined heave, the Guru was pulled free, leaving both six-inch wooden shoes buried permanently beneath three feet of garden clay!

Carried to the veranda on his disciples' shoulders, the Guru proclaimed: 'The six-inch stilts were magnificent in theory; but the garden clay possessed an unauthorized depth!'
moral: Wearing tall wooden clogs into deep swamp mud turns the walker into a stationary statue.

title: The Feast of the Nine Bitter Gourds
summary: A visiting assembly of ten visiting scholars from Kanchipuram arrived at the ashram at noon.
full_text:
A visiting assembly of ten visiting scholars from Kanchipuram arrived at the ashram at noon.

Guru Paramartha wished to display supreme Ayurvedic hospitality.

Madayan suggested: 'Bitter gourd is the king of purifying vegetables! We shall prepare a nine-course banquet consisting entirely of bitter gourd: bitter gourd soup, fried bitter gourd, boiled bitter gourd with neem, bitter gourd chutney, and bitter gourd pudding!'

The feast was served on clean banana leaves.

The ten visiting scholars took their seats, smiled, and dipped their fingers into the first course: bitter gourd soup.

The overwhelming, eye-watering, throat-searing bitterness struck their palates!

One scholar gagged; another turned pale; a third spit his mouthful into his palm!

They tried the fried gourd: more bitterness! They tried the chutney: pure gall!

The chief visiting scholar rose from his mat, his face pale: 'Guru Paramartha! Did we come to a hermitage or a poison refinery? We asked for lunch, not a therapeutic execution!'

The ten scholars marched out of the ashram, leaving their half-eaten banana leaves behind.

Guru Paramartha sat down and tasted the soup: 'PHTHOO! Madayan, this is vile!'

Madayan sighed: 'Scholars of Kanchipuram lack spiritual endurance; let us give the soup to the village goats!'

Even the goats sniffed the bitter gourd and walked away in disgust.
moral: Serving pure bitterness under the guise of medicinal hospitality clears the room of guests.

title: The Stolen Cow and the Green Paint
summary: A rogue who had stolen a white cow from a neighboring village wished to hide her from the police. Knowing the reputation of Guru Paramartha's ashram for gullibility, the rogue b...
full_text:
A rogue who had stolen a white cow from a neighboring village wished to hide her from the police. Knowing the reputation of Guru Paramartha's ashram for gullibility, the rogue brought the cow to the gate, painted her completely green with dye, and told Matti: 'This is a rare Himalayan Emerald Cow! She yields green pistachio milk! I sell her for five rupees!'

Matti ran to the Guru, who purchased the green cow in delight.

They led the green cow to the shed.

Next morning, Matti took a brass bucket and milked the green beast.

The milk poured into the pail: white, pure, ordinary cow's milk!

Matti reported in bewilderment: 'Master! The cow is emerald green, but her milk is ordinary white!'

Madayan explained: 'The green pigment has not yet penetrated the mammary glands! We must feed her green parrot feathers and crushed grass for seven days!'

At that moment, the real owner arrived with the village police.

The police officer threw a bucket of warm water over the cow: the green dye washed off, revealing the stolen white cow!

The rogue was arrested, and the Guru lost his five rupees.

Guru Paramartha noted in his diary: 'Note: Green cows are susceptible to moisture; verify authenticity before milking.'
moral: Painting a stolen cow green does not change the flavor of her milk.

title: The Disciples Who Counted the Waves
summary: Visiting the seashore at Mahabalipuram, Guru Paramartha looked upon the rolling, foamy waves of the Bay of Bengal.
full_text:
Visiting the seashore at Mahabalipuram, Guru Paramartha looked upon the rolling, foamy waves of the Bay of Bengal.

The Guru mused: 'How many waves strike this shore between sunrise and sunset? If we calculate the waves, we can deduce the pulse of the cosmic ocean!'

Matti and Madayan volunteered to count the waves.

They stood at the water's edge, holding bamboo sticks, and began counting aloud as each wave broke upon the sand:

'One... two... three... forty-seven... eighty-eight...'

A large breaker surged forward, soaked their dhotis to the waist, and broke into three separate foaming surges!

Matti argued: 'Was that one large wave, or three small waves?'

Madayan declared: 'It was a composite triad wave! Count it as two and a half!'

Then an enormous roller crashed over their heads, knocking both disciples onto the sand, tumbling them into the foam, and washing away their measuring sticks!

Sputtering salt water, Matti climbed out: 'The ocean is cheating! It sent a rogue wave to wipe out our calculations!'

By sunset, they had arrived at forty thousand, two hundred, and six waves, with three lost in the foam.

The Guru accepted the report: 'A satisfactory census; the ocean may now retire for the night!'
moral: Counting the rolling waves of the ocean leaves you wet, weary, and none the wiser.

title: The Shadow of the Banyan Tree
summary: A cunning village merchant owned a small tea stall next to a magnificent, sprawling banyan tree that cast an enormous, cool shadow across the road.
full_text:
A cunning village merchant owned a small tea stall next to a magnificent, sprawling banyan tree that cast an enormous, cool shadow across the road.

The merchant told Guru Paramartha: 'Master, the land belongs to the village, but the shade of this banyan tree belongs to me! If you wish your disciples to rest in my shadow, you must pay me two silver rupees rent!'

The Guru paid the two silver rupees, and the disciples sat peacefully in the cool shade.

As the sun moved across the sky, the banyan shadow shifted toward the east, leaving the disciples sitting in the blazing, scorching sun!

Matti ran to the merchant: 'Merchant! We paid for the shade, but the shade has moved across the ditch into your tea garden!'

The merchant smiled: 'You purchased the shadow at ten o'clock, not the afternoon shadow! Pay two more rupees for the moving shade!'

The Guru was about to pay, when a passing lawyer intervened:

'If you own the shadow, merchant, then your shadow has trespassed onto the public highway and damaged the holy men's comfort! Pay them four rupees damages for trespassing shade!'

Terrified of a lawsuit, the merchant returned the Guru's two rupees and offered free tea.

The Guru praised the lawyer: 'Legal dialectic is almost as potent as Vedic philosophy!'
moral: Purchasing a moving shadow leaves you standing in the hot sun by afternoon.

title: The Thief Who Left His Turban
summary: A night burglar entered the ashram kitchen, stole two brass pots, but in his haste to squeeze through the window, his red cotton turban caught on an iron nail and remained hangi...
full_text:
A night burglar entered the ashram kitchen, stole two brass pots, but in his haste to squeeze through the window, his red cotton turban caught on an iron nail and remained hanging on the sill.

Next morning, Matti found the red turban: 'Master! The thief escaped, but his headpiece was captured!'

Guru Paramartha convened a court on the veranda.

The red turban was placed upon a wooden stool.

Madayan addressed the turban: 'Accused Turban! You were caught at the scene of the burglary! Where are the two stolen brass pots?'

The turban remained motionless.

'Contempt of court!' roared the Guru. 'Sentence the accused to twenty lashes of the cane!'

The disciples beat the red turban with bamboo switches until it was frayed to threads.

Then, Guru Paramartha sentenced the turban to imprisonment: 'Lock the turban in the iron trunk for seven years!'

They locked the battered turban in the chest, proud of their swift justice, while the real thief sold the two brass pots in the next village for four rupees.
moral: Arresting a turban for a burglary lets the thief walk away with the loot.

title: The River Ferry and the Missing Farthing
summary: Reaching a broad river during their travels, the ferryman demanded six copper coins to row the Guru and his five disciples across: one copper per head.
full_text:
Reaching a broad river during their travels, the ferryman demanded six copper coins to row the Guru and his five disciples across: one copper per head.

The Guru opened his purse: he possessed exactly five copper coins and one silver rupee.

The Guru refused to break the silver rupee: 'The fee is six coppers! We have five! Ferryman, row five of us across, and let Matti swim!'

Matti was terrified of water: 'Master! The river has crocodiles!'

Madayan negotiated: 'Ferryman! What is the theological value of one copper coin? It is a fleeting worldly illusion! Accept five coppers and ferry all six in honor of philosophy!'

The ferryman refused: 'No six coppers, no ferry!'

The disciples spent four hours on the bank debating the ethics of transportation. They missed their banquet, their robes were soaked in the rain, and night fell.

Finally, hungry, cold, and exhausted, the Guru broke his silver rupee, paid the six coppers, and gave the ferryman a tip of two more coppers!

Madayan observed: 'We preserved our philosophical integrity for four hours at a cost of only three coppers per hour!'
moral: Spending ten rupees on philosophical arguments to save one copper coin is expensive economy.

title: The Final Triumph of Guru Paramartha
summary: After decades of extraordinary philosophical misadventures, having crossed sleeping rivers on all fours, rescued the moon from the well, roasted in the steam blanket, and painte...
full_text:
After decades of extraordinary philosophical misadventures, having crossed sleeping rivers on all fours, rescued the moon from the well, roasted in the steam blanket, and painted elephants emerald green, Guru Paramartha celebrated his seventieth birthday in the ashram.

The village elders, the headman, the blacksmith, the barber, the tailor, and hundreds of peasants from twenty neighboring villages crowded into the courtyard, laden with gifts of flowers, fruits, and sweets.

The village headman presented the Guru with a magnificent, carved sandalwood staff, speaking with heartfelt warmth:

'Venerable Guru Paramartha! Your logic has often defied mathematics, your physics has astonished the blacksmiths, and your disciples have confounded the astrologers. Yet in all these years, your ashram has never harbored malice, greed, cruelty, or deceit. You have brought laughter, innocence, and wonder to our lives, reminding us that pompous arrogance is the true folly of the world, while a gentle, humble heart is the greatest wisdom.'

Guru Paramartha stroked his silver beard, his eyes shining with tears of genuine joy.

Turning to his five faithful disciples—Matti, Madayan, Peedan, Asadan, and Mudan—who stood proudly beside him, the Guru smiled with fatherly love:

'My faithful children! We have explored the cosmos, tested the laws of nature, and survived our own experiments! Let the world laugh at our philosophy; for he who can laugh at himself walks with the gods in eternal joy!'

The disciples cheered: 'HAIL GURU PARAMARTHA! OCEAN OF WISDOM AND FATHER OF JOY!'

And the entire village joined in a magnificent feast of sweet pongal and golden laddoos, celebrating the timeless, immortal laughter of Guru Paramartha and his five beloved disciples.
moral: Laughter and innocence outlive all pretentious pomp; true affection forgives a lifetime of folly.
